preamble: An Act to consolidate and amend the provisions relating to offences and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

glossary.short title: The informal, citable name of an Act — here 'the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023' — fixed by Section 1(1) regardless of the Act's formal number (45 of 2023).
glossary.staggered commencement: A drafting technique (Section 1(3)) where an Act does not come into force on the date the President assents to it, but on a later date the Central Government notifies in the Official Gazette — giving the executive time to prepare rules, infrastructure, and transition from the old law (here, the Indian Penal Code, 1860) before the new one binds anyone.
glossary.extraterritorial jurisdiction: The principle, carried from Section 1(4)-(5) of the BNS (mirroring the old IPC Sections 3-4), that Indian criminal law can reach acts committed outside India's territory if the offender is an Indian citizen, is on an Indian-registered ship or aircraft anywhere, or targets a computer resource located in India — so 'offence under this Sanhita' is not confined to acts physically committed within Indian soil.
glossary.offence targeting a computer resource: A new ground of jurisdiction under Section 1(5)(c) BNS (no IPC equivalent) — any person, of any nationality, anywhere in the world, who commits an offence under the Sanhita that targets a computer resource located in India can be tried as if the offence occurred within India. This was added to address cross-border cybercrime that the IPC's territorial scheme could not reach.
glossary.mutiny and desertion savings clause: Section 1(6), which expressly carves military offences of mutiny and desertion by members of the Army, Navy, or Air Force out of the BNS's reach where they are already governed by the Army Act, 1950, the Navy Act, 1957, or the Air Force Act, 1950 — preventing double jeopardy between the general criminal code and the special military codes.
glossary.dishonestly: Defined in Section 2(10) BNS: doing something with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another. It is the mental element that separates many property offences (like theft and cheating) from innocent dealings in property — the focus is on transferring entitlement wrongfully, not merely on dishonesty in a lay moral sense.
glossary.fraudulently: Defined in Section 2(12) BNS: a person is said to do a thing fraudulently if they do it with intent to defraud but not otherwise. Courts read this as requiring both deception and an intention to cause actual injury (to person, property, or rights) — deception alone, without that injurious intent, does not satisfy the definition.
glossary.document (BNS definition): Defined in Section 2(9) BNS to mean any matter expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures, or marks, or by more than one of those means, intended to be used or which may be used as evidence of that matter — deliberately medium-neutral so it covers paper writings, electronic records, photographs, and any other durable recording of information capable of evidentiary use.
glossary.public servant (BNS definition): Defined in Section 2(28) BNS through ten lettered sub-clauses (a) to (j) listing categories such as Armed Forces officers, judges, court officers, jurors/assessors, arbitrators, local-authority officers, government-remunerated officers, election officials, and any officer whose duty is to maintain public order or protect the public interest, or who holds office empowering them to exercise government-like functions. The definition is deliberately broad to capture any person performing a public function, regardless of exact appointment mode or pay source.
glossary.offence (BNS definition): Defined in Section 2(25) BNS: an act or omission made punishable by any law for the time being in force, and includes any act in respect of which a complaint may be made under Section 20 of the Cattle-trespass Act, 1871. This cross-referencing definition is what lets the BNS's General Part (definitions, exceptions, abetment, etc.) apply to offences created outside the Sanhita itself, in special and local laws, unless those laws say otherwise.
glossary.voluntarily: Defined in Section 2(38) BNS: a person is said to cause an effect 'voluntarily' when they cause it by means whereby they intended to cause it, or by means which, at the time of employing those means, they knew or had reason to believe to be likely to cause it. This definition anchors offences like voluntarily causing hurt — the actor need not have specifically intended the exact harm, only known it was a likely consequence of the means chosen.
glossary.wrongful gain and wrongful loss: Correlative terms in Section 2(39) BNS: 'wrongful gain' is gain of property by unlawful means to which the person gaining is not legally entitled; 'wrongful loss' is loss of property by unlawful means to which the person losing it is legally entitled. The clause also fixes the doctrinal point that a person can both wrongfully gain and wrongfully lose by keeping property as well as by acquiring it. These definitions anchor 'dishonestly' and the whole scheme of property offences.
glossary.good faith: Defined in Section 2(14) BNS: nothing is said to be done or believed in 'good faith' which is done or believed without due care and attention. This is a demanding, objective standard — mere honest belief is not enough; the person must have exercised the care and attention a reasonable person would, making 'good faith' a frequently litigated gateway to defences and exceptions throughout the Sanhita (e.g. the General Exceptions in Chapter III).
glossary.valuable security: Defined in Section 2(37) BNS: a document which is, or purports to be, a document whereby any legal right is created, extended, transferred, restricted, extinguished, or released, or whereby any person acknowledges that they lie under a legal liability or have not a certain legal right. Forgery, cheating, and extortion offences frequently turn on whether the instrument obtained or altered qualifies as a 'valuable security' in this technical sense.
glossary.child (BNS definition): Defined in Section 2(7) BNS to mean any person below the age of eighteen years — a single, Sanhita-wide definition that feeds into aggravating provisions throughout the Act (e.g. offences against children, kidnapping, trafficking) wherever the text uses the word 'child' rather than 'minor' or a specific numeric age threshold of its own.
glossary.General Exceptions overlay: The effect of Section 3(1) BNS, which provides that the General Exceptions contained in Chapter III (e.g. mistake of fact, accident, necessity, consent, private defence) apply to every provision of the Sanhita in the same manner as if each exception were repeated within the text of every defining section — so a defendant can always invoke Chapter III even though an individual offence-defining section never mentions it.
glossary.constructive possession: The concept, embedded in Section 3(5)-(6) BNS, that a person is deemed to be 'in possession' of movable property not only when they hold it directly but also when it is in the possession of another person who holds it subject to that person's control, or who holds it on that person's behalf — relevant to theft, criminal misappropriation, and similar property offences where physical custody and legal possession diverge.
glossary.acts extending to illegal omissions: A drafting rule in Section 3(2) BNS: wherever the Sanhita uses a word that denotes an act done, that word (unless a contrary intention appears) also covers an illegal omission to act — so offences framed in terms of 'doing' something can, in appropriate cases, be committed by unlawfully failing to act where there was a legal duty to act.
glossary.common intention: The principle under Section 3(8) BNS (the BNS's version of the former IPC Section 34) that when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention, each of them is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by them alone — a constructive-joint-liability doctrine requiring a shared pre-arranged plan or meeting of minds, illustrated in the Sanhita by the three-person beating example.
glossary.common criminal knowledge or intention: The principle under Section 3(9) BNS (the BNS's version of the former IPC Section 35): whenever an act is criminal only because of the criminal intention or knowledge of the person doing it, several persons who join in that act are liable only to the extent of their own individual criminal intention or knowledge — so joint participants can incur different degrees of liability for the same physical act, unlike the equal liability imposed under 'common intention.'
glossary.cooperation in several acts constituting: Section 3(7) BNS: when an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally cooperates in the commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, commits that offence — covering division-of-labour scenarios where no single participant performs every act that makes up the offence.
glossary.differential liability among co-particip: The outcome illustrated under Section 3(9) BNS: where criminal liability turns on each individual's own knowledge or intention rather than a shared common intention, co-participants in the same physical act can be convicted of offences of different gravity — e.g. one participant convicted of murder while another, lacking the requisite knowledge or intention, is convicted only of a lesser offence for the very same incident.
glossary.punishment ladder: The exhaustive list of six punishment types set out in Section 4 BNS — death, imprisonment for life, imprisonment (rigorous or simple), forfeiture of property, fine, and Community Service — from which every specific offence in the Sanhita must draw its prescribed sentence.
glossary.rigorous imprisonment: One of the two descriptions of imprisonment under Section 4(c)(1) BNS, meaning imprisonment with hard labour, as opposed to simple imprisonment.
glossary.simple imprisonment: One of the two descriptions of imprisonment under Section 4(c)(2) BNS, meaning imprisonment without the compulsory hard labour that rigorous imprisonment entails.
glossary.forfeiture of property: A punishment listed in Section 4(d) BNS under which the offender's property is confiscated by the State as part of the sentence, distinct from a fine (a monetary penalty) and from attachment or confiscation ordered under other special statutes.
glossary.community service (BNS punishment): A punishment newly introduced in Section 4(f) BNS — with no equivalent in the former IPC's Section 53 — under which an offender is required to perform unpaid work benefiting the community, reflecting a restorative-justice alternative to incarceration or fines for less grave offences.
glossary.commutation of sentence: The executive's power under Section 5 BNS to substitute a lighter form of punishment for the one a court has imposed (e.g. death to life imprisonment), exercised by the 'appropriate Government' without needing the offender's consent, following the procedure in BNSS Section 474.
glossary.appropriate Government: Defined in the Explanation to Section 5 BNS: the Central Government, where the sentence is death or concerns a Union-executive-power subject matter; or the State Government where the offender is sentenced, for sentences concerning a State-executive-power subject matter — the body authorised to commute a given sentence.
glossary.fractions of terms of punishment: A calculation concept governed by Section 6 BNS: whenever some other provision requires working out a fraction of a sentence and the base sentence is imprisonment for life, that life term is treated as equivalent to twenty years for the purpose of the calculation, unless otherwise provided.
glossary.life imprisonment as twenty years: The deeming equivalence fixed by Section 6 BNS for calculation purposes only — it does not mean a life sentence actually expires after twenty years in practice, but supplies the number to use whenever another provision needs a fraction of a life sentence computed (e.g. Section 8(3)'s one-fourth default-imprisonment cap).
glossary.discretion to mix rigorous and simple im: The power under Section 7 BNS allowing a sentencing court, where an offence's punishment may be of either description, to direct that the imprisonment be wholly rigorous, wholly simple, or partly rigorous and partly simple within a single sentence.
glossary.unlimited but not excessive fine: The default rule under Section 8(1) BNS: where an offence's punishment clause does not specify a maximum fine amount, the fine a court may impose is not capped by any fixed sum, but the amount imposed must still not be excessive.
glossary.default sentence for non-payment of fine: A term of imprisonment a court may direct under Section 8(2) BNS to be served if a fine it has imposed goes unpaid — always in addition to (not instead of) any other imprisonment already imposed or liable under a commutation of sentence.
glossary.one-fourth cap on default imprisonment: The ceiling fixed by Section 8(3) BNS on default imprisonment for non-payment of a fine: where the offence is punishable with both imprisonment and fine, the default term cannot exceed one-fourth of the maximum imprisonment fixed for that offence.
glossary.proportional discharge on part-payment: The rule under Section 8(6)(b) BNS that if part of a fine is paid or levied before the default imprisonment term expires, and that part is proportionate to the imprisonment already served, the offender is discharged early — illustrated in the Sanhita by the worked ₹1,000-fine/four-month example.
glossary.six-year levy period for unpaid fines: The limitation window fixed by Section 8(7) BNS: an unpaid fine (or any unpaid part of it) may be levied from the offender within six years of sentencing, or for longer if the custodial sentence itself exceeds six years — and this liability survives the offender's death, remaining recoverable from their estate.
glossary.offence made up of several offences: The situation addressed by Section 9(1) BNS, where a single offence is composed of smaller parts that are each individually also offences (e.g. a beating made up of many separate blows) — the offender is punished once for the composite offence, not separately for every component part, unless some law expressly provides for cumulative punishment.
glossary.overlapping definitions of offences: The situation addressed by Section 9(2) BNS, where the same act falls within two or more separate legal definitions of offences, or where several individually-punishable acts combine into a distinct composite offence — in either case the court is barred from awarding a punishment more severe than it could award for any single one of those offences.
glossary.double jeopardy within one transaction: The Sanhita-level protection worked by Section 9 BNS against punishing an offender more than once for what is really the same underlying act or transaction — distinguished, per the section's own illustrations, from genuinely separate acts (e.g. a blow struck at a different victim) occurring within the same episode, which remain separately punishable.
glossary.benefit of doubt as to which offence was: The sentencing safeguard in Section 10 BNS: where a court's judgment finds the accused guilty of one of several specified offences but is unable to determine which one specifically, the accused must be sentenced for whichever of those offences carries the lowest punishment, unless all carry the same punishment.
glossary.solitary confinement: A severe form of custodial isolation that a court may, under Section 11 BNS, order as part of a sentence of rigorous imprisonment, subject to an overall three-month ceiling that scales with the length of the sentence (one, two, or three months depending on whether the term is up to six months, between six months and a year, or over a year).
glossary.rigorous-imprisonment prerequisite for s: The precondition under Section 11 BNS that solitary confinement may only be ordered where rigorous imprisonment is itself an available punishment for the offence in question — it cannot be attached to a sentence of simple imprisonment alone.
glossary.fourteen-day execution cap: The rule under Section 12 BNS that, in actually carrying out a sentence of solitary confinement, no single continuous spell may exceed fourteen days, and each such spell must be followed by a rest interval of at least equal length.
glossary.mandatory rest intervals between solitar: The requirement in Section 12 BNS that periods of solitary confinement — whether under the fourteen-day-per-spell rule or the seven-day-per-month rule for terms exceeding three months — must each be separated by a rest interval at least as long as the preceding spell of confinement.
glossary.recidivist enhanced punishment: The elevated sentencing ceiling (life imprisonment, or imprisonment of either description up to ten years) imposed by Section 13 BNS on a person who, having already been convicted of a Chapter X or Chapter XVII offence carrying three years' imprisonment or more, commits a further offence under either chapter carrying the same three-year-plus threshold.
glossary.repeat-offender liability under Chapters: The specific scope restriction of Section 13 BNS's enhanced-punishment regime: both the prior conviction and the fresh offence must fall under Chapter X (Offences Against the Public Tranquillity) or Chapter XVII (Offences Against Property) and each must independently carry a three-year-or-more imprisonment threshold before the enhancement applies.
glossary.mistake of fact bound by law: The exception in Section 14 BNS: a person who is, or in good faith and due to a mistake of fact (never a mistake of law) believes himself to be, legally bound to do an act commits no offence by doing it — illustrated by a soldier obeying a lawful order, or a court officer arresting the wrong person after a genuine, careful enquiry.
glossary.ignorantia juris non excusat: The Latin maxim ('ignorance of the law excuses no one') underlying Sections 14 and 17 BNS — a mistaken belief about what the law requires or permits gives no defence; only a good-faith mistake about the underlying facts can.
glossary.judicial immunity: The protection under Section 15 BNS for a Judge acting judicially in the exercise of a power actually given, or in good faith believed to be given, to them by law — it covers only judicial acts, not a Judge's personal or administrative conduct.
glossary.acts warranted by court judgment or orde: The protection under Section 16 BNS for a person who acts in pursuance of, or as warranted by, a still-valid court judgment or order, even if the court lacked jurisdiction to pass it, provided the person in good faith believed the court had jurisdiction.
glossary.act justified by law or mistaken belief: The exception in Section 17 BNS, the permissive counterpart to Section 14's mandatory one: a person actually justified by law, or who in good faith mistakenly believes (due to a mistake of fact) that they are justified, commits no offence — illustrated by a citizen's lawful power to apprehend an apparent offender.
glossary.pure accident defence: The exception in Section 18 BNS for harm that results purely by accident or misfortune, without criminal intention or knowledge, while doing a lawful act, lawfully, with proper care and caution — illustrated by a hatchet-head accidentally flying off during lawful work.
glossary.necessity defence: The exception in Section 19 BNS (also called the choice-of-evils defence): an act known to be likely to cause harm is not an offence if done without criminal intent and in good faith to prevent or avoid a different, greater harm to person or property, with the proportionality of the risk taken assessed objectively as a question of fact.
glossary.choice-of-evils harm prevention: Another name for the necessity defence under Section 19 BNS, capturing its core logic: knowingly risking a lesser harm is excused when done in good faith to avoid a more serious and imminent harm, illustrated by the ship-captain and fire-fighting scenarios in the section's own illustrations.
glossary.doli incapax under seven: The absolute, age-based bar in Section 20 BNS: a child under seven years of age is conclusively incapable of committing any offence under the Sanhita, with no inquiry into the child's actual understanding.
glossary.doli incapax seven to twelve: The case-specific defence in Section 21 BNS for a child between seven and twelve years of age, available only where it is proved the child had not, on the specific occasion, attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of their conduct.
glossary.unsoundness of mind defence: The insanity defence under Section 22 BNS: a person who, due to unsoundness of mind at the time of the act, was incapable of knowing either the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law, commits no offence — India's long-standing M'Naghten-derived cognitive-incapacity test.
glossary.M'Naghten-style insanity test: The historical label for the cognitive-incapacity standard codified in Section 22 BNS (carried over from the former IPC), which asks whether unsoundness of mind left the accused incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that it was wrong or illegal — not whether the accused has a diagnosed mental illness as such.
glossary.involuntary intoxication defence: The defence under Section 23 BNS, paralleling the insanity test, available only where the intoxicating substance was administered without the person's knowledge or against their will and rendered them incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or illegal.
glossary.imputed sobriety for voluntary intoxicat: The rule under Section 24 BNS that, for offences requiring a particular knowledge or intent, a voluntarily intoxicated person is treated as if they had the knowledge they would have had while sober — voluntary intoxication cannot be used to deny the required mental element, unless the intoxication was itself involuntary.
glossary.consent defence for non-fatal non-grievo: The baseline consent exception under Section 25 BNS: an act neither intended nor known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt is not an offence against an adult (above eighteen) who consented to suffer the harm or take the risk of it, illustrated by consensual fencing for sport.
glossary.consensual medical treatment defence: The exception under Section 26 BNS protecting good-faith medical and surgical treatment: an act not intended to cause death is not an offence, even if known likely to cause death, when done in good faith for the benefit of a person who consented, illustrated by a surgeon performing a risky but beneficial operation with the patient's consent.
glossary.guardian-consented treatment of minors a: The exception under Section 27 BNS extending consent-based protection to children under twelve and persons of unsound mind via their guardian's or lawful custodian's consent, subject to four provisos barring intentional killing, unjustified death-likely acts, unjustified voluntary grievous hurt, and unprotected abetment.
glossary.vitiated consent: The definitional bar in Section 28 BNS specifying when a purported 'consent' does not count as valid consent anywhere in the Sanhita: consent obtained under fear of injury or a known factual misconception, consent from someone incapable of understanding it due to unsoundness of mind or intoxication, and (absent contrary context) consent from a child under twelve.
glossary.offences independent of consent-related: The limitation in Section 29 BNS confirming that consent-based exceptions (Sections 25-27) excuse only the harm caused to the consenting person, not an act that is independently defined as an offence regardless of that harm — illustrated by causing miscarriage, which remains an offence despite the woman's consent, except where done in good faith to save her life.
glossary.emergency-necessity defence without cons: The exception under Section 30 BNS covering true emergencies: a good-faith act for a person's benefit is not an offence by reason of harm caused, where it was genuinely impossible to obtain consent in time (the person being unconscious or incapable with no guardian reachable), subject to the same four provisos as Section 27.
glossary.mere pecuniary benefit exclusion: The Explanation attached to Section 30 BNS (and cross-applied to Sections 26 and 27) clarifying that purely financial advantage does not count as 'benefit' for the purposes of the good-faith consent and necessity exceptions.
glossary.good-faith communication defence: The exception under Section 31 BNS protecting a communication made in good faith for the recipient's benefit from being treated as an offence merely because it causes harm — illustrated by a surgeon's honest, fatal-shock-inducing disclosure of a grim prognosis.
glossary.duress by threat of instant death: The compulsion/duress defence under Section 32 BNS: an act compelled by threats reasonably causing apprehension of instant death is not an offence — except murder and death-punishable offences against the State, which can never be excused this way — provided the actor did not voluntarily place themselves in that dangerous situation.
glossary.de minimis harm defence: The 'law does not concern itself with trifles' exception under Section 33 BNS: an act causing, intending, or known likely to cause harm so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain of it is not an offence, judged by an objective reasonable-person standard.
glossary.right of private defence (general bar): The opening, umbrella rule of Section 34 BNS: any act genuinely done in the exercise of the right of private defence is not an offence, with the actual scope and limits of that right worked out across the subsequent Sections 35-44.
glossary.private defence of body: The branch of the private-defence right under Section 35(a) BNS permitting every person to defend their own body or any other person's body against any offence affecting the human body, subject to Section 37's restrictions.
glossary.private defence of property: The branch of the private-defence right under Section 35(b) BNS permitting every person to defend their own or any other person's movable or immovable property against theft, robbery, mischief, criminal trespass, or attempts at these, subject to Section 37's restrictions.
glossary.private defence against a non-culpable a: The rule under Section 36 BNS that private defence remains available against an attacker who is personally non-culpable due to youth, immaturity, unsoundness of mind, intoxication, or honest misconception — the defender has exactly the same right as if the attacker's act had been a full offence.
glossary.no private defence against good-faith pu: The restriction in Section 37(1)(a)-(b) BNS barring private defence against a good-faith, colour-of-office act (or directed act) of a public servant that does not reasonably threaten death or grievous hurt, even if not strictly lawful — subject to the defender's knowledge of the actor's public-servant status (Explanations 1-2).
glossary.time-to-seek-public-authorities bar: The restriction in Section 37(1)(c) BNS denying the right of private defence wherever there was time to seek the protection of public authorities instead of acting unilaterally.
glossary.necessity limit on private defence: The proportionality cap in Section 37(2) BNS: the right of private defence never extends to inflicting more harm than is genuinely necessary for the purpose of defence.
glossary.private defence extending to death — bod: The expanded right under Section 38 BNS permitting voluntary causing of death in defence of the body, but only against seven enumerated grave categories of assault — reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, rape, unnatural-lust gratification, kidnapping/abduction, wrongful confinement without recourse to authorities, and acid-throwing or attempted acid-throwing.
glossary.acid-attack ground for lethal private de: The seventh category added in Section 38(g) BNS — throwing or administering acid, or attempting to do so, in circumstances reasonably causing apprehension of grievous hurt — as a ground on which lethal private defence of the body is permitted, reflecting the specific gravity the BNS attaches to acid attacks.
glossary.private defence capped below death: The default rule under Section 39 BNS: for any assault not matching Section 38's seven grave categories, the right of private defence of the body never extends to causing death, only to causing harm short of death, subject to Section 37's restrictions.
glossary.temporal window of private defence of bo: The commencement-and-continuance rule under Section 40 BNS: the right of private defence of the body begins as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger arises from an attempt or threat, even before any offence is committed, and lasts only as long as that reasonable apprehension continues.
glossary.private defence extending to death — pro: The expanded right under Section 41 BNS permitting voluntary causing of death in defence of property, but only against four enumerated grave categories: robbery, night house-breaking (sunset-to-sunrise), arson or explosive mischief against a dwelling or property-custody structure, and theft/mischief/house-trespass under circumstances reasonably raising apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
glossary.private defence of property capped below: The default rule under Section 42 BNS: for theft, mischief, or criminal trespass not matching Section 41's four grave categories, the right of private defence of property never extends to causing death, only to causing harm short of death, subject to Section 37's restrictions.
glossary.temporal window of private defence of pr: The set of commencement-and-continuance rules under Section 43 BNS: the right of private defence of property always begins once a reasonable apprehension of danger to the property arises, but its end point differs by offence — tied to the thief's retreat/recovery/authority-assistance for theft, continuing danger/fear for robbery, continuation of the trespass/mischief itself, or continuation of the house-trespass begun by night house-breaking.
glossary.private defence with incidental risk to: The closing safety-valve of the private-defence scheme under Section 44 BNS: where a defender facing an assault reasonably threatening death cannot effectively exercise private defence without risking incidental harm to an innocent bystander, the right extends to running that risk — illustrated by firing into a threatening mob that includes children.
glossary.abetment: The umbrella concept defined in Section 45 BNS for three distinct ways a person can be complicit in another's wrongdoing: instigating it, engaging in a conspiracy towards it with an act or illegal omission in pursuance of that conspiracy, or intentionally aiding its doing by act or illegal omission — the foundation of Chapter IV's entire liability scheme.
glossary.instigation: One of the three modes of abetment under Section 45(a) BNS, widened by Explanation 1 to cover not just direct urging but also wilful misrepresentation or wilful concealment of a fact one is bound to disclose, where that conduct voluntarily causes or procures (or attempts to cause or procure) a thing to be done.
glossary.intentional aiding: One of the three modes of abetment under Section 45(c) BNS: facilitating, by any act or illegal omission, before or during the commission of the principal act, the actual commission of that act — Explanation 2 confirms the facilitation can occur at any time up to and including the moment of commission.
glossary.engaging in a conspiracy: The second mode of abetment under Section 45(b) BNS: joining with one or more others in a conspiracy for the doing of a thing, which amounts to abetment only once an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy and in order to the doing of that thing.
glossary.abettor: Defined in Section 46 BNS as a person who abets either the commission of an offence, or the commission of an act that would be an offence if done by someone legally capable of committing an offence with the same intention or knowledge as the abettor — a definition deliberately written to survive the principal's incapacity or differing mental state.
glossary.incapacity of the person abetted: The scenario addressed by Section 46 BNS's Explanation 3 and illustrations: an abettor remains fully liable even where the person actually abetted — e.g. a child under seven, or a person of unsound mind — is legally incapable of committing the offence themselves, with the abettor punished as though that person had been capable and had committed it.
glossary.abetment of an abetment: The chained-liability principle in Section 46 BNS's Explanation 4: since the abetment of an offence is itself an offence, abetting that abetment (e.g. A instigates B to instigate C to murder Z) is also independently punishable, with liability running up the chain to each instigator.
glossary.engaging in a conspiracy without concert: The principle in Section 46 BNS's Explanation 5: to be liable as an abettor by conspiracy, a person need not have directly concerted the offence with the person who ultimately commits it — it is enough that they engaged in the same conspiracy in pursuance of which the offence was committed, even via intermediaries who never named them.
glossary.abetment in India of offences outside In: The extraterritorial abetment rule in Section 47 BNS: a person who, while in India, abets the commission of an act outside India is guilty of abetment under the Sanhita if that act would have been an offence had it been committed in India — regardless of the nationality of the person who actually commits it abroad.
glossary.abetment outside India for offence in In: The mirror-image extraterritorial rule in Section 48 BNS: a person who, while outside India, abets the commission of an act within India is guilty of abetment under the Sanhita, so long as that act constitutes an offence if committed in India — closing the jurisdictional gap left open by Section 47 for abetment flowing the opposite direction.
glossary.punishment of abetment where offence is: The default rule in Section 49 BNS: where an abetted offence is actually committed in consequence of the instigation, conspiracy, or aid that constituted the abetment, and no other Sanhita provision specially fixes a punishment for that abetment, the abettor is liable to exactly the same punishment as for the completed offence itself.
glossary.abetment with differing intention betwee: The rule in Section 50 BNS fixing the abettor's punishment by reference to the abettor's own intention or knowledge, not the executor's — where the person abetted acts with a different intention or knowledge than the abettor had, the abettor is punished as if the offence corresponding to the abettor's own state of mind had actually occurred.
glossary.probable-consequence liability for a dif: The extended-liability rule in Section 51 BNS: where a different act is done instead of (or in addition to) the one actually abetted, the abettor remains liable for that different act to the same extent as if directly abetted, provided it was a probable consequence of the abetment and was done under the instigation's influence, aid, or in pursuance of the conspiracy — illustrated by the mistaken-target poisoning (within scope) versus opportunistic theft during an abetted arson (a distinct, unconnected act, outside scope).
glossary.cumulative punishment for act abetted an: The rule in Section 52 BNS that where the different act made punishable under Section 51 is committed in addition to (not instead of) the act actually abetted, and the two constitute distinct offences, the abettor — like the principal — is liable to separate punishment for each offence, not merely one combined sentence.
glossary.liability for an unintended effect known: The rule in Section 53 BNS covering cases where the act abetted is carried out as intended but produces a different (typically graver) effect than the abettor meant — the abettor is liable for the actual effect caused, as if it had been intended, provided the abettor knew that effect was a likely consequence of the act abetted (e.g. instigated grievous hurt escalating to death, attracting a murder-level punishment).
glossary.presence at the scene deeming abettor a: The deeming rule of Section 54 BNS: a person who would otherwise be liable only as an absent abettor is, if actually present when the abetted act or offence is committed, deemed to have committed that act or offence themselves — collapsing the abettor/principal distinction purely on the fact of presence.
glossary.abetment of an offence punishable with d: The specific punishment scheme in Section 55 BNS for abetting an offence that itself carries death or imprisonment for life, where the offence is not actually committed in consequence of the abetment: up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine as the base, rising to up to fourteen years plus fine if the abetted act nonetheless causes hurt to any person.
glossary.abetment of an imprisonment-only offence: The parallel punishment scheme in Section 56 BNS to Section 55, but for offences punishable only with imprisonment (not death or life imprisonment): up to one-fourth of the offence's longest imprisonment term (or fine, or both) as the base, doubled to up to one-half where the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant whose duty was to prevent that very offence.
glossary.public-servant enhancement for duty-boun: The aggravating factor in Section 56 BNS that doubles the abettor's maximum exposure (from one-fourth to one-half of the offence's longest imprisonment term) where either the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant whose official duty was to prevent the very offence that was abetted.
glossary.abetment directed at the public or a cla: The specialised offence in Section 57 BNS punishing abetment not aimed at a single identifiable person but at the public generally or any number or class exceeding ten persons, with a flat punishment of up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, irrespective of whether the mass-abetted offence is actually committed.
glossary.concealment of design to commit a death/: The offence in Section 58 BNS of voluntarily concealing, by act, omission, encryption, or other information-hiding tool, or by knowingly false representation, a known design to commit an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment, where the concealment is intended or known likely to facilitate that offence — punished up to seven years if the offence is committed, up to three years if not, plus fine.
glossary.public servant's heightened duty to disc: The aggravated concealment offence in Section 59 BNS, applicable only to a public servant who conceals a design to commit an offence that it was specifically that public servant's official duty to prevent — graded more severely than the general Section 58 offence, up to one-half of the offence's longest term, or a flat ten years where the concealed offence itself carries death or life imprisonment.
glossary.concealment of design to commit an impri: The residual, least severe tier of the concealment-of-design scheme under Section 60 BNS, covering designs to commit offences punishable only with imprisonment: up to one-fourth of the longest imprisonment term if the offence is committed, and only up to one-eighth if it is not.
glossary.encryption or information-hiding tool: A phrase appearing in Sections 58 and 59 BNS extending the concept of 'concealment' of a known criminal design to cover digital concealment methods — encryption or any other information-hiding tool — a deliberate modernisation with no direct textual equivalent in the former IPC's corresponding Sections 118-119.
glossary.criminal conspiracy: Defined in Section 61(1) BNS as an agreement between two or more persons with the common object to do, or cause to be done, an illegal act, or a legal act by illegal means — a distinct substantive offence under the Sanhita (not merely one mode of abetment under Section 45(b)), subject to the proviso's overt-act requirement for agreements not themselves aimed at committing an offence.
glossary.agreement as the gist of conspiracy: The core principle of Section 61(1) BNS's proviso: where the conspirators' agreement is itself to commit an offence, the bare agreement is enough to constitute criminal conspiracy — no further overt act is required, unlike other agreements within the definition.
glossary.overt-act requirement for non-offence ag: The proviso to Section 61(1) BNS: for any agreement within the definition of criminal conspiracy other than an agreement to commit an offence, some act besides the bare agreement must be done by one or more parties in pursuance of it before the agreement amounts to a criminal conspiracy.
glossary.attempt to commit an offence: The residual offence defined in Section 62 BNS: attempting to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment for life or any other imprisonment, doing some act towards its commission, where no other Sanhita provision specially punishes that attempt — drawing up to one-half of the maximum punishment for the completed offence.
glossary.act towards the commission of the offenc: The threshold requirement of Section 62 BNS distinguishing a punishable attempt from mere preparation: the accused must have actually done some act directed towards carrying out the offence, not merely planned or prepared for it.
glossary.impossible attempt: The principle illustrated in Section 62 BNS by the empty-box and empty-pocket examples: an attempt remains punishable even where it was factually impossible to succeed (e.g. there were no jewels in the box, nothing in the pocket) — liability turns on the act done towards commission, not on the possibility of actually completing the offence.
glossary.rape (BNS definition): Defined in Section 63 BNS through four acts, (a)-(d) — penetration, insertion, manipulation, or application of mouth — committed in any of seven circumstances (i)-(vii) covering absence of consent, consent vitiated by fear, fraud, or impersonation, incapacity to consent, and intercourse with a girl under eighteen — subject to Exceptions 1-2 for medical procedures and the marital exception.
glossary.absence of consent: The first and central circumstance under Section 63(i) BNS that converts the specified sexual acts into rape: the act is done against the woman's will or without her consent, consent being Explanation 2's unequivocal voluntary agreement communicated by words, gestures, or other verbal/non-verbal communication — mere non-resistance or silence does not by itself amount to consent.
glossary.consent obtained by fear: One of the consent-vitiating circumstances under Section 63(ii) BNS: consent obtained by putting the woman or any person she is interested in, in fear of death or hurt is treated in law as no consent at all, so intercourse procured that way is rape.
glossary.consent obtained by impersonation of hus: The circumstance under Section 63(iii) BNS where a woman consents believing the man to be the husband she is lawfully married to, when in fact he is not — the consent is legally vitiated by the impersonation and the act is rape.
glossary.inability to communicate consent: The circumstance under Section 63(v) BNS covering a woman who, at the time of the act, is unable to communicate consent by reason of unsoundness of mind, intoxication, or any other cause — intercourse with such a woman is rape regardless of apparent acquiescence, since she is legally incapable of giving consent.
glossary.statutory rape (under eighteen): The circumstance under Section 63(vii) BNS (read with Explanation 1) that intercourse with a woman under eighteen years of age is rape with or without her consent — consent is legally irrelevant below that age, reinforced by Section 65's heightened punishment tiers for victims under sixteen and under twelve.
glossary.marital exception to rape: Exception 2 to Section 63 BNS, carving sexual intercourse or acts by a man with his own wife, provided the wife is not under eighteen, out of the definition of rape — a controversial carry-over from the former IPC's Exception 2 to Section 375 that leaves marital rape of an adult wife outside the Sanhita's rape provision (subject to the separate, lesser offence in Section 67 for intercourse during judicial separation).
glossary.aggravated rape by persons in custodial: The thirteen-category list under Section 64(2)(a)-(m) BNS of offenders — police officers, public servants, armed forces personnel, jail/remand-home/hospital staff, persons in a position of trust or authority, and others — whose rape of a woman within or by abuse of that very position attracts a markedly higher punishment band than the base offence under Section 64(1).
glossary.rape of a minor under sixteen: The first aggravated-victim tier under Section 65(1) BNS, prescribing a minimum punishment of twenty years' rigorous imprisonment (extendable to life, meaning imprisonment for the remainder of natural life) plus fine for rape of a woman under sixteen years of age — markedly more severe than the base Section 64 punishment.
glossary.rape of a minor under twelve: The most severe victim-age tier under Section 65(2) BNS: rape of a girl under twelve years carries a minimum of twenty years' rigorous imprisonment extendable to life imprisonment for the remainder of natural life, or death — the only BNS rape provision that opens the door to capital punishment.
glossary.capital punishment for rape of a child u: The death-penalty option created by Section 65(2) BNS for rape of a girl under twelve years of age — one of the few capital offences in the Sanhita, reflecting the legislature's escalated response to child sexual assault introduced originally by the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2018 and carried into the BNS.
glossary.death resulting from rape: The aggravated offence in Section 66 BNS where an act of rape (under Sections 63-65, 70, or 71) causes the victim's death or leaves her in a persistent vegetative state — punished with a minimum of twenty years' rigorous imprisonment extendable to life imprisonment for the remainder of natural life, or death.
glossary.persistent vegetative state of victim: A specifically named aggravating outcome in Section 66 BNS, placed on equal statutory footing with causing the victim's death — if the act of rape results in the victim being reduced to a persistent vegetative state, the same elevated punishment band (minimum twenty years to life, or death) applies as for causing death.
glossary.non-consensual intercourse during marita: The distinct, lesser offence created by Section 67 BNS for a man having sexual intercourse with his own wife, who is living separately under a decree of separation or otherwise, without her consent — punished with two to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, bridging the gap left by the marital exception to rape for separated (but not divorced) couples.
glossary.inducement by criminal intimidation or a: The operative mechanism of the Section 68 BNS offence (sexual intercourse by a person in authority): a person in a position of authority or fiduciary relationship — a public servant, superintendent of a custodial institution, or manager/staff of a hospital — who abuses that position or fiduciary relationship to induce or seduce a woman in their custody/charge/presence into sexual intercourse not otherwise amounting to rape, is separately punishable.
glossary.false promise to marry: One of the two deceitful-means grounds in Section 69 BNS for sexual intercourse obtained by making a promise to marry without any intention of fulfilling it — punishable with up to ten years' rigorous imprisonment plus fine, provided the Explanation's definition of 'deceitful means' (including false promise of employment/promotion or marriage after suppressing identity) is satisfied.
glossary.sexual intercourse by deceitful means: The Section 69 BNS offence of having sexual intercourse with a woman by deceitful means — defined in the Explanation to include a false promise to marry made without intention of fulfilling it, a false promise of employment or promotion, or inducement after suppressing one's identity to marry — where the act does not amount to rape under Section 63.
glossary.gang rape: The constructive-liability offence in Section 70(1) BNS: where a woman is raped by one or more persons constituting a group, or acting in furtherance of a common intention, each such person is deemed to have committed rape and is punishable with rigorous imprisonment of not less than twenty years, extendable to life, plus fine payable to the victim — liability attaches to every member of the group regardless of which individual physically committed the act.
glossary.constructive liability for group offence: The doctrinal principle underlying Section 70 BNS's gang-rape provision: when multiple persons act as a group or in furtherance of a common intention to commit rape, the law deems every participant to have committed the complete offence themselves, sidestepping the need to prove which individual performed the specific penetrative act.
glossary.victim-payable fine: A recurring sentencing feature across the Section 64-71 BNS rape provisions: the fine imposed on conviction must be just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses and rehabilitation of the victim, and is paid directly to the victim — a restorative, victim-centred departure from fines simply paid to the State treasury.
glossary.repeat sexual-offence conviction: The enhanced-punishment regime in Section 71 BNS for a person previously convicted of an offence under Section 64, 65, 66, or 70 BNS who is subsequently convicted of any of those same offences again — punishable with imprisonment for life (meaning for the remainder of natural life) or death, reflecting zero tolerance for repeat sexual offenders.
glossary.disclosure of victim identity: The offence in Section 72(1) BNS of printing or publishing the name, or any matter that may make known the identity, of a woman against whom certain sexual offences are alleged or found to have been committed — punishable with up to two years' imprisonment plus fine, aimed at protecting survivors from social stigma and secondary victimisation.
glossary.exceptions to identity-disclosure bar: The three carve-outs in the proviso to Section 72(1)/(2) BNS permitting disclosure of a sexual-offence victim's identity: by or with the authorisation in writing of the victim; by the next of kin where the victim is dead, a minor, of unsound mind, or (with the authority's written authorisation) incapacitated; or where the disclosure is made by/under the order of the court concerned.
glossary.unauthorised publication of court procee: The offence in Section 73 BNS of printing or publishing any matter in relation to proceedings before a court in respect of specified sexual offences without the court's prior permission — punishable with up to two years' imprisonment plus fine, subject to the exception permitting publication of the judgment of a High Court or the Supreme Court.
glossary.outraging the modesty of a woman: The core phrase defining the offence in Section 74 BNS: assault or use of criminal force on a woman intending to outrage her modesty, or with knowledge that the act is likely to outrage it — punishable with one to five years' imprisonment plus fine, one of the Sanhita's most frequently invoked modesty-protection provisions.
glossary.sexual harassment (BNS definition): Defined in Section 75(1) BNS through four clauses (i)-(iv): physical contact and advances involving unwelcome and explicit sexual overtures; a demand or request for sexual favours; showing pornography against a woman's will; or making sexually coloured remarks — each separately constituting the offence of sexual harassment under Section 75(2)/(3).
glossary.sexually coloured remarks: One of the four limbs of sexual harassment under Section 75(1)(iv) BNS — making sexually coloured remarks — the least physically intrusive of the four clauses, drawing the lower punishment band of up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both, under Section 75(3), compared to the up-to-three-year band for the other three clauses.
glossary.intent to disrobe or compel nakedness: The aggravating mental element defining the Section 76 BNS offence (distinct from the general Section 74 modesty offence): assault or use of criminal force with the intention of disrobing a woman or compelling her to be naked, or with knowledge that such disrobing/nakedness is a likely consequence — punished more severely, with a minimum of three years' imprisonment extendable to seven, plus fine.
glossary.voyeurism: The offence in Section 77 BNS of watching or capturing the image of a woman engaging in a private act in circumstances where she would usually expect not to be observed, or disseminating such an image — a technology-conscious offence covering both the act of surveillance and the later sharing of images captured even with consent, once dissemination exceeds that consent.
glossary.private act (BNS definition): Defined in the Explanation to Section 77 BNS to include an act carried out in a place which, in the circumstances, would reasonably be expected to provide privacy, and where the victim's genitals, posterior, or breasts are exposed/covered only in underwear, or the victim is using a lavatory, or doing a sexual act not ordinarily done in public — the threshold concept for the voyeurism offence.
glossary.dissemination exceeding consent: The second limb of the voyeurism offence under Section 77 BNS's Explanation: even where a woman consented to the capture of an image of a private act, if that image is further disseminated beyond what she consented to (e.g. shared with others or made public), the disseminator is deemed to have committed voyeurism.
glossary.stalking: The offence in Section 78(1) BNS, with two limbs — physically following, contacting, or attempting to contact a woman despite her clear disinterest, and monitoring her use of the internet, email, or any other form of electronic communication — punishable with up to three years (first conviction) or up to five years (repeat conviction), plus fine.
glossary.electronic monitoring as stalking: The second, technology-specific limb of the stalking offence under Section 78(1)(ii) BNS: monitoring a woman's use of the internet, email, or any other form of electronic communication amounts to stalking on the same footing as physically following or contacting her, extending the offence into digital surveillance.
glossary.statutory defences to stalking: The three-ground proviso to Section 78(1) BNS exempting conduct from the stalking offence: where it is proved that the pursuit was for the purpose of preventing or detecting crime and the accused was entrusted with that responsibility by the State; was pursued under a specific law or to comply with a condition/requirement imposed by any person under a legal enactment; or was reasonable and justified in the particular circumstances.
glossary.insult to the modesty of a woman by word: The residual catch-all offence in Section 79 BNS: uttering any word, making any sound or gesture, or exhibiting any object, intending that word/sound/gesture/object be seen or heard by a woman and thereby intruding upon her privacy, or intending to insult her modesty — punishable with up to three years' imprisonment plus fine, covering conduct too minor or indirect to fit Sections 74-78.
glossary.intrusion upon privacy: One of the two alternative mental elements of the Section 79 BNS residual modesty offence (the other being intent to insult modesty) — exhibiting an object or making a sound/gesture intending to intrude upon a woman's privacy satisfies the offence even absent a specific intent to insult her modesty.
glossary.dowry death: Defined in Section 80(1) BNS: where a woman's death is caused by burns, bodily injury, or otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of marriage, and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relatives in connection with a dowry demand, the husband/relative is deemed to have caused her death and is liable for 'dowry death' — punishable with a minimum of seven years' imprisonment extendable to life.
glossary.seven-year marriage window: The temporal precondition in Section 80(1) BNS limiting the dowry-death presumption to deaths occurring within seven years of the woman's marriage — a death occurring after that window falls outside this specific deeming provision, though other offences (e.g. murder, cruelty) may still apply.
glossary.soon before death cruelty or harassment: The causal-proximity requirement in Section 80(1) BNS: the dowry-related cruelty or harassment must have occurred 'soon before' the woman's death for the Section 80 presumption of dowry death to arise — courts treat this as a flexible, proximate-in-time test rather than a fixed number of days, requiring a live link between the harassment and the death.
glossary.cruelty (BNS definition): Defined in Section 86 BNS (via the Explanation incorporated by reference into Section 85) through two clauses: (a) wilful conduct likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or cause grave injury/danger to life, limb, or health; or (b) harassment with a view to coercing her or her relatives to meet an unlawful property demand, or on account of failure to meet such a demand.
glossary.cruelty by husband or his relative: The offence in Section 85 BNS of a husband or his relative subjecting a woman to cruelty (as defined in Section 86), punishable with up to three years' imprisonment plus fine — the Sanhita's direct successor to the former IPC's Section 498A, a frequently invoked matrimonial-cruelty provision.
glossary.unlawful property demand harassment: The second limb of 'cruelty' under Section 86(b) BNS: harassment of a woman with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet an unlawful demand for property or valuable security, or harassment arising from failure to meet such a demand — the dowry-harassment pattern most frequently pleaded alongside Section 80's dowry-death provision.
glossary.bigamy: The offence in Section 82(1) BNS of a person marrying again during the lifetime of a husband or wife, where such second marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of the first spouse — punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, subject to the seven-year-absence exception.
glossary.seven-year presumption of death exceptio: The exception to Section 82 BNS's bigamy offence: the provision does not extend to a person whose former marriage has been declared void by a competent court, or who contracts a second marriage after the former spouse has been continually absent for seven years and not heard of as alive, provided the facts are disclosed to the person the second marriage is contracted with.
glossary.concealed bigamy: The aggravated form of bigamy under Section 82(2) BNS: where a person conceals from the person they marry the fact of the former marriage, the punishment rises to up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine — concealment is treated as a distinct, more culpable aggravation of the base bigamy offence.
glossary.fraudulent marriage ceremony: The offence in Section 83 BNS of dishonestly or fraudulently going through a marriage ceremony knowing that one is not thereby lawfully married — punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, distinct from bigamy in that it does not require a subsisting prior valid marriage, only knowledge that the ceremony itself does not create a lawful marriage.
glossary.enticing away a married woman: One limb of the Section 84 BNS offence: taking or enticing away a married woman, or concealing or detaining her, with intent that she may have illicit intercourse with any person, or knowing it to be likely that she will have such intercourse — punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.concealment or detention of a married wo: The alternative limb of the Section 84 BNS offence alongside enticement: concealing or detaining a married woman with the intent or knowledge that illicit intercourse is intended or likely, treated on the same footing and drawing the same punishment as actively taking or enticing her away.
glossary.kidnapping or abducting a woman to compe: The offence in Section 87 BNS of kidnapping or abducting any woman with intent that she may be compelled to marry any person against her will, or in order that she may be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse, or by means of criminal intimidation inducing her to go from any place — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine.
glossary.causing miscarriage: The base offence in Section 88 BNS of voluntarily causing a woman with child to miscarry, unless done in good faith for the purpose of saving the woman's life — punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both, rising to up to seven years if the woman is 'quick with child.'
glossary.good-faith life-saving exception for mis: The exception built directly into Section 88 BNS's definition: causing a miscarriage done in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the pregnant woman is excluded from the offence entirely — the sole statutory justification recognised within the provision itself, separate from the general Chapter III exceptions.
glossary.quick with child: A common-law-derived phrase used as an aggravating threshold in Section 88 BNS: where the woman whose miscarriage is caused is 'quick with child' (i.e., the fetus's movements can be felt), the maximum punishment rises from three to seven years' imprisonment, reflecting the advanced stage of pregnancy.
glossary.causing miscarriage without consent: The escalated offence in Section 89 BNS, punishable with imprisonment for life or up to ten years plus fine, where a miscarriage is caused without the pregnant woman's consent — regardless of whether she is quick with child, the absence of consent alone drives the punishment far above the Section 88 consensual-miscarriage offence.
glossary.death resulting from an act intended to: The offence in Section 90 BNS where an act done with intent to cause a woman's miscarriage results in her death — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine if the act was not done in good faith to save her life, and more severely if done without her consent, irrespective of whether the accused knew the act was likely to cause death.
glossary.preventing live birth or causing death a: The offence in Section 91 BNS of doing any act, before a child's birth, with intent to prevent that child from being born alive, or causing it to die after birth, where the act is not done in good faith to save the mother's life — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.culpable-homicide-equivalent act causing: The offence in Section 92 BNS treating an act causing the death of a quick unborn child as akin to culpable homicide if the act would have amounted to culpable homicide had it instead caused the mother's death — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine, bridging the conceptual gap between homicide offences (which require a 'person' already born) and harm to an unborn child.
glossary.exposure and abandonment of a child unde: The offence in Section 93 BNS of a parent or person having care of a child under twelve years exposing or leaving that child in any place with the intention of wholly abandoning it — punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment, fine, or both, with an Explanation preserving liability for culpable homicide or murder if the exposure/abandonment in fact causes the child's death.
glossary.concealment of birth by secret disposal: The offence in Section 94 BNS of secretly burying or otherwise disposing of the dead body of a child, whether the child died before, at, or after birth, with the intention of concealing the birth — punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both, independent of and separate from any liability for causing the child's death.
glossary.hiring or engaging a child to commit an: The offence in Section 95(1) BNS of hiring, employing, or engaging a child to commit an offence — punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, and drawing rigorous imprisonment up to ten years where the offence actually committed by the child carries that higher threshold under the Explanation's sexual-exploitation/pornography extension.
glossary.cumulative liability for the resulting o: The stacking principle in Section 95(2) BNS: a person who hires, employs, or engages a child to commit an offence is liable not only for the hiring/engaging itself under Section 95(1) but also, cumulatively, for the offence actually committed by the child as a direct result — mirroring the double-liability structure seen elsewhere in the abetment scheme.
glossary.procuration of a child for illicit inter: The offence in Section 96 BNS of inducing a child to go from any place, or doing any act, with intent that the child may be, or knowing it to be likely that the child will be, forced or seduced into illicit intercourse with another person — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine.
glossary.illicit intercourse (BNS definition): A phrase used throughout the Section 84-96 BNS offences (enticement, kidnapping to compel marriage, procuration) denoting sexual intercourse outside a lawful marital relationship that the law treats as an aggravating purpose justifying criminal liability against whoever induces, forces, or facilitates it, without itself independently defining or punishing the intercourse.
glossary.kidnapping a child under ten to steal fr: The offence in Section 97 BNS of kidnapping or abducting a child under ten years of age with the intent to take dishonestly any movable property from the person of that child — punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, a property-crime-motivated kidnapping offence distinct from the sexual/marital kidnapping offences elsewhere in the Chapter.
glossary.selling a child for prostitution or illi: The offence in Section 98(1) BNS of selling, letting to hire, or otherwise disposing of any person under eighteen with intent that such person be used for prostitution, illicit intercourse, or any unlawful/immoral purpose — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine.
glossary.statutory presumption of prostitution in: The reverse-burden presumption attached to both Sections 98 and 99 BNS: where a female under eighteen is sold, let to hire, or disposed of to a prostitute or brothel-keeper (or otherwise to a person who keeps/manages a brothel), the person disposing of/buying her is presumed, unless the contrary is proved, to have done so with the intent that she be used for prostitution.
glossary.buying a child for prostitution or illic: The mirror-image offence to Section 98 BNS, created by Section 99 BNS: buying, hiring, or otherwise obtaining possession of a person under eighteen with intent that they be used for prostitution, illicit intercourse, or unlawful/immoral purposes — punishable with a mandatory minimum of seven years' rigorous imprisonment extendable to fourteen years, plus fine.
glossary.minimum mandatory sentence: A sentencing structure used across several BNS provisions in Chapter V (e.g. Sections 65, 70, 71, 99) that fixes a statutory floor below which a court cannot sentence on conviction, even where it might otherwise exercise downward sentencing discretion — reflecting the legislature's intent to guarantee a severe baseline punishment for specified offences against women and children.
glossary.abuse of position of authority or fiduci: The operative aggravating ground for the Section 68 BNS offence (sexual intercourse by a person in authority): a public servant, superintendent or manager of a jail/remand home/other custodial institution, or a member of hospital staff who abuses the position of authority or fiduciary relationship they hold over a woman in their custody, charge, or presence to induce or seduce her into sexual intercourse not amounting to rape commits this distinct offence.
glossary.deceitful inducement of belief in lawful: The offence in Section 81 BNS of a man, by deceit, causing any woman who is not lawfully married to him to believe that she is lawfully married to him and to cohabit or have sexual intercourse with him in that belief — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine, distinct from bigamy since it requires no actual prior or subsequent marriage ceremony, only the deceitful inducement of belief.
glossary.culpable homicide: Defined in Section 100 BNS as causing death by an act done with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death — the genus of which murder (Section 101) is a narrower, more culpable species; the three Explanations clarify that death of a person suffering a prior disorder/disease/infirmity still counts if accelerated, that causing death of a child not yet born alive does not count, and that causing the death of a quick unborn child may fall under a separate offence (Section 92).
glossary.accelerating an existing disorder: Explanation 1 to Section 100 BNS: a person who causes bodily injury to another already labouring under a disorder, disease, or bodily infirmity, and thereby accelerates that person's death, is deemed to have caused their death — a pre-existing vulnerability of the victim is no defence to a culpable homicide charge.
glossary.live-birth threshold for homicide: Explanation 2 to Section 100 BNS: causing the death of a child in the mother's womb is not culpable homicide, but causing the death of a living child who has not completely come out of its mother's womb may amount to culpable homicide — the dividing line is whether any part of the child has been brought forth alive, even if the umbilical cord is not yet cut.
glossary.murder (BNS definition): Defined in Section 101 BNS: culpable homicide is murder if the act causing death is done with the intention of causing death (clause a), or with intention to cause bodily injury the offender knows to be likely to cause death (clause b), or with intention to cause bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death (clause c), or with knowledge the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death or such injury, without any excuse for incurring that risk (clause d) — subject to the five Exceptions that downgrade murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
glossary.grave and sudden provocation exception: Exception 1 to Section 101 BNS: culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, deprived of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation or of any other person by mistake or accident — subject to the proviso that the provocation must not be sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender, must not be given by anything done in obedience to law or by a public servant acting lawfully, and must not be given by anything done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence.
glossary.private defence exceeding power exceptio: Exception 2 to Section 101 BNS: culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given by law and causes death without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than necessary for the purpose of such defence.
glossary.public servant exceeding power exception: Exception 3 to Section 101 BNS: culpable homicide is not murder if a public servant, or a person aiding a public servant acting for the advancement of public justice, exceeds the powers given by law and causes death by an act believed in good faith to be lawful and necessary for the due discharge of duty, without ill-will towards the person whose death is caused.
glossary.sudden fight exception: Exception 4 to Section 101 BNS: culpable homicide is not murder if it is committed without premeditation in a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, without the offender having taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner — the Explanation clarifies it is immaterial which party offers the provocation or commences the assault.
glossary.consent to death exception: Exception 5 to Section 101 BNS: culpable homicide is not murder if the person whose death is caused, being above eighteen years of age, suffers death or takes the risk of death with their own consent.
glossary.transferred malice in homicide: The doctrine codified in Section 102 BNS: where a person, intending or knowing their act likely to cause the death of one person, by doing an act causes the death of a different person whose death they neither intended nor knew likely, the culpable homicide committed is of the same description as it would have been against the intended victim — malice is 'transferred' to the actual victim, illustrated by the mistaken-target shooting example.
glossary.mob lynching provision: Section 103(2) BNS, a provision with no IPC equivalent: when a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on grounds including race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief, or any other similar ground, each member of that group is punishable with death or life imprisonment plus fine — a direct legislative response to mob lynching incidents.
glossary.discriminatory-ground group murder: The identity of the aggravating grounds listed in Section 103(2) BNS for mob-lynching-type group murder — race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief, or any other similar ground — mirroring the discriminatory-ground language also used for group grievous hurt under Section 117(4) BNS.
glossary.life-convict committing a further murder: Section 104 BNS: a person already under sentence of imprisonment for life who commits murder is punishable with death or imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life — a distinct, more severe punishment provision from the general murder punishment in Section 103, reflecting the aggravation of reoffending while already serving a life sentence.
glossary.culpable homicide not amounting to murde: Section 105 BNS fixes a two-tier punishment scheme for culpable homicide not amounting to murder (i.e., homicide falling within one of Section 101's five Exceptions, or otherwise not meeting murder's threshold): imprisonment for life or up to ten years plus fine if the act was done with intention of causing death or injury likely to cause death, or up to ten years plus fine if done only with knowledge that death was a likely consequence, without intent to cause death.
glossary.causing death by negligence: Section 106 BNS: causing death by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, punishable with up to five years' imprisonment plus fine — distinguished from culpable homicide by the complete absence of intention or knowledge that death was a likely consequence, the fault lying purely in a failure to exercise reasonable care.
glossary.registered medical practitioner carve-ou: The proviso to Section 106(1) BNS capping punishment at two years' imprisonment (instead of five) where the rash or negligent act causing death was committed by a registered medical practitioner performing a medical procedure — a protective carve-out for doctors acting in a professional capacity, absent in the former IPC's Section 304A.
glossary.hit-and-run enhancement: Section 106(2) BNS, a new provision with no IPC equivalent: whoever causes death by rash or negligent driving of a vehicle and escapes without reporting to a police officer or Magistrate soon after the incident is punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine — a sharp escalation from the base five-year punishment, targeting hit-and-run flight from the scene.
glossary.abetment of suicide of a vulnerable pers: Section 107(2) BNS: where a child, a person of unsound mind, an intoxicated person, or a person in a delirious or otherwise incapacitated state is abetted to commit suicide, the abettor is punishable with death or imprisonment for life or imprisonment up to ten years plus fine — a far more severe band than the general abetment-of-suicide offence under Section 108, reflecting the victim's inability to make a genuinely autonomous choice.
glossary.abetment of suicide (general): Section 108 BNS: the general offence of abetting the commission of suicide by any person (not falling within the vulnerable-person category of Section 107(2)), punishable with imprisonment of either description up to ten years, plus fine.
glossary.attempt to murder: Section 109 BNS: doing an act with such intention or knowledge, and under such circumstances, that if death were caused the offender would be guilty of murder, is punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine as the base, rising to up to life imprisonment plus fine where hurt is actually caused to any person by the act.
glossary.life-convict attempting murder causing h: Section 109(2) BNS: where a person already under sentence of imprisonment for life attempts to commit murder and hurt is caused, the offender is punishable with death or imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life — the attempt-stage mirror of Section 104's completed-murder life-convict enhancement.
glossary.attempt to commit culpable homicide not: Section 110 BNS: the lighter mirror of Section 109, punishing an attempt to commit culpable homicide not amounting to murder with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both, rising to up to seven years plus fine where hurt is actually caused to any person by the act done.
glossary.organised crime: Defined and comprehensively punished under Section 111 BNS, a provision with no IPC equivalent modelled on state organised-crime statutes like MCOCA: any continuing unlawful activity including kidnapping, robbery, extortion, cyber-crime, or trafficking, carried out by an individual singly or jointly as a member of an organised crime syndicate, by violence, threat, intimidation, corruption, or other unlawful means, to obtain direct or indirect material benefit including financial gain.
glossary.organised crime syndicate: Defined within Section 111 BNS as a group of two or more persons acting in concert, singly or jointly, as a syndicate or gang, involved in continuing unlawful activity — the structural predicate that distinguishes organised crime from an ordinary single offence committed by one or more individuals acting without that ongoing criminal enterprise structure.
