glossary.continuing unlawful activity: A core element of the Section 111 BNS organised-crime definition: an unlawful activity that is a cognizable offence punishable with three years' imprisonment or more, undertaken singly or jointly, as a member of an organised crime syndicate, in respect of which more than one chargesheet has been filed before a competent court within the preceding ten years and that court has taken cognizance of the offence — the repeated, pattern-based element distinguishing it from an isolated crime.
glossary.economic offence (organised crime): A category expressly brought within Section 111 BNS's organised-crime definition: criminal breach of trust, forgery, counterfeiting of currency notes, bank notes or Government stamps, mass-marketing fraud, or running any scheme to defraud multiple persons — recognising that large-scale financial crime syndicates fall within the same organised-crime framework as violent crime syndicates.
glossary.membership of an organised crime syndica: An independently punishable act under Section 111 BNS: being a member of an organised crime syndicate is itself an offence (punishable with five to ten years' imprisonment plus fine of not less than five lakh rupees), separate from actually participating in a specific continuing unlawful activity — mere membership suffices for liability.
glossary.harbouring an organised-crime offender: An offence under Section 111 BNS of harbouring or concealing, or attempting to harbour or conceal, any member of an organised crime syndicate, punishable with three to five years' imprisonment plus fine of not less than five lakh rupees — subject to an express proviso exempting the spouse of the offender from liability under this specific clause.
glossary.unaccounted property linked to organised: A presumption-shifting provision within Section 111 BNS: possessing property known or reasonably believed to be derived from the commission of an organised crime, or possessing property on behalf of another member of an organised crime syndicate where the person cannot satisfactorily account for the possession, is independently punishable — targeting the proceeds and financial infrastructure of organised-crime networks, not just the predicate acts.
glossary.petty organised crime: Section 112 BNS, a new offence with no IPC equivalent: a group or gang of persons engaged in theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorised selling of tickets, unfair means in examinations, or similar criminal acts affecting daily or economic life, committed with the motive to fill the void of committing petty crime through habitual and organised criminals — punishable up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, sitting below the heavier Section 111 organised-crime offence.
glossary.terrorist act (BNS definition): Defined and punished under Section 113 BNS, a provision with no IPC equivalent modelled on the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967: any act committed with intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, security, or economic security of India, or to strike terror in the people, using bombs, dynamite, firearms, poisonous gases, biological or chemical weapons, or any other means of a nature to cause death, injury, or damage to property or essential supplies/services, falling within clauses (a) to (c) of the section.
glossary.public functionary: A specific aggravating target identified within Section 113 BNS's terrorist-act definition: an act that causes death of, or injury to, any public functionary with the intent to compel the Government or any other person to do or abstain from doing any act, or that threatens the unity and integrity of India, falls squarely within the terrorist-act offence.
glossary.counterfeit Indian currency: Listed within Section 113 BNS's terrorist-act definition as a method by which a terrorist act may be committed — the production, smuggling, or circulation of high-quality counterfeit Indian paper currency, coin, or any other material, destabilising the monetary or financial system of the country, is itself treated as capable of constituting a terrorist act.
glossary.terrorist training camp: An independently punishable activity under Section 113 BNS: organising or causing to be organised any camp or camps for imparting training in terrorism, punishable with imprisonment for life or any term of years with fine — targeting the infrastructure that produces terrorist operatives, not just the completed terrorist act.
glossary.membership of a terrorist organisation: An independently punishable act under Section 113 BNS, parallel to organised-crime-syndicate membership: being a member of a terrorist organisation involved in a terrorist act is itself an offence, punishable with imprisonment for life or up to ten years plus fine.
glossary.harbouring a terrorist: An offence under Section 113 BNS of harbouring or concealing, or attempting to harbour or conceal, a person known to be a terrorist, punishable with imprisonment for life or up to ten years plus fine — subject to the same express proviso exempting the spouse of such a person from liability under this clause as applies to harbouring an organised-crime offender under Section 111.
glossary.UAPA overlap for terrorist act: The Explanation to Section 113 BNS clarifying that an officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police decides whether a case registered under the Sanhita is to be investigated under the BNS or under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 — acknowledging the deliberate overlap between this new BNS terrorist-act provision and the pre-existing specialised anti-terror statute.
glossary.hurt (BNS definition): Defined in Section 114 BNS as causing bodily pain, disease, or infirmity to any person — the broad foundational definition from which the entire hurt/grievous-hurt offence ladder (Sections 115-125 BNS) is built, requiring none of the eight specific grievous-hurt categories of Section 116.
glossary.voluntarily causing hurt: Section 115 BNS: the base offence of voluntarily causing hurt (as defined in Section 114), punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both under sub-section (2); sub-section (1) separately criminalises hurt caused other than by dangerous weapons or means with community service as an available punishment where no grievous hurt results.
glossary.grievous hurt (BNS definition): Defined in Section 116 BNS through eight exhaustive categories (a) to (h): emasculation; permanent privation of sight or hearing of either eye or ear; privation of any member or joint; destruction or permanent impairing of the powers of any member or joint; permanent disfiguration of the head or face; fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth; any hurt endangering life or causing severe bodily pain or inability to follow ordinary pursuits for twenty days; and any hurt leading to a person being in a persistent vegetative state.
glossary.voluntarily causing grievous hurt: Section 117(1)-(2) BNS: voluntarily causing hurt, if the hurt caused is grievous hurt as defined in Section 116, is punishable with imprisonment of either description up to seven years, plus fine — the escalated counterpart to the base voluntarily-causing-hurt offence under Section 115.
glossary.grievous hurt of a different kind than i: A principle embedded in Section 117 BNS's structure (and illustrated across the hurt provisions): a person who voluntarily causes hurt, intending or knowing it likely to cause grievous hurt of one kind, is liable under Section 117 even if the grievous hurt actually caused is of a different kind than intended or known to be likely — liability tracks the grievous character of the injury, not an exact match to the specific category anticipated.
glossary.permanent disability or persistent veget: Section 117(3) BNS: where the grievous hurt caused results in permanent disability or a persistent vegetative state of the victim, the offender is punishable with imprisonment of not less than ten years, extendable to imprisonment for life, plus the obligation to pay fine or compensation to the victim covering medical expenses — a severe escalation beyond the general seven-year grievous-hurt band in Section 117(1)-(2).
glossary.discriminatory-ground group grievous hur: Section 117(4) BNS: a group of five or more persons acting in concert who cause grievous hurt to a person on grounds of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief, or any other similar ground, with each member punishable with imprisonment of seven years to life plus fine — the grievous-hurt mirror of the Section 103(2) mob-lynching group-murder provision.
glossary.voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous we: Section 118 BNS: an aggravated offence for voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt using any instrument for shooting, stabbing, or cutting, or any instrument likely to cause death if used as a weapon of offence, or by means of fire or any heated substance, poison, corrosive substance, explosive substance, or any substance deleterious to the human body to inhale, swallow, or receive into the blood, or by means of any animal — drawing substantially higher punishment than the plain hurt/grievous-hurt offences because of the dangerous method employed.
glossary.voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hur: Section 119 BNS: voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt in order to extort property or a valuable security, or to constrain any person to do anything illegal that may facilitate extortion of property or valuable security, punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment (up to fourteen years for grievous hurt) plus fine.

Section 120 BNS: voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort a confession, or information that may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or to compel restoration of property or satisfaction of a claim/demand, or to induce a person to give false evidence — the section whose illustrations expressly address custodial torture by police and revenue officers.
glossary.custodial torture: A fact pattern expressly illustrated under Section 120 BNS: a police officer who causes hurt to extort a confession of guilt or a revenue officer who causes hurt to extort a confession regarding concealed property both fall squarely within the offence of voluntarily causing hurt/grievous hurt to extort a confession — giving BNS a textual hook for prosecuting custodial violence by law-enforcement and revenue officials.
glossary.voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hur: Section 121 BNS: voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter any person, including a public servant, from discharging their lawful duty as such public servant, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment (up to ten years for grievous hurt) plus fine.

Section 122 BNS: a mitigated punishment band for voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on grave and sudden provocation, provided the offender did not intend to cause hurt to any person other than the one who gave the provocation — mirroring the same grave-and-sudden-provocation logic as Exception 1 to Section 101's murder definition, carried down to the hurt-offence level.
glossary.causing hurt by poison to facilitate an: Section 123 BNS: administering to or causing any person to take poison or any stupefying, intoxicating, or unwholesome drug/substance, with intent to cause hurt, or to commit or facilitate the commission of an offence, or knowing it likely that hurt will thereby be caused — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine.
glossary.acid attack: Section 124(1)-(2) BNS: voluntarily causing grievous hurt by throwing acid on, or administering acid to, any person, or by any other means, with intent to cause permanent or partial damage, deformity, burns, maiming, disfigurement, or disability, or to cause grievous hurt — punishable with rigorous imprisonment of not less than ten years, extendable to imprisonment for life, plus fine payable to the victim to meet medical expenses.
glossary.attempt to throw or administer acid: Section 124(2) BNS: a lesser but still severe offence covering an attempt to throw or administer acid, or an attempt to cause permanent or partial damage, deformity, burns, maiming, disfigurement, disability, or grievous hurt by acid, punishable with five to seven years' imprisonment plus fine — the inchoate-offence counterpart to the completed acid-attack offence in Section 124(1).
glossary.acid (BNS definition): The Explanation to Section 124 BNS defining 'acid' to include any substance which is acidic or corrosive in nature and is capable of causing bodily injury leading to scars, disfigurement, temporary or permanent disability, partial or total blindness — a functional definition keyed to the substance's injurious effect rather than any single chemical formula.
glossary.irreversibility not required for acid-at: A principle drawn from Section 124 BNS's wording ('permanent or partial damage'): the acid-attack offence is made out whether the deformity, burns, or disability caused is permanent or only partial/temporary — the offender need not have succeeded in causing irreversible harm for liability to attach.
glossary.act endangering life or personal safety: Section 125 BNS: doing any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or the personal safety of others, graded by outcome — up to three months' imprisonment, fine up to two thousand five hundred rupees, or both for mere endangerment; rising to up to six months/five thousand rupees if hurt is caused; and up to two years/ten thousand rupees if grievous hurt is caused.
glossary.wrongful restraint: Defined and punished in Section 126 BNS: voluntarily obstructing a person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which they have a right to proceed, punishable with up to one month's imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both, or community service — the lighter of the two liberty-restricting offences, not involving total confinement.
glossary.good-faith claim of right to obstruct a: The Exception to Section 126 BNS: the obstruction of a private way over land or water which a person in good faith believes themselves to have a lawful right to obstruct is not wrongful restraint — a defence available only where the belief in the right to obstruct is both genuine and exercised in good faith.
glossary.wrongful confinement: Defined and punished in Section 127 BNS: wrongfully restraining a person in a manner that prevents that person from proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits, punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both as the base offence under sub-section (2), with escalating punishment under sub-sections (3)-(8) keyed to duration and aggravating circumstances.
glossary.confinement defying a writ of liberation: Section 127(6) BNS: wrongfully confining a person and keeping that person so confined after receiving a writ of habeas corpus (or any other lawful direction) for that person's release, punishable with imprisonment for up to two years in addition to any other punishment to which the offender may be liable for the original wrongful confinement.
glossary.secret confinement concealing whereabout: Section 127(7) BNS: wrongfully confining a person in such a manner as to indicate an intention that the confinement may not be known to any person interested in the confined person, or to any public servant, or that the place of confinement may not be known to or discovered by any such person — punishable with imprisonment up to seven years, plus fine, reflecting the aggravated danger of secretive, undiscoverable confinement.
glossary.wrongful confinement to extort property: Section 127(8) BNS (extortion-of-property limb): wrongfully confining a person for the purpose of extorting property or a valuable security from the person confined or any interested person, or to constrain any person to do anything illegal that may facilitate such extortion, punishable with imprisonment of up to three years, plus fine.
glossary.wrongful confinement to extort confessio: The companion limb within Section 127(8) BNS: wrongfully confining a person to extort a confession, or information that may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, punishable with imprisonment of up to three years, plus fine — paralleling the extort-property limb within the same sub-section.
glossary.force (BNS definition): Defined in Section 128 BNS as causing motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to another person or to a substance that then contacts that person's body, clothing, or carried items, or affects their sense of feeling -- but only where the actor brings this about by their own bodily power, by arranging a substance so the motion occurs without further action, or by inducing an animal to move. A morally neutral physical concept, narrowed into criminal force by Section 129.
glossary.cessation of motion: One of the three physical effects captured by Section 128 BNS's definition of 'force' -- stopping an already-moving person or object counts as using force just as much as starting or changing its motion, illustrated by A seizing the pole of Z's palanquin and halting it.
glossary.contact affecting sense of feeling: The qualifying requirement in Section 128 BNS: force is only made out where the motion caused brings a substance into contact with the victim's body, clothing, or carried items, or is otherwise so situated that the contact affects the victim's sense of feeling -- illustrated by pouring boiling water into a bath where the heat itself affects Z even without direct skin contact.
glossary.criminal force: Defined in Section 129 BNS as the intentional use of force (per Section 128) to any person, without that person's consent, done either in order to commit an offence or with intention or knowledge that it is likely to cause injury, fear, or annoyance to that person -- the operative, punishable concept built on the neutral physical definition of force.
glossary.absence of consent for force: The second of Section 129 BNS's two defining conditions for criminal force: the force must be used without the consent of the person to whom it is applied -- consensual physical contact, however forceful, does not become criminal force merely because it causes incidental injury, fear, or annoyance.
glossary.injury fear or annoyance: The disjunctive mental-element trigger in Section 129 BNS: criminal force requires either that the force was used in order to commit an offence, or that the actor intended or knew it likely to cause injury, fear, or annoyance to the victim -- any one of these three outcomes (injury, fear, or mere annoyance) suffices, reflecting how low the threshold is set.
glossary.assault (BNS definition): Defined in Section 130 BNS as making any gesture or preparation, intending or knowing it likely to cause a person present to apprehend that criminal force is about to be used against them -- an anticipatory offence requiring no actual physical contact, only the creation of a reasonable apprehension of imminent criminal force.
glossary.apprehension of criminal force: The core mental result required by Section 130 BNS's assault definition: the victim must be caused to apprehend that the person making the gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force against them -- fear of future force, not the force itself, is what completes the offence of assault.
glossary.mere words not amounting to assault: The Explanation to Section 130 BNS: words alone, however threatening, never by themselves amount to an assault -- but words can give an otherwise ambiguous gesture or preparation the meaning needed to make it an assault, illustrated by A picking up a stick while saying 'I will give you a beating.'
glossary.punishment for base assault or criminal: The default punishment fixed by Section 131 BNS for simple assault or criminal force not committed on grave and sudden provocation: imprisonment of either description up to three months, fine up to one thousand rupees, or both -- the residual provision that applies unless one of the more specific, heavier Sections 132-135 (public servant, dishonour, theft, or confinement contexts) is engaged.
glossary.grave and sudden provocation defence to: The mitigating circumstance recognised by Sections 131 and 136 BNS: an assault or use of criminal force committed on grave and sudden provocation from the victim draws a much lighter punishment (Section 136) than the same act committed otherwise (Section 131) -- but the mitigation is unavailable where the provocation was self-sought, arose from lawful official conduct, or arose from lawful exercise of the right of private defence.
glossary.assault or criminal force to deter a pub: Section 132 BNS: an aggravated assault offence, punishable up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both, covering assault or criminal force used on a public servant in execution of duty, or with intent to deter that duty, or in consequence of duty lawfully discharged -- the assault-level counterpart to the hurt-level offence in Section 121.
glossary.assault or criminal force with intent to: Section 133 BNS: assault or criminal force committed with the specific intention of dishonouring the victim, otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation, punishable up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- the dishonouring intent is what elevates this above the base Section 131 offence.
glossary.assault or criminal force in attempt to: Section 134 BNS: assault or criminal force used while attempting to steal property that the victim is then wearing or carrying (e.g. chain-snatching, bag-snatching), punishable up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.assault or criminal force in attempt wro: Section 135 BNS: assault or criminal force used while attempting to wrongfully confine a person, punishable up to one year's imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both -- the attempt-stage precursor to a completed wrongful confinement under Section 127.
glossary.assault or criminal force on grave and s: Section 136 BNS: the mitigated mirror of Section 131, punishing assault or criminal force genuinely triggered by grave and sudden provocation from the victim with only simple imprisonment up to one month, fine up to one thousand rupees, or both -- subject to the same disqualifying circumstances as Section 131's Explanation 1.
glossary.kidnapping (BNS definition): Defined in Section 137(1) BNS as being of two kinds -- kidnapping from India and kidnapping from lawful guardianship -- punishable under sub-section (2) with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine; it opens the 'Of kidnapping, abduction, slavery and forced labour' sub-chapter and is distinguished from the separately defined 'abduction' (Section 138), which requires force or deceitful inducement but is not independently punishable.
glossary.kidnapping from India: The first kind of kidnapping under Section 137(1)(a) BNS: conveying any person beyond the limits of India without the consent of that person, or of someone legally authorised to consent on their behalf -- the victim's own territorial removal, not confinement or guardianship, is the gravamen.
glossary.kidnapping from lawful guardianship: The second kind of kidnapping under Section 137(1)(b) BNS: taking or enticing a child or a person of unsound mind out of the keeping of their lawful guardian without that guardian's consent -- the victim's own consent is irrelevant here since the law deems children and persons of unsound mind incapable of consenting to being taken away.
glossary.good-faith illegitimate-father exception: The Exception to Section 137(1)(b) BNS: a person who in good faith believes himself to be the father of an illegitimate child, or believes himself entitled to the child's lawful custody, is not guilty of kidnapping from lawful guardianship by taking that child -- unless the act is committed for an immoral or unlawful purpose, in which case the exception does not apply.
glossary.abduction (BNS definition): Defined in Section 138 BNS as compelling a person by force, or inducing them by deceitful means, to go from any place -- unlike kidnapping, abduction is not by itself a punishable offence under the Sanhita; it becomes punishable only when combined with a specific wrongful purpose under later sections such as 140 or 142.
glossary.kidnapping a child for begging: Section 139(1) BNS: kidnapping a child, or obtaining custody of a child without being the lawful guardian, in order that the child be employed or used for begging, punishable with rigorous imprisonment of ten years to life plus fine -- a severe child-protection provision targeting organised begging rackets.
glossary.maiming a child for begging: Section 139(2) BNS: the even more severe offence of actually maiming a child in order that the child may be employed or used for begging, punishable with a minimum twenty years' imprisonment up to life (meaning the remainder of the person's natural life), plus fine.
glossary.presumption of begging-related kidnappin: Section 139(3) BNS: where any person other than a child's lawful guardian employs or uses that child for begging, it is presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the person kidnapped or otherwise obtained custody of the child for the purpose of begging -- a reversed burden of proof that significantly eases the prosecution's task once child-begging-by-a-non-guardian is shown.
glossary.begging (BNS definition): Defined in Section 139(4) BNS to include soliciting or receiving alms in a public place under any pretence (singing, dancing, fortune-telling, tricks, selling articles, or otherwise), entering private premises to solicit alms, exhibiting a sore, wound, injury, deformity or disease (of oneself, another, or an animal) to obtain or extort alms, and using a child as an exhibit to solicit alms.
glossary.kidnapping or abducting to murder: Section 140(1) BNS: kidnapping or abducting a person in order that they may be murdered, or exposed to the danger of being murdered, punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years' rigorous imprisonment plus fine -- illustrated by kidnapping someone to be sacrificed to an idol, or carrying someone away from home in order that they be murdered.
glossary.kidnapping or abducting for ransom: Section 140(2) BNS: kidnapping or abducting a person, or detaining them after such kidnapping or abduction, and threatening death or hurt (or causing a reasonable apprehension of it), or actually causing hurt or death, in order to compel a Government, foreign State, international organisation, or any person to act, abstain from acting, or pay a ransom -- punishable with death or life imprisonment, the most severe tier within Section 140.
glossary.kidnapping or abducting for secret wrong: Section 140(3) BNS: kidnapping or abducting a person with intent that they be secretly and wrongfully confined, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine -- the lightest of Section 140's four purpose-based tiers.
glossary.kidnapping or abducting to subject to gr: Section 140(4) BNS: kidnapping or abducting a person in order that they be subjected (or exposed to the danger of being subjected) to grievous hurt, slavery, or the unnatural lust of any person, punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine.
glossary.importation of girl or boy for illicit i: Section 141 BNS: importing into India from any foreign country a girl under twenty-one years or a boy under eighteen years, with intent or knowledge that they will likely be forced or seduced into illicit intercourse with another person, punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine -- notable for its asymmetric age thresholds between girls and boys, and for requiring a cross-border importation element that the general trafficking offence (Section 143) does not.
glossary.wrongfully concealing a kidnapped or abd: Section 142 BNS: a person who, knowing that someone has been kidnapped or abducted, wrongfully conceals or confines them is punished exactly as if they themselves had committed the kidnapping or abduction with the same intention, knowledge, or purpose underlying the concealment -- a derivative-liability provision that borrows its punishment from whichever purpose-specific tier of Section 140 matches the concealer's own purpose.
glossary.derivative liability for concealment mat: The operative mechanism of Section 142 BNS: the concealer of a kidnapped or abducted person does not face a fixed, independent punishment, but is instead punished as if they had committed the underlying kidnapping or abduction themselves, calibrated to the same intention, knowledge, or purpose that motivates their own act of concealment or confinement.
glossary.trafficking of person (BNS definition): Defined in Section 143(1) BNS as recruiting, transporting, harbouring, transferring, or receiving a person for the purpose of exploitation, by any of six specified means -- threats, force or coercion, abduction, fraud or deception, abuse of power, or inducement (including payments or benefits) to secure the consent of whoever controls the victim -- the Sanhita's comprehensive anti-trafficking provision, carrying a punishment ladder from seven years to mandatory life depending on aggravating factors.
glossary.exploitation (trafficking definition): Defined in Explanation 1 to Section 143 BNS to include any act of physical exploitation, any form of sexual exploitation, slavery or practices similar to slavery, servitude, beggary, or forced removal of organs -- the broad purpose element that, combined with one of Section 143(1)'s six listed means, completes the offence of trafficking.
glossary.victim consent immaterial in trafficking: Explanation 2 to Section 143 BNS: the consent of the victim is expressly made immaterial in determining whether the offence of trafficking has been committed -- a trafficked person's apparent agreement to be recruited, transported, harboured, transferred, or received does not provide any defence once the exploitation purpose and one of the specified means is established.
glossary.aggravated trafficking of a child: The escalated punishment tiers within Section 143 BNS keyed to child victims: ten years to life for trafficking a single child (sub-section 4), fourteen years to life for trafficking more than one child (sub-section 5), and mandatory imprisonment for the remainder of natural life for a repeat conviction of child trafficking (sub-section 6) -- reflecting the Sanhita's markedly harsher treatment of trafficking offences against children.
glossary.public servant or police officer traffic: Section 143(7) BNS: where a public servant or police officer is involved in trafficking any person, that public servant or police officer is punishable with imprisonment for the remainder of their natural life plus fine -- a mandatory-life aggravation reflecting the particular betrayal of public trust when state functionaries participate in trafficking.
glossary.repeat child-trafficking conviction: Section 143(6) BNS: a person convicted of child trafficking on more than one occasion must be punished with imprisonment for life, meaning imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, plus fine -- a mandatory (not merely discretionary) life sentence triggered purely by the fact of a repeat conviction.
glossary.exploitation of a trafficked person: Section 144 BNS: a demand-side offence distinct from Section 143's supply-side trafficking offence -- knowingly or having reason to believe a person has been trafficked, and then engaging that person for sexual exploitation, is independently punishable with five to ten years' imprisonment where the victim is a child, or three to seven years where the victim is an adult.
glossary.habitual dealing in slaves: Section 145 BNS: a standalone anti-slavery offence punishing habitual importing, exporting, removing, buying, selling, trafficking in, or dealing in slaves, with life imprisonment or up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine -- the 'habitually' requirement distinguishes it from a single, isolated transaction.
glossary.unlawful compulsory labour: Section 146 BNS, the final provision of Chapter VI: unlawfully compelling any person to labour against their will, punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both -- a general, comparatively lightly punished forced-labour offence for situations not otherwise captured by the more specific slavery or trafficking provisions.
glossary.waging war against the Government of Ind: The gravest offence under Section 147 BNS, opening Chapter VII ('Of Offences Against the State'): waging war, attempting to wage war, or abetting the waging of war against the Government of India, punishable with death or life imprisonment plus fine -- illustrated simply by A joining an insurrection, showing that mere participation, not leadership or organisation, suffices.
glossary.abetting the waging of war: One of the three modes of liability under Section 147 BNS alongside actually waging war and attempting to wage war -- abetting another's war-waging against the Government of India draws the identical death-or-life-imprisonment punishment as the completed offence itself.
glossary.conspiracy to wage war: Punished under Section 148 BNS with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine: conspiring, whether within or outside India, to commit any offence punishable under Section 147 -- distinguished from the general criminal-conspiracy offence (Section 61) by the Explanation dispensing with any overt-act requirement, given the gravity of the subject matter.
glossary.conspiracy to overawe the Government by: The second limb of Section 148 BNS: conspiring, by means of criminal force or the show of criminal force, to overawe the Central Government or any State Government, carries the same life-imprisonment-or-ten-years punishment as conspiring to wage war under the same section.
glossary.mere-agreement conspiracy against the St: The Explanation to Section 148 BNS: unlike most agreements falling within the general definition of criminal conspiracy (Section 61), which require an overt act before becoming punishable, a conspiracy to wage war or to overawe Government under Section 148 is complete upon the bare agreement alone -- no act or illegal omission in pursuance of it need ever occur.
glossary.preparation to wage war against the Gove: Section 149 BNS: collecting men, arms, or ammunition, or otherwise preparing to wage war, with intention of either actually waging war or merely being prepared to do so, against the Government of India, punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine -- notably complete even where the offender has only readied themselves without a settled plan to attack.
glossary.concealment of a design to wage war: Section 150 BNS: concealing, by act or illegal omission, the existence of a known design to wage war against the Government of India, intending or knowing likely that the concealment will facilitate that war, punishable with up to ten years plus fine -- the State-security-specific counterpart to the general concealment-of-design offences in Sections 58-60.
glossary.assaulting the President or a Governor t: Section 151 BNS: assaulting, wrongfully restraining (or attempting to), or overawing by criminal force or its show (or attempting to), the President of India or a State Governor, with intention of inducing or compelling them to exercise or refrain from exercising any lawful power, punishable with up to seven years plus fine -- an elevated offence reflecting the constitutional-office status of the victim.
glossary.act endangering sovereignty unity and in: Section 152 BNS, the Sanhita's replacement for the former IPC's sedition provision (Section 124A): purposely or knowingly exciting or attempting to excite secession, armed rebellion, or subversive activities, or encouraging separatist feelings, or otherwise endangering India's sovereignty or unity and integrity, by words, signs, visible representation, electronic communication, or financial means -- punishable with life imprisonment or up to seven years plus fine, subject to an express lawful-dissent Explanation.
glossary.exciting secession or armed rebellion: The core prohibited conduct under Section 152 BNS: purposely or knowingly exciting, or attempting to excite, secession or armed rebellion or subversive activities against India, by any of the means listed in the section (words, signs, visible representation, electronic communication, or financial means) -- the central element distinguishing the modern offence from mere criticism of Government.
glossary.lawful-dissent exception to Section 152: The Explanation to Section 152 BNS: comments expressing disapprobation of Government measures or administrative action, made with a view to obtaining their alteration by lawful means, do not constitute an offence under this section, provided they do not excite or attempt to excite secession, armed rebellion, or subversive activities -- the key textual safeguard for critical political speech distinguishing lawful dissent from the punishable conduct.
glossary.waging war against a friendly foreign St: Section 153 BNS: waging war, attempting to wage war, or abetting the waging of war against the Government of any foreign State at peace with the Government of India, punishable with life imprisonment plus optional fine, up to seven years plus optional fine, or fine alone -- the 'at peace with India' qualifier is the operative condition limiting the section's reach.
glossary.depredation on a friendly foreign State': Section 154 BNS: committing, or merely preparing to commit, depredation (plundering or raiding) on the territory of a foreign State at peace with India, punishable with up to seven years plus fine, plus forfeiture of property used, intended to be used, or acquired by the depredation -- complete even at the mere-preparation stage.
glossary.forfeiture of depredation property: The additional punishment under Section 154 BNS stripping an offender of any property used, intended to be used in, or acquired by committing depredation on a friendly foreign State's territory, over and above the imprisonment and fine otherwise prescribed.
glossary.receiving property taken by war or depre: Section 155 BNS: knowingly receiving property taken in the commission of an offence under Section 153 (waging war against a friendly foreign State) or Section 154 (depredation on its territory), punishable with up to seven years plus fine, plus forfeiture of the property received -- the knowledge of the property's tainted origin is the essential mental element.
glossary.public servant voluntarily allowing a St: Section 156 BNS: a public servant having custody of a State prisoner or prisoner of war who voluntarily allows that prisoner to escape is punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine -- the deliberate nature of the lapse draws a far heavier punishment than the negligent version under Section 157.
glossary.public servant negligently suffering esc: Section 157 BNS, the negligence-based mirror of Section 156: a public servant who, through mere carelessness rather than voluntary conduct, allows a State prisoner or prisoner of war in their custody to escape is punishable with simple imprisonment up to three years plus fine -- a much lighter band reflecting the absence of deliberate facilitation.
glossary.aiding escape of a State prisoner or pri: One of four modes of outsider liability under Section 158 BNS: knowingly aiding or assisting a State prisoner or prisoner of war to escape from lawful custody, punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine -- applicable to any person, not just the public servant in direct custody.
glossary.harbouring an escaped State prisoner or: Another mode of liability under Section 158 BNS: harbouring or concealing a State prisoner or prisoner of war who has already escaped from lawful custody, carrying the same life-imprisonment-or-ten-years punishment as actively aiding the escape itself.
glossary.resisting recapture of an escaped prison: The fourth mode of liability under Section 158 BNS: offering or attempting to offer any resistance to the recapture of an escaped State prisoner or prisoner of war, punishable identically to aiding escape, rescuing, or harbouring such a prisoner under the same section.
glossary.parole limits as custody under Section 1: The Explanation to Section 158 BNS: a State prisoner or prisoner of war permitted to be at large on parole within certain limits in India is deemed to 'escape from lawful custody' if they go beyond those permitted limits -- extending the section's reach to anyone who then harbours or aids such a parolee who has strayed outside their geographic bounds.
glossary.collecting arms or men to wage war: A shorthand for the preparatory conduct criminalised under Section 149 BNS -- collecting men, arms, or ammunition, or otherwise preparing to wage war against the Government of India, with the intention of waging war or merely being prepared to do so.
glossary.abetting mutiny: The first limb of Section 159 BNS: abetting the committing of mutiny by an officer, soldier, sailor, or airman of the Army, Navy, or Air Force of the Government of India, punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine regardless of whether the mutiny actually results -- escalated to death-or-life exposure under Section 160 if mutiny is in fact committed in consequence.
glossary.seducing a soldier sailor or airman from: The second limb of Section 159 BNS: attempting to seduce an officer, soldier, sailor, or airman from his allegiance or duty to the Government of India's Army, Navy, or Air Force, carrying the same life-imprisonment-or-ten-years punishment as abetting mutiny under the same section, complete upon the attempt itself without any further consequence required.
glossary.abetment of mutiny resulting in actual m: Section 160 BNS: the consequence-triggered escalation of Section 159 -- where mutiny is actually committed in consequence of the abetment, the abettor's punishment rises to death or life imprisonment, or up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine, mirroring the Sanhita's broader pattern of doubling an abettor's exposure once the abetted offence actually materialises.
glossary.abetment of assault on a superior office: Section 161 BNS: abetting an assault by an officer, soldier, sailor, or airman on a superior officer who is in the execution of his office, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment plus fine irrespective of whether the assault actually occurs -- escalated under Section 162 if the assault is in fact committed.
glossary.abetment of assault on superior officer: Section 162 BNS: the consequence-triggered escalation of Section 161 -- where the abetted assault on a superior officer in execution of office is actually committed, the abettor's maximum punishment rises from three years to up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine.
glossary.abetment of desertion: Section 163 BNS: abetting the desertion of any officer, soldier, sailor, or airman of the Army, Navy, or Air Force, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- the lightest punishment band among the Chapter VIII abetment offences, reflecting desertion's comparatively lower gravity relative to mutiny or assault on a superior officer.
glossary.harbouring a deserter: Section 164 BNS: knowingly or with reason to believe that a person has deserted from the Army, Navy, or Air Force, harbouring that deserter, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both, subject to the spousal exception that removes liability where the harbourer is the deserter's own spouse.
glossary.spousal exception to harbouring a desert: The Exception to Section 164 BNS: the harbouring-deserter offence does not extend to harbour given by the spouse of the deserter -- a recurring carve-out across the Sanhita's harbouring-type offences (compare Sections 111 and 113) that recognises the practical reality of spousal cohabitation.
glossary.negligent concealment of a deserter on a: Section 165 BNS: an unusual strict, negligence-based penalty of up to three thousand rupees on the master or person in charge of a merchant vessel aboard which a deserter is concealed, even if actually ignorant of the concealment, where that ignorance stems from the master's own neglect of duty or a want of discipline on board -- notable for imposing only a monetary penalty, not imprisonment, and for attaching liability on a constructive-knowledge basis.
glossary.abetment of insubordination: Section 166 BNS: knowingly abetting an act of insubordination by a member of the Army, Navy, or Air Force, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both, but only where the insubordination is actually committed in consequence of the abetment -- unlike mutiny and assault-on-superior abetment, there is no lesser outcome-independent counterpart for insubordination.
glossary.savings clause for the special military: Section 167 BNS: a jurisdiction-clearing provision stating that persons subject to the Air Force Act 1950, the Army Act 1950, or the Navy Act 1957 are not liable to punishment under the Sanhita for any offence defined in Chapter VIII, preventing double jeopardy between the Sanhita's general military-offence provisions and the special service-specific military codes -- the Chapter-specific reinforcement of the mutiny/desertion savings clause already found in Section 1(6).
glossary.impersonating a soldier sailor or airman: Section 168 BNS, closing Chapter VIII: a civilian who wears a garb or carries a token resembling that used by a soldier, sailor, or airman, with the intention that it be believed they are such a person, is punishable with up to three months' imprisonment, fine up to two thousand rupees, or both -- the specific intention to deceive observers into believing genuine service status distinguishes this from innocent costume-wearing.
glossary.candidate (election offences definition): Defined in Section 169(a) BNS, opening Chapter IX, as a person who has been nominated as a candidate at any election -- the threshold status that triggers the protections and offences built around candidates throughout the Chapter (bribery, undue influence, personation, false statements, illegal payments).
glossary.electoral right: Defined in Section 169(b) BNS as the right of a person to stand, or not to stand as, or to withdraw from being, a candidate, or to vote or refrain from voting at an election -- the core interest that Chapter IX's bribery and undue-influence offences protect from interference or corrupt inducement.
glossary.bribery at an election: Section 170 BNS: giving a gratification to induce or reward the exercise of an electoral right, or accepting a gratification as a reward for exercising or inducing the exercise of such a right -- punishable under Section 173 with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both, subject to the treating proviso and the public-policy declaration carve-out.
glossary.gratification deemed given: Section 170(2) BNS: a person who merely offers, agrees to give, or offers or attempts to procure a gratification is deemed to have given it -- extending bribery liability on the giving side to the offer or attempt stage without requiring actual delivery of the gratification.
glossary.gratification deemed accepted: Section 170(3) BNS: a person who obtains, agrees to accept, or attempts to obtain a gratification is deemed to have accepted it, and accepting as a motive for conduct not intended or as a reward for conduct not performed is deemed acceptance as a reward -- extending bribery liability on the receiving side to agreements and attempts.
glossary.public-policy declaration carve-out: The proviso to Section 170 BNS: a declaration of public policy or a promise of public action is not an offence of bribery -- protecting ordinary campaign promises and policy platforms from being mischaracterised as corrupt inducements under the election-bribery offence.
glossary.undue influence at an election: Section 171 BNS: voluntarily interfering, or attempting to interfere, with the free exercise of any electoral right, punishable under Section 174 with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both -- illustrated (non-exhaustively) by threats of injury and threats of Divine displeasure or spiritual censure under sub-section (2).
glossary.threat of injury to a candidate or voter: One of the two deemed forms of undue influence under Section 171(2)(a) BNS: threatening a candidate, voter, or any person in whom either is interested, with injury of any kind, is deemed to interfere with the free exercise of that candidate's or voter's electoral right.
glossary.spiritual or divine-displeasure threats: The second deemed form of undue influence under Section 171(2)(b) BNS: inducing or attempting to induce a candidate or voter to believe that they or someone they care about will become an object of Divine displeasure or spiritual censure, deemed to interfere with the free exercise of the electoral right.
glossary.personation at an election: Section 172 BNS: applying for a voting paper in the name of another person (living or dead) or a fictitious name, voting a second time in one's own name at the same election, or abetting/procuring any such fraudulent voting, punishable under Section 174 with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both, subject to the proxy-voting carve-out.
glossary.proxy-voting carve-out from personation: The proviso to Section 172 BNS: the personation offence does not apply to a person lawfully authorised to vote as proxy for an elector, so far as that person votes strictly as the authorised proxy for that elector.
glossary.punishment for bribery at an election: Section 173 BNS: fixes the punishment for Section 170 bribery at up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both, with bribery by treating punished by fine only under the section's proviso.
glossary.bribery by treating: The Explanation to Section 173 BNS: 'treating' is that form of election bribery where the gratification consists in food, drink, entertainment, or provision, and under the section's proviso is punishable by fine only, not imprisonment -- a lighter band than ordinary bribery.
glossary.punishment for undue influence or person: Section 174 BNS: fixes a single, identical punishment of up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both, for both undue influence (Section 171) and personation (Section 172) at an election.
glossary.false statement about a candidate's pers: Section 175 BNS: making or publishing, with intent to affect an election's result, a statement of fact about a candidate's personal character or conduct known or believed to be false, or not believed to be true, punishable with fine only -- a narrow electoral-context, intent-and-falsity-specific offence distinct from genuine policy criticism.
glossary.illegal election expenses without candid: Section 176 BNS: incurring or authorising expenses for promoting or procuring a candidate's election (public meetings, advertisements, circulars, publications, or otherwise) without that candidate's general or special written authority, punishable with fine up to ten thousand rupees.
glossary.retrospective approval of small election: The proviso to Section 176 BNS: unauthorised election expenses not exceeding ten rupees are deemed to have been incurred with the candidate's authority if the candidate gives written approval within ten days of the expense being incurred -- a narrow safety valve for small, good-faith campaign spending.
glossary.failure to keep election expense account: Section 177 BNS, closing Chapter IX: failing to keep accounts of election-related expenses where required to do so by law or a rule having the force of law, punishable with fine up to five thousand rupees -- a pure recordkeeping offence tied to an external statutory duty, typically under election law.
glossary.counterfeiting coin: Defined in the Explanation to Section 178 BNS: causing a genuine coin to appear like a different coin, intending or knowing it likely that deception will be practised thereby -- expressly extended to include diminishing a coin's weight or altering its composition or appearance, not just creating an outright fake. Punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine.
glossary.counterfeiting Government stamp: Defined in the Explanation to Section 178 BNS: counterfeiting by causing a genuine Government revenue stamp of one denomination to appear like a genuine stamp of a different denomination -- punishable, together with coin, currency-note, and bank-note counterfeiting, with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine.
glossary.bank-note (BNS definition): Defined in the Explanation to Section 178 BNS as a promissory note or engagement for payment of money to bearer on demand, issued by any banking business anywhere in the world, or by or under the authority of any State or Sovereign Power, intended to be used as equivalent to or a substitute for money.
glossary.coin (BNS definition): Section 178 BNS's Explanation gives 'coin' the same meaning as section 2 of the Coinage Act, 2011, and includes metal currently used as money, stamped and issued by or under the authority of any State or Sovereign Power intended to be so used.
glossary.using forged or counterfeit currency as: Section 179 BNS: importing, exporting, selling, delivering, buying, receiving, trafficking in, or otherwise using as genuine, any forged or counterfeit coin, stamp, currency-note, or bank-note, knowing or having reason to believe it is forged or counterfeit -- punishable identically to counterfeiting itself, with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine.
glossary.trafficking in forged or counterfeit coi: A shorthand for the full scope of dealing-conduct criminalised under Section 179 BNS -- importing, exporting, buying, selling, delivering, or receiving forged or counterfeit coin, stamps, currency-notes, or bank-notes, knowing or having reason to believe they are forged or counterfeit.
glossary.possession of forged or counterfeit curr: Section 180 BNS: possessing forged or counterfeit coin, stamp, currency-note, or bank-note, knowing or having reason to believe it is forged, with intent to use it or allow its use as genuine, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- subject to the lawful-source defence.
glossary.lawful-source defence to possession of c: The Explanation to Section 180 BNS: if a person establishes that their possession of forged or counterfeit coin, stamp, currency-note, or bank-note is from a lawful source, no offence under that section is constituted -- a complete defence once possession and the forged/counterfeit character are shown.
glossary.making or possessing counterfeiting inst: Section 181 BNS: making, mending, buying, selling, disposing of, or possessing any machinery, die, instrument, or material intended, or known/believed to be intended, for forging or counterfeiting coin, Government revenue stamps, currency-notes, or bank-notes, punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine -- the same maximum punishment as actual counterfeiting under Section 178.
glossary.document resembling a currency-note or b: Section 182(1) BNS: making, causing to be made, using, or delivering any document purporting to be, or so nearly resembling as to be calculated to deceive, a currency-note or bank-note, punishable with fine up to three hundred rupees -- a lesser, deception-adjacent offence distinct from true counterfeiting under Section 178.
glossary.refusal to disclose maker of a currency-: Section 182(2) BNS: a person named on a document whose making is an offence under Section 182(1) who refuses, without lawful excuse, to disclose to a police officer the name and address of who printed or made it, is punishable with fine up to six hundred rupees -- a heavier fine than the underlying document offence itself.
glossary.presumption of causing a currency-resemb: Section 182(3) BNS: where a person's name appears on a document charged under Section 182(1), or on any other document used or distributed in connection with it, it may be presumed, until the contrary is proved, that the person caused the document to be made -- a rebuttable evidentiary presumption shifting the practical burden to the named person.
glossary.effacing writing from a Government-stamp: Section 183 BNS: fraudulently or with intent to cause loss to Government, removing or effacing from a substance bearing a Government revenue stamp the writing or document for which the stamp was used, so the stamp can be reused for a different writing or document, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.removing a used Government stamp to reus: The second limb of Section 183 BNS: fraudulently or with intent to cause Government loss, removing from a writing or document a Government revenue stamp that has been used for it, in order that the stamp may be used for a different writing or document -- part of the same three-year-maximum offence as effacing the underlying writing.
glossary.using a previously used Government reven: Section 184 BNS: fraudulently or with intent to cause Government loss, using for any purpose a Government revenue stamp known to have been used before, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- the completion offence to Section 183's stamp-detachment conduct.
glossary.erasing the used-mark from a Government: Section 185 BNS: fraudulently or with intent to cause Government loss, erasing or removing from a Government revenue stamp the mark denoting it has been used, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- the evidence-destruction limb completing the Sections 183-185 stamp-reuse fraud chain.
glossary.possessing or dealing in a stamp with it: The second and third limbs of Section 185 BNS: knowingly possessing, selling, or disposing of a Government revenue stamp from which the used-denoting mark has been erased or removed, or selling or disposing of any such stamp known to have been used -- carrying the same up-to-three-years punishment as the erasure itself.
glossary.fictitious stamp: Defined in Section 186(3) BNS as any stamp falsely purporting to be issued by Government to denote a rate of postage, or any facsimile, imitation, or representation of a Government postage stamp -- making, uttering, dealing in, selling, using, or possessing one without lawful excuse is punishable with fine up to two hundred rupees under Section 186(1).
glossary.forfeiture of fictitious-stamp-making ma: Section 186(2) BNS: any fictitious stamp, die, plate, instrument, or material found in a person's possession for making a fictitious stamp may be seized and, if seized, shall be forfeited -- an automatic forfeiture consequence alongside the fine-only punishment under Section 186(1).
glossary.extended meaning of Government for posta: Section 186(4) BNS: for postage-stamp purposes across Sections 178-181 and 183-185, 'Government' is deemed to include whoever is authorised by law to administer executive government anywhere in India or in any foreign country, notwithstanding the Sanhita's general Section 2(12) definition -- recognising the often cross-border character of postal stamp fraud.
glossary.mint employee causing coin of wrongful w: Section 187 BNS: a person employed in a lawfully established Indian mint who does, or omits a legally required, act with the intention of causing coin issued from that mint to deviate from its legally fixed weight or composition, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine -- an insider-sabotage offence distinct from the general counterfeiting provisions.
glossary.unlawfully taking a coining instrument f: Section 188 BNS, closing Chapter X: taking any coining tool or instrument out of a lawfully established Indian mint without lawful authority, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine -- complete on the unauthorised removal alone, with no need to prove any intended counterfeiting use of the tool.
glossary.unlawful assembly: Defined in Section 189(1) BNS as an assembly of five or more persons whose common object falls within five categories: overawing government by criminal force, resisting execution of law, committing mischief/criminal trespass/an offence, forcibly taking property or rights, or compelling illegal conduct -- the foundational concept for the whole Chapter XI public-tranquillity offence cluster.
glossary.membership of an unlawful assembly: Section 189(2) BNS: being aware of the facts that render an assembly unlawful and intentionally joining or continuing in it, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, fine, or both -- the base liability tier, escalated under sub-section (3) if the member joins or continues after a lawful dispersal order.
glossary.armed member of an unlawful assembly: Section 189(4) BNS: being a member of an unlawful assembly while armed with a deadly weapon, or anything likely to cause death if used as a weapon, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- the same armed-escalation pattern recurs for rioting under Section 191(3).
glossary.hiring persons to join an unlawful assem: Section 189(6) BNS: hiring, engaging, employing, promoting, or conniving at the hiring/engagement/employment of any person to join or become a member of an unlawful assembly -- punishable as a member of that assembly, and as if personally responsible for any offence committed by the hired person as a member pursuant to that hiring.
glossary.harbouring persons hired for an unlawful: Section 189(7) BNS: harbouring, receiving, or assembling, in premises under one's occupation, charge, or control, persons known to have been or about to be hired, engaged, or employed to join an unlawful assembly, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.constructive liability of unlawful assem: Section 190 BNS: if an offence is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object, or as members knew likely in prosecution of that object, every person who was a member at the time is guilty of that offence -- a powerful vicarious-liability rule requiring no proof of individual participation in the specific act, only membership at the critical moment.
glossary.rioting: Section 191(1) BNS: the offence committed by every member of an unlawful assembly, or any member of it, the moment force or violence is used in prosecution of the common object -- punishable under Section 191(2) with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.rioting armed with a deadly weapon: Section 191(3) BNS: the aggravated form of rioting committed while armed with a deadly weapon, or anything likely to cause death if used as a weapon, punishable with up to five years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- more than double the base rioting punishment.
glossary.wantonly provoking a riot: Section 192 BNS: malignantly, or wantonly through illegal conduct, provoking a person intending or knowing it likely that rioting will result, punishable with up to one year if rioting actually follows, or up to six months if it does not -- a consequence-triggered escalation mirroring the Sanhita's abetment-escalation pattern elsewhere.
glossary.liability of landowner for unlawful asse: Section 193(1) BNS: a fine up to one thousand rupees on an owner, occupier, or interest-holder in land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes place, who, knowing of or having reason to believe in it, fails to notify the nearest police station and fails to use all lawful means to prevent or suppress it -- an omission-based offence, not liability for the riot itself.
glossary.liability of riot beneficiary: Section 193(2) BNS: a fine on a person for whose benefit or on whose behalf a riot is committed (typically a land interest-holder or party to the underlying dispute) who, having reason to believe the riot or the unlawful assembly behind it was likely, fails to use all lawful means to prevent or suppress it.
glossary.liability of agent or manager for riot b: Section 193(3) BNS: the parallel fine liability imposed on the agent or manager of a riot beneficiary under Section 193(2), where that agent or manager, having reason to believe the riot or unlawful assembly was likely, fails to use all lawful means to prevent or suppress it.
glossary.affray: Defined in Section 194(1) BNS as two or more persons fighting in a public place in a manner that disturbs the public peace, punishable under Section 194(2) with up to one month's imprisonment, fine up to one thousand rupees, or both -- the lightest public-order offence in Chapter XI, requiring no prior unlawful assembly or common object.
glossary.assaulting or obstructing a public serva: Section 195(1) BNS: assaulting, obstructing, or using criminal force on a public servant discharging duty to disperse an unlawful assembly or suppress a riot or affray, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment plus a mandatory minimum fine of twenty-five thousand rupees.
glossary.threatening or attempting to obstruct a: Section 195(2) BNS: the lesser-punished attempt/threat version of Section 195(1) -- threatening to assault, or attempting to obstruct or use criminal force on, a public servant engaged in dispersing an unlawful assembly or suppressing a riot/affray, punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.promoting enmity between groups: Section 196(1)(a) BNS: promoting or attempting to promote, through any medium (spoken/written words, signs, visible representations, or electronic communication), disharmony or feelings of enmity, hatred, or ill-will between groups defined by religion, race, birthplace, residence, language, caste, community, or any other ground -- punishable with up to three years, escalated to up to five years plus fine if committed in a place of worship.
glossary.acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmo: Section 196(1)(b) BNS: committing any act prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony between religious, racial, language, or regional groups, castes, or communities, which disturbs or is likely to disturb public tranquillity -- the second limb of the Section 196 group-harmony offence.
glossary.organising or participating in paramilit: Section 196(1)(c) BNS: organising or participating in a drill, exercise, movement, or similar activity intended, or known likely, to train participants to use criminal force or violence against a religious, racial, language, regional, caste, or community group, where the activity causes or is likely to cause fear, alarm, or insecurity among that group's members.
glossary.offence committed in a place of worship: Section 196(2) BNS: committing any offence under Section 196(1) in a place of worship, or in an assembly engaged in religious worship or ceremonies, escalates the punishment to up to five years' imprisonment plus mandatory fine -- the same place-of-worship enhancement structure recurs in Section 197(2) for the national-integration offence.
glossary.imputation of disloyalty against a class: Section 197(1)(a) BNS: making or publishing an imputation that a class of persons cannot, by reason of their religious, racial, language, regional, caste, or community membership, bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution or uphold India's sovereignty and integrity, punishable with up to three years, escalated to five years plus fine in a place of worship.
glossary.denial of citizenship rights on group gr: Section 197(1)(b) BNS: asserting, counselling, advising, propagating, or publishing that a class of persons should, by reason of group membership (religion, race, language, region, caste, community), be denied or deprived of their rights as citizens of India.
glossary.assertion of group obligation causing di: Section 197(1)(c) BNS: making or publishing an assertion, counsel, plea, or appeal about the obligations of a class of persons by reason of their group membership, where it causes or is likely to cause disharmony, enmity, hatred, or ill-will between that class and others.
glossary.false or misleading information jeopardi: Section 197(1)(d) BNS: making or publishing false or misleading information that jeopardises the sovereignty, unity, integrity, or security of India -- a disinformation-specific limb with no direct IPC equivalent, read alongside Section 152's sedition-replacement offence but without a comparably developed lawful-dissent boundary.
glossary.public servant knowingly disobeying a le: Section 198 BNS, opening Chapter XII: a public servant who knowingly disobeys a legal direction governing their official conduct, intending or knowing it likely to cause injury to any person, is punishable with up to one year's simple imprisonment, fine, or both -- the general catch-all public-servant misconduct offence, illustrated by an execution officer who knowingly flouts the legal procedure for seizing property to a decree-holder's detriment.
glossary.public servant unlawfully compelling att: Section 199(a) BNS: a public servant who knowingly disobeys a legal prohibition against requiring a person's attendance at a place for investigation into an offence or other matter, punishable with a mandatory minimum of six months' rigorous imprisonment up to two years, plus fine.
glossary.public servant violating investigation p: Section 199(b) BNS: a public servant who knowingly disobeys, to a person's prejudice, any other legal direction regulating how an investigation must be conducted, carrying the same mandatory-minimum six-months-to-two-years rigorous imprisonment plus fine as the other limbs of Section 199.
glossary.public servant failing to record cogniza: Section 199(c) BNS: a public servant who fails to record information given under BNSS Section 173(1) relating to specified cognizable offences (including sexual offences, acid attacks, and trafficking-related provisions under BNS Sections 64-79, 124, 143, and 144), punishable with a mandatory minimum six months' rigorous imprisonment up to two years, plus fine -- an accountability mechanism against suppression of serious complaints at the police-station stage.
glossary.non-treatment of victim by a hospital in: Section 200 BNS: a person in charge of any hospital, public or private, who contravenes BNSS Section 397's requirement to provide immediate free treatment to victims of specified offences, punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both -- the penal backstop ensuring hospitals cannot lawfully refuse emergency treatment to such victims.
glossary.public servant framing an incorrect docu: Section 201 BNS: a public servant charged with preparing or translating a document or electronic record who deliberately frames, prepares, or translates it in a manner known or believed to be incorrect, intending or knowing it likely to cause injury to any person, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.public servant unlawfully engaging in tr: Section 202 BNS: a public servant legally bound by the terms of office not to engage in trade who does so anyway, punishable with up to one year's simple imprisonment, fine, or both, or with community service -- one of the few BNS offences expressly offering community service as an alternative sentence, reflecting its administrative, non-violent character.
glossary.public servant unlawfully purchasing or: Section 203 BNS: a public servant legally bound not to purchase or bid for certain property (typically property connected to their official duties) who does so anyway, whether in their own name, another's name, jointly, or in shares, punishable with up to two years' simple imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.confiscation of property unlawfully purc: The mandatory consequence attached to Section 203 BNS: if the public servant actually completes the unlawful purchase, the property itself shall be confiscated, over and above the imprisonment or fine imposed on the offender personally.
glossary.personating a public servant: Section 204 BNS: falsely pretending to hold a particular public-servant office one does not hold, or falsely personating a specific person who does hold such office, and going on to do or attempt an act under colour of that assumed office, punishable with a mandatory minimum six months' up to three years' imprisonment plus fine.
glossary.wearing garb or carrying a token of a pu: Section 205 BNS, closing Chapter XII: wearing a garb or carrying a token resembling that used by a particular class of public servants, with intention or knowledge that it is likely to be believed the wearer belongs to that class, punishable with up to three months' imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both -- the general public-servant counterpart to Section 168's military-impersonation offence.
glossary.absconding to avoid service of summons: Section 206 BNS, opening Chapter XIII: deliberately absconding to avoid being served with a summons, notice, or order from a competent public servant, punishable with up to one month's simple imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees, escalated under limb (b) to up to six months plus fine up to ten thousand rupees where the dodged process required attendance or document production in a Court.
glossary.tiered punishment for court-summons absc: The recurring two-band punishment structure used across much of Chapter XIII BNS: a lighter general punishment for contempt-adjacent conduct directed at non-Court public-servant process, and a heavier punishment reserved specifically for conduct touching a Court's own summons, notice, order, or document-production requirement.
glossary.preventing service of summons notice or: The first limb of Section 207 BNS: intentionally preventing the serving, on oneself or any other person, of a summons, notice, or order from a public servant legally competent to issue it -- punishable under the same one-month/six-month tiered structure as Section 206.
glossary.removing an affixed summons or notice: A further limb of Section 207 BNS: intentionally removing a summons, notice, or order from a place to which it has been lawfully affixed, treated identically to preventing its service or its lawful affixing in the first place.
glossary.preventing publication of a proclamation: The final limb of Section 207 BNS: intentionally preventing the lawful making of a proclamation directed under the authority of a public servant legally competent to direct it -- part of the same offence covering sabotage of service, affixing, and proclamation of official process.
glossary.non-attendance in obedience to a public: Section 208 BNS: intentionally omitting to attend at a place and time one is legally bound to attend per a summons, notice, order, or proclamation, punishable with up to one month (escalated to six months for Court attendance) -- illustrated by witnesses who simply fail to appear before a High Court or a District Judge.
glossary.premature departure from a place of requ: The second limb of Section 208 BNS: departing from a place of required attendance before the time at which it is lawful to depart, punished identically to outright non-attendance under the same section.
glossary.non-appearance under a BNSS Section 84 p: Section 209 BNS: failing to appear at the place and time specified in a proclamation published under BNSS Section 84(1) (the procedure for proclaiming a person absconding to avoid arrest), punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or community service.
glossary.proclaimed offender punishment escalatio: Section 209 BNS's heavier tier: where a declaration under BNSS Section 84(4) has pronounced the non-appearing person a 'proclaimed offender,' the punishment for non-appearance escalates sharply to up to seven years' imprisonment plus mandatory fine.
glossary.omission to produce a document or electr: Section 210 BNS: intentionally omitting to produce or deliver up a document or electronic record one is legally bound to produce to a public servant, punishable with up to one month (escalated to six months where the document was owed to a Court) -- the 'electronic record' language extends the duty to digital files, not just physical documents.
glossary.omission to give notice or information t: Section 211 BNS: intentionally omitting to give notice or furnish information one is legally bound to give to a public servant, in the manner and time required by law, with a three-tier punishment structure escalating where the withheld information concerns an offence's commission, prevention, or an offender's apprehension, or is required by a BNSS Section 394 order.
glossary.offence-related information withholding: The limb (b) escalation of Section 211 BNS: where the notice or information a person is legally bound to give concerns the commission of an offence, is required to prevent an offence, or is required to apprehend an offender, the omission to give it draws up to six months' imprisonment rather than the base one-month band.
glossary.BNSS Section 394 order non-compliance: The limb (c) tier of Section 211 BNS: failing to give notice or information specifically required by an order passed under BNSS Section 394, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, or fine up to one thousand rupees, or both.
glossary.furnishing false information to a public: Section 212 BNS: the active-falsehood counterpart to Section 211 -- furnishing, as true, information to a public servant one is legally bound to inform, knowing or having reason to believe it false, punishable with up to six months (escalated to two years where the false information concerns an offence's commission, prevention, or an offender's apprehension).
glossary.extraterritorial offence and offender fo: The shared Explanation to Section 212 BNS: for both Sections 211 and 212, 'offence' is extended to include specified acts committed outside India that would be punishable under BNS Sections 103, 105, 307, 309(2)-(4), 310(2)-(5), 311, 312, 326(f)-(g), 331(4)(6)-(8), and 332(a)-(b) if committed in India, and 'offender' is extended to anyone merely alleged to have committed such an act.
glossary.refusing an oath or affirmation when dul: Section 213 BNS: refusing to bind oneself by an oath or affirmation to state the truth when lawfully required to do so by a competent public servant, punishable with up to six months' simple imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both -- the foundational offence underlying Sections 214-216's truth-telling duties.
glossary.refusing to answer a public servant's la: Section 214 BNS: refusing to answer a question lawfully demanded by a public servant in exercise of their legal powers, where the person is legally bound to state the truth on that subject, punishable identically to oath-refusal under Section 213.
glossary.refusing to sign a statement: Section 215 BNS: refusing to sign one's own statement when lawfully required to do so by a competent public servant, punishable with up to three months' imprisonment, fine up to three thousand rupees, or both -- the lightest of the Sections 213-215 non-cooperation offences.
glossary.false statement on oath or affirmation t: Section 216 BNS: making a statement known or believed false, or not believed true, while legally bound by oath or affirmation to state the truth to a public servant or other legally authorised administrator, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment plus mandatory fine -- the Chapter XIII sibling of Section 227's judicial-proceeding false-evidence offence.
