glossary.false information intended to misuse a p: Section 217 BNS: giving a public servant information known or believed false, intending or knowing it likely to cause that public servant to act wrongly or to misuse their lawful power to someone's injury or annoyance, punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both.
glossary.false information causing wrongful dismi: The illustrative scenarios under Section 217 BNS: a false neglect-of-duty complaint engineered to get a subordinate officer dismissed, and a false contraband tip engineered to trigger an annoying search of someone's premises -- both captured as examples of misusing a public servant's lawful power through deliberate falsehood.
glossary.resistance to lawful taking of property: Section 218 BNS: offering resistance to the taking of property under the lawful authority of a public servant, knowing or having reason to believe the taker is such a public servant, punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both.
glossary.obstructing a sale of property conducted: Section 219 BNS: intentionally obstructing a sale of property offered for sale under a public servant's lawful authority, punishable with up to one month's imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both -- a lighter offence than Section 218's resistance-to-taking.
glossary.illegal purchase or bid at a lawful publ: Section 220 BNS: purchasing or bidding at a public-servant-authority sale on account of a person known to be legally incapable of purchasing at that sale, punishable with up to one month's imprisonment, fine up to two hundred rupees, or both.
glossary.sham bidding without intent to perform: The second limb of Section 220 BNS: bidding for property at a lawful public-servant sale without any genuine intention of performing the obligations the bid creates, punished identically to bidding on behalf of a legally incapable purchaser.
glossary.obstructing a public servant in discharg: Section 221 BNS: the general-purpose obstruction offence -- voluntarily obstructing a public servant while they discharge their public functions, punishable with up to three months' imprisonment, fine up to two thousand five hundred rupees, or both.
glossary.omission to assist a public servant when: Section 222 BNS: intentionally omitting to render assistance to a public servant in execution of public duty, where legally bound to furnish it, punishable with up to one month (escalated to six months where the assistance was demanded for Court-process execution, offence prevention, riot/affray suppression, or apprehending an offender or escapee).
glossary.refusal of posse comitatus-style assista: A description of Section 222 BNS's underlying rationale: the modern statutory equivalent of the common-law duty of ordinary citizens to assist public authority when lawfully called upon, with refusal in serious circumstances (riot suppression, apprehending escapees) drawing the heavier six-month punishment band.
glossary.disobedience to a lawfully promulgated p: Section 223 BNS: knowing disobedience of a lawfully promulgated public-servant order directing abstention from an act or specified property handling, punishable with up to six months where the disobedience causes or risks obstruction/annoyance/injury to a lawfully employed person, escalating to up to one year where it causes or risks danger to life, health, safety, or a riot/affray.
glossary.no-intent-to-harm requirement for order: The Explanation to Section 223 BNS: liability does not require intent to produce harm or contemplation that disobedience is likely to produce harm -- mere knowledge of the order plus disobedience that produces or is likely to produce harm suffices, a comparatively strict liability standard within the Sanhita.
glossary.threat of injury to a public servant to: Section 224 BNS: holding out a threat of injury to a public servant, or to a person believed to interest that public servant, for the purpose of inducing them to act, forbear, or delay in their public functions, punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
glossary.threat to deter a legal application for: Section 225 BNS: holding out a threat of injury to a person to induce them to refrain from, or abandon, a legal application for protection to a public servant empowered to give it, punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both -- an access-to-justice protection complementing Section 224.
glossary.attempt to commit suicide to compel or r: Section 226 BNS, closing Chapter XIII: attempting suicide with intent to compel or restrain a public servant from discharging official duty, punishable with up to one year's simple imprisonment, fine, or both, or with community service.

sections.title: Short title, commencement and application
sections.raw_text:
(1) This Act may be called the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
(2) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint, and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Sanhita.
(3) Every person shall be liable to punishment under this Sanhita and not otherwise for every act or omission contrary to the provisions thereof, of which he shall be guilty within India.
(4) Any person liable, by any law for the time being in force in India, to be tried for an offence committed beyond India shall be dealt with according to the provisions of this Sanhita for any act committed beyond India in the same manner as if such act had been committed within India.
(5) The provisions of this Sanhita shall also apply to any offence committed by—
(a) any citizen of India in any place without and beyond India;
(b) any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be;
(c) any person in any place without and beyond India committing offence targeting a computer resource located in India.
Explanation.—In this section, the word “offence” includes every act committed outside India which, if committed in India, would be punishable under this Sanhita.
Illustration.—A, who is a citizen of India, commits a murder in any place without and beyond India. He can be tried and convicted of murder in any place in India in which he may be found.
(6) Nothing in this Sanhita shall affect the provisions of any Act for punishing mutiny and desertion of officers, soldiers, sailors or airmen in the service of the Government of India or the provisions of any special or local law.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 1 is the Sanhita's opening gateway clause: it names the Act, hands the Central Government a notification-based switch to bring different provisions into force on different dates rather than all at once, lays down the basic rule that criminal liability in India flows only from this Sanhita (not any residual common-law notion of crime), and then extends that liability outward to Indian citizens abroad, to anyone on an Indian-registered ship or aircraft anywhere in the world, and — reflecting a problem the 1860 Penal Code never had to address — to anyone sitting outside India who targets a computer resource located inside India. A closing savings clause keeps military mutiny/desertion law and other special or local laws untouched.
essential_elements: Clause (1): fixes the short title as 'the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023'
Clause (2): staggered-commencement power — the Central Government may notify different dates for different provisions, not necessarily one single commencement date for the whole Sanhita
Clause (3): the core territorial principle — liability for acts/omissions within India arises under this Sanhita 'and not otherwise'
Clause (4): extraterritorial offences are tried exactly as if committed within India

Clause (5): three specific extraterritorial hooks — (a) Indian citizens anywhere abroad, (b) anyone on an Indian-registered ship or aircraft, (c) anyone abroad who targets a computer resource located in India
Clause (6): preserves military mutiny/desertion legislation and other special or local laws from being displaced by this Sanhita's general scheme
exceptions_and_qualifications: The extraterritorial clause (5)(c) targeting a computer resource located in India is a new addition with no equivalent in the old Indian Penal Code, 1860 — it is the hook used to prosecute cross-border cyber-offences

Clause (6) is a savings/non-obstante-style carve-out, not a substantive exception to who is liable — it only confirms this Sanhita does not override military discipline law or other special/local statutes

Because commencement can be staggered under clause (2), different BNS sections can theoretically take effect on different notified dates even though the Sanhita as a whole was brought into force in a single notification
breakdown.how_to_read: Read clause (5) as the extraterritorial reach provision — in practice its sub-clause (c) is the one practitioners cite for cross-border cyber-crime jurisdiction. Clause (6) should never be read as narrowing the Sanhita's own scope; it is purely a non-displacement clause protecting other statutes.

sections.title: Definitions

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 2 is the Sanhita's master glossary — 39 numbered clauses defining the vocabulary every later offence-definition relies on. Most carry forward almost word-for-word from the old Indian Penal Code's Section 8 to Section 52A (dishonestly, fraudulently, document, voluntarily, public servant, valuable security, and so on), so decades of IPC case law construing these exact phrases remains directly relevant. A few are updated or new: 'document' now expressly includes electronic and digital records, 'gender' is defined by cross-reference to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, and clause (39) imports any term the Sanhita itself leaves undefined from the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (the companion criminal-procedure code).
essential_elements: Clauses (1)-(39) each define a single term or term-pair used throughout the Sanhita's substantive offence provisions
Clause (8) 'document' is explicitly widened beyond paper to include electronic and digital records — a change from the undiluted IPC-era definition

Clause (24) 'offence' has a split meaning: the default sense (punishable only under this Sanhita) is overridden for an enumerated list of sections, where 'offence' instead reaches conduct punishable under any special or local law too

Clause (28) 'public servant' is an exhaustive ten-category list (commissioned officers, Judges, Court officers, panchayat members, arbitrators, confinement-empowered officers, law-enforcement officers, revenue/pecuniary officers, local-rights officers, election officials, and government-service personnel) plus two deeming Explanations
Clause (39) is a residual cross-reference clause pulling in undefined terms from the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (24)'s 'offence' definition is itself subject to two carve-outs (sub-clauses (a) and (b)) listing dozens of specific sections where the narrower IPC-style meaning does not apply — always check whether the section you are working with appears on either list before assuming the default definition governs

Clause (28)(k)(ii)'s 'public servant' extension to local-authority and government-company employees depends on cross-referenced definitions in the General Clauses Act, 1897 and the Companies Act, 2013, so confirming public-servant status for such an employee requires checking those external definitions too

Because most definitions reproduce IPC wording verbatim, pre-2024 Supreme Court and High Court judgments interpreting the identical IPC phrase remain persuasive (often binding) authority for the BNS equivalent
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this section as a lookup table, not a provision to memorise wholesale — when an offence section uses a defined term in quotation marks, cross-check its exact clause here first, since several terms (especially 'offence', 'document', and 'public servant') carry carve-outs or extensions that change the outcome of a case.

sections.title: General explanations
sections.raw_text:
(1) Throughout this Sanhita every definition of an offence, every penal provision, and every Illustration of every such definition or penal provision, shall be understood subject to the exceptions contained in the Chapter entitled “General Exceptions”, though those exceptions are not repeated in such definition, penal provision, or Illustration.
Illustrations.—(a) The sections in this Sanhita, which contain definitions of offences, do not express that a child under seven years of age cannot commit such offences; but the definitions are to be understood subject to the general exception which provides that nothing shall be an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age. (b) A, a police officer, without warrant, apprehends Z, who has committed murder. Here A is not guilty of the offence of wrongful confinement; for he was bound by law to apprehend Z, and therefore the case falls within the general exception which provides that “nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is bound by law to do it”.
(2) Every expression which is explained in any Part of this Sanhita, is used in every Part of this Sanhita in conformity with the explanation.
(3) When property is in the possession of a person’s spouse, clerk or servant, on account of that person, it is in that person’s possession within the meaning of this Sanhita. Explanation.—A person employed temporarily or on a particular occasion in the capacity of a clerk or servant, is a clerk or servant within the meaning of this sub-section.
(4) In every Part of this Sanhita, except where a contrary intention appears from the context, words which refer to acts done extend also to illegal omissions.
(5) When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone.
(6) Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge or intention.
(7) Wherever the causing of a certain effect, or an attempt to cause that effect, by an act or by an omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by an omission is the same offence.
Illustration.—A intentionally causes Z’s death, partly by illegally omitting to give Z food, and partly by beating Z. A has committed murder.
(8) When an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally cooperates in the commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, commits that offence.
Illustrations.—(a) A and B agree to murder Z by severally and at different times giving him small doses of poison. A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty of the offence though their acts are separate. (b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose. Z dies of hunger. Both A and B are guilty of the murder of Z. (c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z’s death, illegally omits to supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B, A is guilty only of an attempt to commit murder.
(9) Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be guilty of different offences by means of that act.
Illustration.—A attacks Z under such circumstances of grave provocation that his killing of Z would be only culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged in causing Z’s death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide.
key_terms: cooperation in several acts constituting one offence

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 3 lays down nine interpretive ground rules that apply across the entire Sanhita rather than to any single offence. The most important is clause (1): every offence-definition is automatically read subject to Chapter III's General Exceptions even though those exceptions are never repeated section by section — so, for example, the fact that a seven-year-old cannot be convicted of murder is never stated in the murder section itself, only in the General Exceptions chapter. The remaining clauses fix constructive-possession rules, extend act-based language to cover illegal omissions, and — most consequentially for group crime — establish that persons acting with a common intention, a shared criminal knowledge/intention, or merely cooperating through separate acts in the same offence are each liable as if they alone had committed the whole offence; yet clause (9)'s illustration shows participants in the same criminal episode can still end up convicted of genuinely different offences depending on their individual mental state.
essential_elements: Clause (1): every offence definition, penal provision, and illustration is automatically subject to Chapter III's General Exceptions, even without express repetition
Clause (2): a term explained anywhere in the Sanhita carries that same meaning everywhere else in the Sanhita
Clause (3): property held by a person's spouse, clerk, or servant on that person's account counts as being in that person's own possession
Clause (4): references to 'acts' extend to illegal omissions unless a contrary intention appears
Clause (5): common-intention liability — each participant in a group act done in furtherance of the common intention of all is liable as if he alone did the whole act
Clause (6): common-knowledge-or-intention liability for acts that are criminal only because of the knowledge/intention behind them
Clause (7): causing an effect partly by act and partly by omission is treated as the same offence as causing it wholly by act or wholly by omission
Clause (8): cooperating in any one of several acts that together constitute an offence makes a person guilty of that offence
Clause (9): several persons engaged in one criminal act or transaction may nonetheless be convicted of different offences from each other, depending on individual intent or circumstance
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (1) is an interpretive default, not an independent defence — a defendant must still actually satisfy the elements of a specific General Exception (e.g. the age, unsoundness-of-mind, or compulsion provisions in Chapter III) for it to apply

Clause (3)'s constructive-possession rule only reaches spouse/clerk/servant relationships 'on account of' the person — mere physical custody by an unrelated third party does not automatically transfer possession

Clause (9) is the key qualification on clauses (5)-(8): shared participation in one transaction does not force identical liability on every participant — grave provocation, lack of prior common intention, or absence of the requisite knowledge can produce different convictions (e.g. murder for one, culpable homicide not amounting to murder for another) out of the same episode
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat clauses (5) and (6) as the Sanhita's general group-liability engine (the BNS's equivalent of the old IPC's 'common intention' and 'common object' architecture) — but always test clause (9) against the facts before assuming every co-accused shares the same offence; grave and sudden provocation or absence of common intention is exactly what can split liability within the same group act, as its own illustration demonstrates.

sections.title: Punishments

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 4 is the master menu of punishments available under the BNS: death, imprisonment for life, imprisonment (rigorous or simple), forfeiture of property, fine, and — new to the BNS and not present in the IPC — Community Service. Every offence-defining section later in the Sanhita prescribes punishment by drawing from this closed list; a court cannot invent a sentence outside it.
essential_elements: The list is exhaustive — six categories only, with imprisonment further split into rigorous and simple.
Community Service is a wholly new addition compared to the IPC's equivalent Section 53, reflecting a restorative-justice shift.
Each specific offence section elsewhere in the BNS selects which of these punishments (and what range/term) applies to it.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Section 4 itself defines no offence and prescribes no term — it only catalogues the types of sentence a court may impose when some other section makes an act punishable.

What 'Community Service' actually entails in practice (nature of work, supervising authority) is left to be worked out under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and rules made thereunder, not spelled out in this Sanhita.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Section 4 as a glossary of sentence-types, not a sentencing section in itself — when reading any specific offence (e.g. 'punishable with imprisonment which may extend to X years, or fine, or both'), map the words back to this list to know exactly what kind of punishment is being authorised.

sections.title: Commutation of sentence
sections.raw_text:
The appropriate Government may, without the consent of the offender, commute any punishment under this Sanhita to any other punishment in accordance with section 474 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

Explanation.––For the purposes of this section the expression “appropriate Government” means,––
(a) in cases where the sentence is a sentence of death or is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends, the Central Government; and
(b) in cases where the sentence (whether of death or not) is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends, the Government of the State within which the offender is sentenced.

breakdown.plain_summary: Commutation means substituting a lighter form of punishment for the one originally imposed — for example, converting a death sentence into life imprisonment. Section 5 gives the 'appropriate Government' (Central or State, depending on which executive power the offence falls under) the power to do this unilaterally, without needing the convict's agreement, following the procedure in BNSS Section 474.
essential_elements: The power belongs to the executive (government), not the courts — this is distinct from judicial appeal, review, or revision.
No consent of the offender is required for commutation to operate.

The Explanation splits 'appropriate Government' along the same Union/State executive-power line used throughout Indian constitutional law: death sentences and Union-subject offences go to the Centre; State-subject offences go to the State Government where the offender is sentenced.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section only grants the *power* to commute — the actual procedure (who applies, what the government must consider) is set out in BNSS Section 474, not here.

Commutation is different from a pardon or remission; it changes the nature of the sentence (e.g. death to life) rather than cancelling or shortening it outright, though remission/pardon powers exist separately under the Constitution (Articles 72, 161) and BNSS.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Section 5 together with BNSS Section 474 — this Sanhita tells you *who* may commute and *what counts as* the appropriate Government, while the BNSS tells you *how* the commutation process actually runs.

sections.title: Fractions of terms of punishment
sections.raw_text: In calculating fractions of terms of punishment, imprisonment for life shall be reckoned as equivalent to imprisonment for twenty years unless otherwise provided.

breakdown.plain_summary: Whenever some other provision requires a fraction of a sentence to be calculated (for example, 'one-fourth of the maximum term') and the sentence in question is imprisonment for life, this section tells you what number to use: treat life imprisonment as if it were a fixed term of twenty years, unless a specific provision says otherwise.
essential_elements: This is a deeming/calculation rule, not a statement that life imprisonment actually lasts only twenty years in practice — a life sentence still ordinarily means imprisonment for the remainder of natural life (see Section 4's reference and settled Supreme Court case law).
It applies only when some other provision requires a fractional calculation and the base term is life imprisonment.
The twenty-year figure yields to any provision that 'otherwise provides' a different equivalence for its own purpose.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Does not itself cap or define what life imprisonment means in general — it is a narrow arithmetic convenience provision used, for instance, in default-sentence calculations under Section 8(3).
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this section as a lookup value whenever a formula elsewhere refers to a 'fraction of the term' and the underlying sentence is life imprisonment — plug in twenty years unless that other provision specifies something different.

sections.title: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple
sections.raw_text: In every case in which an offender is punishable with imprisonment which may be of either description, it shall be competent to the Court which sentences such offender to direct in the sentence that such imprisonment shall be wholly rigorous, or that such imprisonment shall be wholly simple, or that any part of such imprisonment shall be rigorous and the rest simple.
key_terms: discretion to mix rigorous and simple imprisonment

breakdown.plain_summary: Where an offence's punishment may be either rigorous (with hard labour) or simple imprisonment, the sentencing court has discretion to make the whole term rigorous, the whole term simple, or split the term so that part is rigorous and the rest simple.
essential_elements: Applies only where the punishment clause for the offence allows imprisonment 'of either description' — if a section mandates only rigorous (or only simple) imprisonment, there is no such discretion.
The discretion includes a hybrid option: part rigorous, part simple, within the same sentence.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Does not apply to offences where the Sanhita prescribes a single fixed description of imprisonment.
breakdown.how_to_read: When an offence's punishment clause reads 'imprisonment of either description,' read Section 7 alongside it to know the court can tailor the rigorous/simple split within that sentence.

sections.title: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where no sum is expressed to which a fine may extend, the amount of fine to which the offender is liable is unlimited, but shall not be excessive.

(2) In every case of an offence––
(a) punishable with imprisonment as well as fine, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine, whether with or without imprisonment;
(b) punishable with imprisonment or fine, or with fine only, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine,
it shall be competent to the Court which sentences such offender to direct by the sentence that, in default of payment of the fine, the offender shall suffer imprisonment for a certain term, in which imprisonment shall be in excess of any other imprisonment to which he may have been sentenced or to which he may be liable under a commutation of a sentence.

(3) The term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned in default of payment of a fine shall not exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which is the maximum fixed for the offence, if the offence be punishable with imprisonment as well as fine.

(4) The imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of a fine or in default of community service may be of any description to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence.

(5) If the offence is punishable with fine or community service, the imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of the fine or in default of community service shall be simple, and the term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned, in default of payment of fine or in default of community service, shall not exceed,—
(a) two months when the amount of the fine does not exceed five thousand rupees;
(b) four months when the amount of the fine does not exceed ten thousand rupees; and
(c) one year in any other case.

(6) (a) The imprisonment which is imposed in default of payment of a fine shall terminate whenever that fine is either paid or levied by process of law;
(b) If, before the expiration of the term of imprisonment fixed in default of payment, such a proportion of the fine be paid or levied that the term of imprisonment suffered in default of payment is not less than proportional to the part of the fine still unpaid, the imprisonment shall terminate.

Illustration.
A is sentenced to a fine of one thousand rupees and to four months’ imprisonment in default of payment. Here, if seven hundred and fifty rupees of the fine be paid or levied before the expiration of one month of the imprisonment, A will be discharged as soon as the first month has expired. If seven hundred and fifty rupees be paid or levied at the time of the expiration of the first month, or at any later time while A continues in imprisonment, A will be immediately discharged. If five hundred rupees of the fine be paid or levied before the expiration of two months of the imprisonment, A will be discharged as soon as the two months are completed. If five hundred rupees be paid or levied at the time of the expiration of those two months, or at any later time while A continues in imprisonment, A will be immediately discharged.

(7) The fine, or any part thereof which remains unpaid, may be levied at any time within six years after the passing of the sentence, and if, under the sentence, the offender be liable to imprisonment for a longer period than six years, then at any time previous to the expiration of that period; and the death of the offender does not discharge from the liability any property which would, after his death, be legally liable for his debts.
key_terms: default sentence for non-payment of fine
six-year levy period for unpaid fines

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 8 is the detailed machinery provision for fines. If an offence's punishment clause does not state a maximum fine amount, the fine is uncapped but must not be excessive. Whenever a court sentences someone to pay a fine, it may also direct a default term of imprisonment to be served if the fine is not paid — but that default term is tightly capped (generally one-fourth of the maximum imprisonment for the offence, or two months/four months/one year depending on the fine amount for fine-only or community-service offences), must be served in addition to any other sentence, and must end immediately once the fine is paid or proportionally reduced through part-payment. Unpaid fines remain recoverable from the offender's estate for up to six years (or longer if the prison term itself exceeds six years).
essential_elements: No stated maximum fine = unlimited fine, subject to the overriding 'not excessive' constraint (sub-section 1).
A default-imprisonment direction is optional ('it shall be competent to the Court') and is always additional/consecutive to any other imprisonment imposed (sub-section 2).
Default imprisonment is capped at one-fourth of the maximum imprisonment term for offences punishable with both imprisonment and fine (sub-section 3).

For fine-only or community-service-only offences, default imprisonment must be simple and is capped on a sliding scale by fine amount: 2 months (≤₹5,000), 4 months (≤₹10,000), 1 year (any higher amount) (sub-section 5).
Default imprisonment terminates immediately on full payment/levy of the fine, and proportionally on part-payment (sub-section 6), illustrated by the worked example.

Unpaid fines (or the unpaid balance) remain leviable from the offender's property for six years after sentencing, or longer if the custodial sentence itself exceeds six years — and this liability survives the offender's death against their estate (sub-section 7).
exceptions_and_qualifications: The one-fourth cap in sub-section (3) applies only where the offence carries both imprisonment and fine as punishment options — a different, fine-amount-based cap applies under sub-section (5) for fine/community-service-only offences.

Sub-section (4) allows default imprisonment of any description (rigorous or simple) generally, but sub-section (5) carves out a specific requirement that default imprisonment must be simple where the underlying offence is punishable with fine or community service only.
Death of the offender does not wipe out an unpaid fine — it becomes a charge recoverable from the deceased's estate, an important point for executors and heirs to note.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Section 8 as a toolkit a court consults every time it imposes a fine: first check whether a cap on the fine exists in the offence's own punishment clause (if not, sub-section 1 applies); then, if a default sentence is being considered, work out which cap applies — the one-fourth rule (imprisonment+fine offences) or the sliding ₹5,000/₹10,000 scale (fine/community-service-only offences) — and remember the default term always evaporates proportionally as the fine gets paid.

sections.title: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where anything which is an offence is made up of parts, any of which parts is itself an offence, the offender shall not be punished with the punishment of more than one of such his offences, unless it be so expressly provided.

(2) Where—
(a) anything is an offence falling within two or more separate definitions of any law in force for the time being by which offences are defined or punished; or
(b) several acts, of which one or more than one would by itself or themselves constitute an offence, constitute, when combined, a different offence,
the offender shall not be punished with a more severe punishment than the Court which tries him could award for any one of such offences.

Illustrations.
(a) A gives Z fifty strokes with a stick. Here A may have committed the offence of voluntarily causing hurt to Z by the whole beating, and also by each of the blows which make up the whole beating. If A were liable to punishment for every blow, he might be imprisoned for fifty years, one for each blow. But he is liable only to one punishment for the whole beating.
(b) But, if, while A is beating Z, Y interferes, and A intentionally strikes Y, here, as the blow given to Y is no part of the act whereby A voluntarily causes hurt to Z, A is liable to one punishment for voluntarily causing hurt to Z, and to another for the blow given to Y.
key_terms: offence made up of several offences

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 9 prevents an offender from being punished multiple times for what is really a single course of criminal conduct. If one offence is really built out of smaller acts that are each individually also offences (like fifty separate blows making up one beating), the offender is punished once for the whole, not once per component. Likewise, if the same conduct happens to fall under two or more overlapping legal definitions of offences, or if several individually-punishable acts combine to create a distinct composite offence, the court cannot impose a punishment heavier than what it could award for any single one of those offences.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): one offence 'made up of parts' that are themselves offences → punish for the whole, not part-by-part, unless a law expressly says otherwise.
Sub-section (2)(a): the same act fitting within multiple overlapping offence definitions → cap punishment at what could be awarded for any single one.
Sub-section (2)(b): several separately-punishable acts combining into a distinct composite offence → same cap.
The two illustrations distinguish 'parts of the same act' (one punishment) from a genuinely separate act directed at a different victim within the same episode (separate, additional punishment).
exceptions_and_qualifications: The protection in sub-section (1) yields wherever some other provision 'expressly provides' for cumulative punishment of the component offences.

The rule protects against punishing the *same* conduct twice over, not against punishing genuinely distinct acts that happen to occur in the same episode (illustration (b)) — this is the doctrinal cousin of the constitutional double-jeopardy protection but is a Sanhita-level, not Constitution-level, rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use the two illustrations as the test: ask whether the additional 'offence' you're looking at is truly just another slice of the same act (Section 9 caps punishment to one), or a factually separate act with its own distinct object/victim arising in the same episode (separate punishment permitted).

sections.title: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, the judgment stating that it is doubtful of which
sections.raw_text: In all cases in which judgment is given that a person is guilty of one of several offences specified in the judgment, but that it is doubtful of which of these offences he is guilty, the offender shall be punished for the offence for which the lowest punishment is provided if the same punishment is not provided for all.
key_terms: benefit of doubt as to which offence was committed

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a court is satisfied the accused is guilty of one of several specified offences but cannot determine with certainty which one, the accused must be sentenced according to whichever of those offences carries the lowest punishment — the benefit of that uncertainty goes to the accused.
essential_elements: Requires the judgment itself to record guilt of 'one of several' specifically identified offences, with genuine doubt as to which exact one applies.
The court must then apply the lowest-punishment offence among those specified, unless all carry the same punishment (in which case the question is moot).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is not a general 'benefit of the doubt' rule about guilt itself — guilt of one of the listed offences must already be established; the doubt is only about which one.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as a sentencing safeguard, not a guilt/acquittal provision — it only operates after the court has already concluded the accused committed one of a specific set of offences.

sections.title: Solitary confinement

breakdown.plain_summary: Where rigorous imprisonment is an available punishment for the offence, the sentencing court may additionally order that some portion of that imprisonment be served in solitary confinement — but only up to a maximum of three months total, and the maximum allowed scales with the length of the overall sentence (one month if the sentence is up to six months; two months if it is between six months and a year; three months if it exceeds a year).
essential_elements: Solitary confinement can only be ordered where rigorous imprisonment is a power available to the court for that offence — it cannot be tacked onto simple imprisonment.
An absolute ceiling of three months applies regardless of how long the overall sentence is.
The permissible solitary-confinement duration is tiered to the length of the imprisonment term itself (six-month, one-year thresholds).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Section 12 (the next section) places a further operational limit on how solitary confinement under this section must actually be executed — the two must be read together.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always cross-check Section 11's permission to *order* solitary confinement against Section 12's rules for *executing* it — the order and the execution are governed by two distinct, linked provisions.

sections.title: Limit of solitary confinement
sections.raw_text: In executing a sentence of solitary confinement, such confinement shall in no case exceed fourteen days at a time, with intervals between the periods of solitary confinement of not less duration than such periods; and when the imprisonment awarded shall exceed three months, the solitary confinement shall not exceed seven days in any one month of the whole imprisonment awarded, with intervals between the periods of solitary confinement of not less duration than such periods.
key_terms: mandatory rest intervals between solitary spells

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 12 regulates how a sentence of solitary confinement authorised under Section 11 must actually be carried out in practice: no single stretch of solitary confinement may exceed fourteen days, and it must be followed by a rest interval at least as long as the confinement spell itself. Additionally, if the total imprisonment term exceeds three months, no more than seven days of solitary confinement may be served in any single month of that term, again with equivalent rest intervals in between.
essential_elements: Maximum fourteen days of solitary confinement per continuous spell, always.
Mandatory rest interval between spells at least equal in length to the preceding spell.
Additional monthly cap of seven days where the overall imprisonment term exceeds three months.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section is purely about execution/implementation mechanics — it does not expand or restate the authority to order solitary confinement in the first place, which comes exclusively from Section 11.
breakdown.how_to_read: Think of Section 11 as the 'can the court order it, and how much in total' question, and Section 12 as the 'how must it actually be scheduled, day by day' question — a sentence that complies with Section 11's three-month ceiling can still be unlawfully executed if it breaches Section 12's fourteen-day/seven-day-per-month scheduling rules.

sections.title: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction
sections.raw_text: Whoever, having been convicted by a Court in India, of an offence punishable under Chapter X or Chapter XVII of this Sanhita with imprisonment of either description for a term of three years or upwards, shall be guilty of any offence punishable under either of those Chapters with like imprisonment for the like term, shall be subject for every such subsequent offence to imprisonment for life, or to imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years.
key_terms: repeat-offender liability under Chapters X and XVII

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a repeat-offender ('recidivism') provision targeting offences against public tranquility (Chapter X) and property offences (Chapter XVII). If a person, already convicted in India of an offence under either of those two chapters that was punishable with three years' imprisonment or more, goes on to commit another offence under either chapter carrying the same (three-year-plus) level of imprisonment, the enhanced punishment for that subsequent offence jumps to either life imprisonment or imprisonment of either description for up to ten years — well beyond what the underlying offence alone might otherwise carry.
essential_elements: Requires a prior conviction by an Indian court specifically under Chapter X or Chapter XVII, for an offence punishable with three years' imprisonment or more.
The subsequent offence must also fall under Chapter X or Chapter XVII and be punishable with 'like imprisonment for the like term' (i.e. also carrying a three-year-plus threshold).

Once triggered, the enhanced ceiling becomes life imprisonment, or imprisonment of either description up to ten years — the court retains discretion between the two, and as to term within the ten-year ceiling.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Does not apply across unrelated chapters — both the earlier and the later offence must come from Chapter X (public tranquility) or Chapter XVII (property offences) specifically, not any other part of the Sanhita.
The three-year threshold must be met on both the prior conviction and the fresh offence for the enhancement to engage.
breakdown.how_to_read: Apply this section as a two-step test: (1) was the earlier conviction under Chapter X or XVII with a three-year-plus imprisonment term, and (2) is the new offence also under Chapter X or XVII with a three-year-plus term — only if both are 'yes' does the enhanced life/ten-year ceiling under Section 13 replace the ordinary punishment for the new offence.

sections.title: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law
sections.raw_text:
Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law in good faith believes himself to be, bound by law to do it.

Illustrations.
(a) A, a soldier, fires on a mob by the order of his superior officer, in conformity with the commands of the law. A has committed no offence.
(b) A, an officer of a Court, being ordered by that Court to arrest Y, and, after due enquiry, believing Z to be Y, arrests Z. A has committed no offence.
key_terms: mistake of fact bound by law

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the first General Exception: a person legally bound to do something, or who in good faith mistakenly but reasonably believes (due to a mistake of *fact*, never a mistake of *law*) that they are bound to do it, commits no offence by doing it.
essential_elements: Applies to a person who is actually bound by law, or who believes in good faith they are bound, due to a mistake of fact.
The mistake must be one of fact, not of law — the old maxim 'ignorance of law is no excuse' still applies.
Good faith is required (see Section 2(14)'s 'due care and attention' standard).
exceptions_and_qualifications: A mistaken belief about what the law itself requires provides no protection under this section — only a mistaken belief about facts, held with due care, does.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair this with Section 17 (acts justified, or believed in good faith to be justified, by law) — Section 14 covers compulsion ('bound to do'), Section 17 covers permission ('justified in doing').

sections.title: Act of Judge when acting judicially
sections.raw_text: Nothing is an offence which is done by a Judge when acting judicially in the exercise of any power which is, or which in good faith he believes to be, given to him by law.

breakdown.plain_summary: A Judge acting in a judicial capacity commits no offence by exercising a power that is actually given to them by law, or that they in good faith believe is given to them by law.
essential_elements: Protection applies only to acts done 'acting judicially' — not to a Judge's purely administrative or personal conduct.
Covers both powers actually conferred by law and powers honestly, carefully believed to be conferred.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Does not immunise acts done outside a judicial capacity, or in bad faith.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside Section 16 (acts done pursuant to a court's judgment/order) — Section 15 protects the Judge who makes the order; Section 16 protects the person who executes it.

sections.title: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court
sections.raw_text: Nothing which is done in pursuance of, or which is warranted by the judgment or order of, a Court; if done whilst such judgment or order remains in force, is an offence, notwithstanding the Court may have had no jurisdiction to pass such judgment or order, provided the person doing the act in good faith believes that the Court had such jurisdiction.
key_terms: acts warranted by court judgment or order

breakdown.plain_summary: A person who acts in pursuance of, or as warranted by, a still-valid court judgment or order commits no offence — even if the court turns out to have lacked jurisdiction to pass it — so long as that person in good faith believed the court had jurisdiction.
essential_elements: The judgment or order must still be in force at the time of the act.
Protection survives even a jurisdictional defect in the underlying order, provided the actor's good-faith belief in the court's jurisdiction.
exceptions_and_qualifications: No protection if the judgment/order has already been set aside or has expired, or if the person acted without the required good-faith belief.
breakdown.how_to_read: This protects enforcement officers and litigants who rely on a court order — focus on whether the order was still in force and whether the actor's belief in the court's jurisdiction meets the good-faith (due care and attention) standard.

sections.title: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law
sections.raw_text:
Nothing is an offence which is done by any person who is justified by law, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law in good faith, believes himself to be justified by law, in doing it.

Illustration.
A sees Z commit what appears to A to be a murder. A, in the exercise, to the best of his judgment exerted in good faith, of the power which the law gives to all persons of apprehending murderers in the fact, seizes Z, in order to bring Z before the proper authorities. A has committed no offence, though it may turn out that Z was acting in self-defence.
key_terms: act justified by law or mistaken belief of justification

breakdown.plain_summary: Mirrors Section 14 but for permissive rather than mandatory legal authority: a person actually justified by law, or who in good faith mistakenly believes (due to a mistake of fact) that they are justified, commits no offence.
essential_elements: Covers both genuine legal justification and a good-faith, fact-based mistaken belief in justification.
The illustration shows a private citizen's lawful power to apprehend an apparent offender, even if the underlying facts later turn out differently.
exceptions_and_qualifications: As with Section 14, a mistake about the law itself (rather than the facts) gives no protection.
breakdown.how_to_read: Think of Section 14 as 'I thought I had to' and Section 17 as 'I thought I was allowed to' — both require the mistake to be factual, held in good faith.

sections.title: Accident in doing a lawful act
sections.raw_text:
Nothing is an offence which is done by accident or misfortune, and without any criminal intention or knowledge in the doing of a lawful act in a lawful manner by lawful means and with proper care and caution.

Illustration.
A is at work with a hatchet; the head flies off and kills a man who is standing by. Here, if there was no want of proper caution on the part of A, his act is excusable and not an offence.

breakdown.plain_summary: A harm that results purely by accident or misfortune — with no criminal intention or knowledge — while doing a lawful act, lawfully, with proper care and caution, is not an offence.
essential_elements: The underlying act itself must be lawful, done by lawful means, in a lawful manner.
The actor must have exercised proper care and caution.
No criminal intention or knowledge of the resulting harm.
exceptions_and_qualifications: If the underlying act was unlawful, or the actor was careless, this defence fails even if the harm was unintended — negligence-based liability can still attach separately.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use the hatchet illustration as the template: ask (1) was the act itself lawful, (2) was it done carefully, and (3) was the resulting harm unintended and unknown — only a 'yes' to all three engages this exception.

sections.title: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm
sections.raw_text:
Nothing is an offence merely by reason of its being done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it be done without any criminal intention to cause harm, and in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property.

Explanation.—It is a question of fact in such a case whether the harm to be prevented or avoided was of such a nature and so imminent as to justify or excuse the risk of doing the act with the knowledge that it was likely to cause harm.

Illustrations.
(a) A, the captain of a vessel, suddenly and without any fault or negligence on his part, finds himself in such a position that, before he can stop his vessel, he must inevitably run down a boat B, with twenty or thirty passengers on board, unless he changes the course of his vessel, and that, by changing his course, he must incur risk of running down a boat C with only two passengers on board, which he may possibly clear. Here, if A alters his course without any intention to run down the boat C and in good faith for the purpose of avoiding the danger to the passengers in the boat B, he is not guilty of an offence, though he may run down the boat C by doing an act which he knew was likely to cause that effect, if it be found as a matter of fact that the danger which he intended to avoid was such as to excuse him in incurring the risk of running down the boat C.
(b) A, in a great fire, pulls down houses in order to prevent the conflagration from spreading. He does this with the intention in good faith of saving human life or property. Here, if it be found that the harm to be prevented was of such a nature and so imminent as to excuse A's act, A is not guilty of the offence.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the Sanhita's 'necessity' defence: doing something known to be likely to cause harm is not an offence if done without criminal intent and in good faith to prevent or avoid a greater harm to person or property — whether the prevented harm was imminent and serious enough to justify the risk taken is always a question of fact.
essential_elements: Knowledge of likely harm is not enough on its own — there must be no criminal intention to cause that harm.
The act must be done in good faith specifically to prevent or avoid a different, other harm.
Whether the prevented harm justified the risk is assessed objectively as a question of fact (the Explanation).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a true necessity/choice-of-evils defence, distinct from private defence (Sections 34-44), which responds to an offence being committed against the defender, not to a general emergency.
breakdown.how_to_read: Apply a proportionality test using the two illustrations: was the harm avoided genuinely severe and imminent enough, viewed objectively, to excuse knowingly risking the lesser harm that actually occurred?

sections.title: Act of a child under seven years of age
sections.raw_text: Nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.

breakdown.plain_summary: A child under seven years of age is conclusively incapable of committing any offence under the Sanhita — this is an absolute, age-based bar, with no inquiry into the child's actual maturity.
essential_elements: Age is determined purely by the calendar — under seven years at the time of the act.
No factual inquiry into the child's actual understanding is undertaken or needed; the bar is absolute.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Contrast with Section 21, which covers children aged seven to twelve and requires proof of immaturity of understanding rather than an absolute age bar.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Section 20 as a bright-line rule (age alone decides) and Section 21 as a case-specific inquiry (age plus proof of immaturity) — do not blend the two tests.

sections.title: Act of a child above seven years of age and under twelve years of age of immature understanding
sections.raw_text: Nothing is an offence which is done by a child above seven years of age and under twelve years of age, who has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge of the nature and consequences of his conduct on that occasion.

breakdown.plain_summary: A child between seven and twelve years of age escapes liability only if, on the specific occasion in question, they had not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of their conduct — unlike Section 20, this requires proof of actual immaturity, not just an age cut-off.
essential_elements: Age bracket: above seven and under twelve years.
Requires a factual finding that the child lacked sufficient maturity to understand the nature and consequences of that specific act, on that specific occasion.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A child in this bracket who did understand the nature and consequences of the act is not protected — maturity, not mere age, is the operative test.
breakdown.how_to_read: Expect this defence to be contested on evidence of the particular child's cognitive development and the circumstances of the specific act — it is not automatic merely because the child falls within the age bracket.

sections.title: Act of a person of unsound mind
sections.raw_text: Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law.

breakdown.plain_summary: The insanity defence: a person who, because of unsoundness of mind at the time of the act, was incapable of knowing either the nature of the act itself, or that it was wrong or contrary to law, commits no offence.
essential_elements: Unsoundness of mind must exist at the time of the act, not merely before or after.
Incapacity must go to either (a) knowledge of the nature of the act, or (b) knowledge that the act was wrong or illegal — either suffices.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Mere eccentricity, odd behaviour, or even a diagnosed mental illness is insufficient on its own — the specific cognitive incapacity described must be established for the moment of the act.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is India's long-standing (M'Naghten-derived) insanity test, carried over from the IPC's equivalent provision — focus on the two alternative cognitive incapacities, not on mental illness as a diagnosis in itself.

sections.title: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will
sections.raw_text: Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, is, by reason of intoxication, incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong, or contrary to law; provided that the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will.

breakdown.plain_summary: Involuntary intoxication can excuse an offence in the same way unsoundness of mind can — but only where the intoxicating substance was administered without the person's knowledge or against their will, and it rendered them incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or illegal.
essential_elements: The incapacity test mirrors Section 22's (nature of act, or wrongfulness/illegality).
The intoxication must have been administered without knowledge or against the person's will — this proviso is the crux of the section.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Voluntary intoxication is never covered here — a person who chose to consume the intoxicant gets no defence under Section 23 (compare Section 24, which deals with voluntary intoxication differently).
breakdown.how_to_read: Always check the 'how did the intoxication happen' question first — if it was voluntary, Section 23 is unavailable and Section 24's knowledge-imputation rule applies instead.

sections.title: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated
sections.raw_text: In cases where an act done is not an offence unless done with a particular knowledge or intent, a person who does the act in a state of intoxication shall be liable to be dealt with as if he had the same knowledge as he would have had if he had not been intoxicated, unless the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where an offence requires proof of a particular knowledge or intent, a voluntarily intoxicated person is treated as if they had the same knowledge they would have had while sober — in effect, voluntary intoxication is no excuse for lack of the required mental element, unless the intoxication was itself involuntary (administered without knowledge or against the person's will).
essential_elements: Applies specifically to offences that require proof of a particular knowledge or intent (not strict-liability or general-intent offences).
The default rule imputes the knowledge the person would have had sober — voluntary intoxication cannot be used to negate that imputed knowledge.
The imputation does not apply where the intoxication was involuntary — that scenario instead falls back on Section 23's true incapacity test.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section does not excuse the act at all for voluntary intoxication — it is the opposite of an exception; it closes off intoxication as a route to deny the required mental state.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Sections 23 and 24 as a matched pair covering the two intoxication scenarios: Section 23 is a full defence for involuntary intoxication causing true incapacity; Section 24 denies voluntary intoxication as an excuse for lacking a required intent/knowledge, by imputing sober-state knowledge.

sections.title: Act not intended and not known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, done by consent
sections.raw_text:
Nothing which is not intended to cause death, or grievous hurt, and which is not known by the doer to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, to any person, above eighteen years of age, who has given consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm; or by reason of any harm which it may be known by the doer to be likely to cause to any such person who has consented to take the risk of that harm.

Illustration.
A and Z agree to fence with each other for amusement. This agreement implies the consent of each to suffer any harm which, in the course of such fencing, may be caused without foul play; and if A, while playing fairly, hurts Z, A commits no offence.
key_terms: consent defence for non-fatal non-grievous harm

breakdown.plain_summary: An act that is neither intended, nor known by the actor to be likely, to cause death or grievous hurt is not an offence as against an adult (above eighteen) who consented to suffer that harm or to take the risk of it — the classic example being consensual sport such as fencing.
essential_elements: The consenting person must be above eighteen years of age.
The act must not be intended to cause, and must not be known to be likely to cause, death or grievous hurt.
Consent may be express or implied (as in the fencing illustration).
exceptions_and_qualifications: If the act is intended to cause, or known to be likely to cause, death or grievous hurt, this exception does not apply at all — see Section 26 for the narrower death-related consent exception, and Section 29's bar on acts that are independently offences.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the baseline consent exception for minor/moderate harm among adults; for anything touching death or grievous hurt, look instead to the stricter, narrower exceptions in Sections 26-30.

sections.title: Act not intended to cause death, done by consent in good faith for person's benefit
sections.raw_text:
Nothing, which is not intended to cause death, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, or be known by the doer to be likely to cause, to any person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, and who has given a consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm, or to take the risk of that harm.

Illustration.
A, a surgeon, knowing that a particular operation is likely to cause the death of Z, who suffers under the painful complaint, but not intending to cause Z's death, and intending, in good faith, Z's benefit, performs that operation on Z, with Z's consent. A has committed no offence.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the core defence protecting consensual medical and surgical treatment: an act not intended to cause death is not an offence — even if it may cause or is known to be likely to cause serious harm or death — when done in good faith for the benefit of a consenting person, as illustrated by a surgeon performing a risky but beneficial operation with the patient's consent.
essential_elements: Death must not be intended (knowledge that death is a likely risk is permitted, unlike intent).
The act must be done in good faith for the benefit of the person harmed.
The person must have given express or implied consent to suffer the harm or take the risk.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Mere pecuniary benefit does not count as 'benefit' for this purpose (Explanation to Section 30, expressly made applicable to Sections 26, 27, and 30).
Does not protect acts intended to cause death, however consensual.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the doctor's/surgeon's shield — the dividing line from Section 25 is that Section 26 permits acts known to be likely to cause death itself (not just grievous hurt), provided death is not intended and the act is in good faith for the patient's benefit.

sections.title: Act done in good faith for benefit of child or person of unsound mind, by, or by consent of guardian
key_terms: guardian-consented treatment of minors and persons of unsound mind

breakdown.plain_summary: Extends the consensual-benefit idea to persons who cannot themselves give effective consent — children under twelve and persons of unsound mind — by allowing a guardian or lawful custodian to consent on their behalf to good-faith beneficial acts, but with four carved-out limits: it never covers intentional killing, acts known likely to cause death except to prevent death/grievous hurt or cure a grievous condition, voluntary grievous hurt except for the same narrow purposes, or abetment of offences the exception itself would not cover.
essential_elements: Protected person: under twelve years of age, or of unsound mind.
Act must be done in good faith for that person's benefit, by or with the guardian/lawful custodian's express or implied consent.
Four provisos strip the protection for intentional death, death-likely acts (outside curative/life-saving purpose), voluntary grievous hurt (outside the same purpose), and derivative abetment.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The four provisos are cumulative limits, not alternatives — any one of them being triggered removes the protection for that particular act.
Explanation under Section 30 (mere pecuniary benefit excluded) applies here too by cross-reference.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use the illustration as the template for the *permitted* zone (risky but curative surgery with guardian consent), and the four provisos as the boundary markers for where guardian consent stops protecting the actor.

sections.title: Consent known to be given under fear or misconception
sections.raw_text:
A consent is not such a consent as is intended by any section of this Sanhita,––
(a) if the consent is given by a person under fear of injury, or under a misconception of fact, and if the person doing the act knows, or has reason to believe, that the fear or consent was given in consequence of such fear or misconception; or
(b) if the consent is given by a person who, from unsoundness of mind, or intoxication, is unable to understand the nature and consequence of that to which he gives his consent; or
(c) unless the contrary appears from the context, if the consent is given by a person who is under twelve years of age.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section defines when a purported 'consent' does not count as valid consent anywhere else in the Sanhita: consent obtained under fear of injury or a factual misconception (known to the actor), consent given by someone incapable of understanding it due to unsoundness of mind or intoxication, and — unless context shows otherwise — consent given by a child under twelve.
essential_elements: Clause (a): fear-of-injury or factual-misconception consent, where the actor knows or has reason to believe this caused the 'consent' — a knowledge requirement on the actor's side.
Clause (b): consent from a person incapable, due to unsoundness of mind or intoxication, of understanding its nature and consequence.
Clause (c): a default rule that consent given by a child under twelve does not count, unless context indicates otherwise.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (c) is a rebuttable default ('unless the contrary appears from the context'), not an absolute bar like the age-twelve threshold used elsewhere in the consent exceptions.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Section 28 as the definitional gatekeeper for every consent-based exception in Sections 25-27 and 29-30 — before relying on 'consent' as a defence anywhere in the Sanhita, check it does not fall into one of these three vitiating categories.

sections.title: Exclusion of acts which are offences independently of harm caused
sections.raw_text:
The exceptions in sections 25, 26 and 27 do not extend to acts which are offences independently of any harm which they may cause, or be intended to cause, or be known to be likely to cause, to the person giving the consent, or on whose behalf the consent is given.

Illustration.
Causing miscarriage (unless caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the woman) is an offence independently of any harm which it may cause or be intended to cause to the woman. Therefore, it is not an offence “by reason of such harm”; and the consent of the woman or of her guardian to the causing of such miscarriage does not justify the act.

breakdown.plain_summary: Consent-based protection under Sections 25, 26, and 27 only ever excuses the *harm* caused to the consenting person — it cannot excuse an act that is a separate, independent offence in its own right regardless of that harm, as illustrated by causing miscarriage, which is independently punishable and is not cured merely because the woman or her guardian consented.
essential_elements: Applies as a limiting cross-reference specifically to the exceptions in Sections 25, 26, and 27.
Distinguishes harm-to-the-consenting-person (which consent can excuse) from independently-defined offences (which consent cannot excuse).
exceptions_and_qualifications: The illustration itself carries its own exception within it: miscarriage caused in good faith to save the woman's life is not independently an offence, so this bar does not apply to that scenario.
breakdown.how_to_read: Whenever invoking the consent exceptions (Sections 25-27), separately ask whether the act is *also* defined as an offence on some basis other than the harm to the consenting person — if so, Section 29 blocks the consent defence regardless of how genuine that consent was.

sections.title: Act done in good faith for benefit of a person without consent
sections.raw_text:
Nothing is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause to a person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, even without that person's consent, if the circumstances are such that it is impossible for that person to signify consent, or if that person is incapable of giving consent, and has no guardian or other person in lawful charge of him from whom it is possible to obtain consent in time for the thing to be done with benefit:
Provided that this exception shall not extend to––
(a) the intentional causing of death, or the attempting to cause death;
(b) the doing of anything which the person doing it knows to be likely to cause death, for any purpose other than the preventing of death or grievous hurt, or the curing of any grievous disease or infirmity;
(c) the voluntary causing of hurt, or to the attempting to cause hurt, for any purpose other than the preventing of death or hurt;
(d) the abetment of any offence, to the committing of which offence it would not extend.

Illustrations.
(1) Z is thrown from his horse, and is insensible. A, a surgeon, finds that Z requires to be trepanned. A, not intending Z's death, but in good faith, for Z's benefit, performs the trepan before Z recovers his power of judging for himself. A has committed no offence.
(2) Z is carried off by a tiger. A fires at the tiger knowing it to be likely that the shot may kill Z, but not intending to kill Z, and in good faith intending Z's benefit. A's bullet gives Z a mortal wound. A has committed no offence.
(3) A, a surgeon, sees a child suffer an accident which is likely to prove fatal unless an operation be immediately performed. There is no time to apply to the child's guardian. A performs the operation in spite of the entreaties of the child, intending, in good faith, the child's benefit. A has committed no offence.
(4) A is in a house which is on fire, with Z, a child. People below hold out a blanket. A drops the child from the house top, knowing it to be likely that the fall may kill the child, but not intending to kill the child, and intending, in good faith, the child's benefit. Here, even if the child is killed by the fall, A has committed no offence.

Explanation.—Mere pecuniary benefit is not benefit within the meaning of sections 26, 27 and this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: The emergency counterpart to Sections 26-27: where it is impossible to obtain consent in time (the person is unconscious, or incapable with no guardian reachable in time), a good-faith act for that person's benefit is not an offence by reason of the harm caused — subject to the same four provisos as Section 27 (no intentional killing, no death-likely acts outside a curative/life-saving purpose, no voluntary hurt outside preventing death/hurt, no unprotected abetment).
essential_elements: Consent must be genuinely impossible to obtain in time — either the person cannot signify it, or is incapable and has no reachable guardian.
The act must be in good faith for that person's benefit.
The same four limiting provisos as Section 27 apply.
The closing Explanation — purely financial benefit does not count as 'benefit' — governs this section as well as Sections 26 and 27.
exceptions_and_qualifications: If consent could have been obtained in time but simply was not sought, this exception does not apply — the impossibility/incapacity condition is a genuine precondition, not a formality.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use the four illustrations (unconscious rider, tiger-mauling victim, injured child with no time to reach the guardian, burning-house rescue) as the paradigm emergency scenarios this section is built for — each shows good-faith, no-time-for-consent, benefit-oriented action.

sections.title: Communication made in good faith
sections.raw_text:
No communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, if it is made for the benefit of that person.

Illustration.
A, a surgeon, in good faith, communicates to a patient his opinion that he cannot live. The patient dies in consequence of the shock. A has committed no offence, though he knew it to be likely that the communication might cause the patient's death.

breakdown.plain_summary: A communication made in good faith, for the recipient's benefit, is not an offence merely because it causes harm to the person it is made to — even fatal psychological shock, as in the illustration of a surgeon honestly disclosing a grim prognosis.
essential_elements: The communication must be made in good faith.
It must be made for the benefit of the person to whom it is communicated.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A communication made recklessly, maliciously, or not genuinely for the recipient's benefit falls outside this protection.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a narrow, specific protection for honest, well-intentioned disclosures (classically, medical prognoses) — it does not protect communications made for some other purpose that merely happen to also be framed as being for the recipient's benefit.

sections.title: Act to which a person is compelled by threats
sections.raw_text:
Except murder, and offences against the State punishable with death, nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is compelled to do it by threats, which, at the time of doing it, reasonably cause the apprehension that instant death to that person will otherwise be the consequence:
Provided that the person doing the act did not of his own accord, or from a reasonable apprehension of harm to himself short of instant death, place himself in the situation by which he became subject to such constraint.

Explanation 1.—A person who, of his own accord, or by reason of a threat of being beaten, joins a gang of dacoits, knowing their character, is not entitled to the benefit of this exception, on the ground of his having been compelled by his associates to do anything that is an offence by law.
Explanation 2.—A person seized by a gang of dacoits, and forced, by threat of instant death, to do a thing which is an offence by law; for example, a smith compelled to take his tools and to force the door of a house for the dacoits to enter and plunder it, is entitled to the benefit of this exception.
key_terms: duress by threat of instant death

breakdown.plain_summary: The duress defence: an act compelled by threats that, at the time, reasonably create an apprehension of instant death to the actor is not an offence — except for murder and offences against the State punishable with death, which can never be excused this way — provided the actor did not voluntarily place themselves in that dangerous situation.
essential_elements: The threat must reasonably cause apprehension of *instant* death — lesser threats (e.g. of being beaten) do not qualify.
The threat must be operating at the time of the act.
The actor must not have voluntarily, or through foreseeable lesser risk, placed themselves in the compelling situation (the proviso).
Murder and offences against the State punishable with death are absolutely excluded from this defence, however severe the threat.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Explanation 1 denies the defence to someone who knowingly joins a criminal gang and is then 'compelled' by associates — foreseeable risk undertaken voluntarily disqualifies the defence.
