Explanation 2 confirms the defence protects someone genuinely seized and threatened with instant death by criminals, illustrated by a forced locksmith.
breakdown.how_to_read: Run through: (1) is the offence murder or a death-punishable State offence (if so, stop — no defence at all); (2) was the threat one of instant death, not lesser harm; (3) did the actor voluntarily walk into the risk beforehand — only a clean path through all three preserves the defence.

sections.title: Act causing slight harm
sections.raw_text: Nothing is an offence by reason that it causes, or that it is intended to cause, or that it is known to be likely to cause, any harm, if that harm is so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain of such harm.

breakdown.plain_summary: The law does not concern itself with trifles: an act causing (or intended to cause, or known to be likely to cause) harm so slight that an ordinary, reasonable person would not even complain about it is not an offence.
essential_elements: The test is objective — whether a person of ordinary sense and temper would complain — not whether the particular victim was unusually sensitive or tolerant.
Covers harm that is caused, intended, or merely known-likely, so long as it meets the slightness threshold.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a narrow, fact-specific defence best suited to genuinely trivial harms — courts apply it conservatively, since almost any physical contact or minor loss could otherwise be dressed up as 'slight.'
breakdown.how_to_read: Apply the 'ordinary sense and temper' reasonable-person standard, not the actual complainant's own reaction — a thin-skinned complainant's objection does not defeat this defence if an ordinary person would have shrugged the harm off.

sections.title: Things done in private defence
sections.raw_text: Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence.

breakdown.plain_summary: The opening, umbrella provision of the private-defence scheme: any act genuinely done in the exercise of the right of private defence is not an offence. The scope and limits of that right are then worked out across Sections 35-44.
essential_elements: A purely gateway provision — it establishes that private defence is a complete defence, but the content of the right is defined by the sections that follow.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Always read together with Sections 35-44, especially Section 37's restrictions — Section 34 alone does not tell you what conduct actually qualifies as 'private defence.'
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Section 34 as a signpost into the private-defence sub-scheme (Sections 35-44) under the heading 'Of right of private defence' — the real analytical work happens in those later sections.

sections.title: Right of private defence of body and of property

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 35 defines the two broad categories of the right of private defence, subject to Section 37's restrictions: defence of the body (one's own or any other person's) against any body-affecting offence, and defence of property (one's own or any other person's, movable or immovable) against theft, robbery, mischief, criminal trespass, or attempts at those offences.
essential_elements: The right extends to defending third parties' bodies and property, not just one's own.
Body-defence applies against 'any offence affecting the human body' — a broad category.
Property-defence is narrower, limited to theft, robbery, mischief, criminal trespass, or attempts at these.
Both branches are expressly made subject to Section 37's restrictions.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Property defence does not cover every property-related wrong — only the four named offences/attempts; a civil property dispute, for instance, is not automatically within this right.
breakdown.how_to_read: Identify first whether you are defending body or property and against what kind of offence — then proceed to Sections 36-44 to work out the restrictions, extent (including whether death may be caused), and duration of that specific branch of the right.

sections.title: Right of private defence against act of a person of unsound mind, etc.
sections.raw_text:
When an act, which would otherwise be a certain offence, is not that offence, by reason of the youth, the want of maturity of understanding, the unsoundness of mind or the intoxication of the person doing that act, or by reason of any misconception on the part of that person, every person has the same right of private defence against that act which he would have if the act were that offence.

Illustrations.
(a) Z, a person of unsound mind, attempts to kill A; Z is guilty of no offence. But A has the same right of private defence which he would have if Z were sane.
(b) A enters by night a house which he is legally entitled to enter. Z, in good faith, taking A for a house-breaker, attacks A. Here Z, by attacking A under this misconception, commits no offence. But A has the same right of private defence against Z, which he would have if Z were not acting under that misconception.
key_terms: private defence against a non-culpable attacker

breakdown.plain_summary: Private defence is available even against an attacker who personally commits no offence because of youth, immaturity, unsoundness of mind, intoxication, or an honest misconception — the defender has exactly the same right of private defence as if the attacker's act had been a full offence.
essential_elements: The attacker's personal lack of culpability (due to the listed excusing factors) does not reduce the victim's right to defend themselves.
The defender's right is measured as if the attacker's act were, in fact, the offence it resembles.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section does not expand the *scope* of private defence beyond what Sections 35 and 37-44 otherwise allow — it only confirms the right exists despite the attacker's personal non-liability.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use the two illustrations (the insane assailant, and the honestly-mistaken house-breaker accusation) to see that private defence protects against the *objective* danger posed by an act, independent of whether the person causing that danger is themselves legally blameworthy.

sections.title: Acts against which there is no right of private defence
sections.raw_text:
(1) There is no right of private defence,––
(a) against an act which does not reasonably cause the apprehension of death or of grievous hurt, if done, or attempted to be done, by a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office, though that act, may not be strictly justifiable by law;
(b) against an act which does not reasonably cause the apprehension of death or of grievous hurt, if done, or attempted to be done, by the direction of a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office, though that direction may not be strictly justifiable by law;
(c) in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.

(2) The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence.

Explanation 1.—A person is not deprived of the right of private defence against an act done, or attempted to be done, by a public servant, as such, unless he knows or has reason to believe, that the person doing the act is such public servant.
Explanation 2.—A person is not deprived of the right of private defence against an act done, or attempted to be done, by the direction of a public servant, unless he knows, or has reason to believe, that the person doing the act is acting by such direction, or unless such person states the authority under which he acts, or if he has authority in writing, unless he produces such authority, if demanded.
key_terms: no private defence against good-faith public servants

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 37 is the master restriction provision for the whole private-defence scheme: there is no right of private defence against a public servant's (or a public servant's directed) act that does not reasonably threaten death or grievous hurt, so long as it is done in good faith under colour of office — even if not strictly lawful; nor is there a right where there was time to seek help from public authorities instead of taking the law into one's own hands. And whatever right does exist is always capped at the harm genuinely necessary for defence, never more.
essential_elements: Clause (a)/(b): bars private defence against good-faith, colour-of-office public-servant action (direct or directed) that does not threaten death/grievous hurt.
Clause (c): bars private defence whenever there was time to seek the protection of public authorities instead.
Sub-section (2): an absolute proportionality cap — never more harm than necessary for defence.
Explanation 1: the public-servant bar only applies if the defender knew or had reason to believe the actor was a public servant.
Explanation 2: the directed-action bar only applies if the defender knew, or the directing authority was properly identified/demonstrated, as acting under such direction.
exceptions_and_qualifications: If the public servant's act does threaten death or grievous hurt, or is not in good faith/under colour of office, the bar in clauses (a)-(b) does not apply and ordinary private-defence rules resume.
The two Explanations are defender-protective — ignorance of the attacker's public-servant status, or absence of proper identification/authority, preserves the defender's right.
breakdown.how_to_read: Run Section 37 as a checklist before concluding private defence was available: public servant involved and good faith/colour of office and no death/grievous-hurt threat (bar applies, subject to the knowledge provisos)? time available to call public authorities (bar applies)? and finally, regardless, was the force used proportionate to what was necessary?

sections.title: When right of private defence of body extends to causing death
key_terms: private defence extending to death — body
acid-attack ground for lethal private defence

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 38 lists the seven categories of assault grave enough that the right of private defence of the body extends all the way to voluntarily causing death to the assailant: reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, assault intending rape, unnatural-lust gratification, kidnapping/abduction, wrongful confinement with no recourse to authorities, and acid-throwing (or attempted acid-throwing) likely to cause grievous hurt — the last being a BNS-era addition reflecting the specific seriousness of acid attacks.
essential_elements: Only these seven enumerated categories of assault justify lethal force in defence of the body.
The right to cause death under this section is itself still subject to Section 37's restrictions (proportionality, no-time-to-seek-help, public-servant carve-outs).
exceptions_and_qualifications: For any assault not falling within these seven categories, Section 39 applies instead — the right does not extend to causing death, only to other harm.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as a closed list — match the attacker's conduct against the seven categories precisely before concluding that lethal private defence of the body was legally available.

sections.title: When such right extends to causing any harm other than death
sections.raw_text: If the offence be not of any of the descriptions specified in section 38, the right of private defence of the body does not extend to the voluntary causing of death to the assailant, but does extend, under the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing to the assailant of any harm other than death.

breakdown.plain_summary: For any assault that does not fall within Section 38's seven grave categories, the right of private defence of the body is capped: it never extends to voluntarily causing the assailant's death, but it does extend to causing any harm short of death, subject to Section 37's restrictions.
essential_elements: This is the default/residual rule for all body-defence scenarios not covered by Section 38's list.
Death is categorically off the table; lesser harm remains available, still bounded by proportionality under Section 37(2).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Always cross-check Section 38 first — if the assault matches one of its seven categories, Section 39's death-ban does not apply.
breakdown.how_to_read: Sections 38 and 39 work as a binary switch: classify the assailant's conduct under Section 38's list first; if it fits, lethal defence is permitted (subject to Section 37); if it does not fit, Section 39 caps the defender at non-lethal harm only.

sections.title: Commencement and continuance of right of private defence of body
sections.raw_text: The right of private defence of the body commences as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises from an attempt or threat to commit the offence though the offence may not have been committed; and it continues as long as such apprehension of danger to the body continues.
key_terms: temporal window of private defence of body

breakdown.plain_summary: The right of private defence of the body is not limited to the moment of actual physical attack — it begins as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger arises from an attempt or threat, even before any offence is actually committed, and it lasts for exactly as long as that reasonable apprehension of danger persists.
essential_elements: Trigger: reasonable apprehension of danger from an attempt or threat — actual commission of the offence is not required to start the clock.
Duration: the right lasts only as long as the reasonable apprehension of danger continues, not indefinitely or retrospectively after the danger has passed.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Once the apprehension of danger genuinely ends (e.g. the attacker retreats or is subdued), continued force is no longer private defence but becomes retaliation — a critical, frequently litigated line.
breakdown.how_to_read: Focus fact-finding on two timestamps: when did reasonable apprehension of bodily danger first arise, and when did it cease — force used outside that window falls outside the protection of private defence of the body.

sections.title: When right of private defence of property extends to causing death
key_terms: private defence extending to death — property

breakdown.plain_summary: Mirroring Section 38 for property, Section 41 lists the four categories of property offence grave enough to justify the defender voluntarily causing death: robbery, house-breaking at night (after sunset, before sunrise), arson/explosive mischief against a dwelling or property-custody structure, and theft/mischief/house-trespass committed under circumstances reasonably raising apprehension of death or grievous hurt if the right is not exercised.
essential_elements: Four enumerated categories only — robbery, night house-breaking, dwelling/custody-structure arson or explosive mischief, and theft/mischief/house-trespass with reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
Still subject to Section 37's restrictions (good-faith public servants, time to seek help, and proportionality).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Ordinary daytime theft or simple trespass not accompanied by a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt does not qualify — see Section 42 for the non-lethal default.
breakdown.how_to_read: Match the specific property offence against these four categories before concluding lethal private defence of property was available — the 'night' element in house-breaking and the 'dwelling/custody-structure' element in arson/mischief are both load-bearing qualifiers, not incidental detail.

sections.title: When such right extends to causing any harm other than death
sections.raw_text: If the offence, the committing of which, or the attempting to commit which occasions the exercise of the right of private defence, be theft, mischief, or criminal trespass, not of any of the descriptions specified in section 41, that right does not extend to the voluntary causing of death, but does extend, subject to the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing to the wrong-doer of any harm other than death.
key_terms: private defence of property capped below death

breakdown.plain_summary: For theft, mischief, or criminal trespass that does not fall within Section 41's four grave categories, the right of private defence of property never extends to causing death — only to causing harm short of death, subject to Section 37's restrictions.
essential_elements: Residual/default rule for property-defence scenarios not covered by Section 41's list.
Death is barred; lesser harm remains available, proportionate under Section 37(2).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Always check Section 41 first — if the offence matches robbery, night house-breaking, dwelling-targeted arson/explosive mischief, or theft/mischief/house-trespass with reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, Section 41 (not Section 42) governs.
breakdown.how_to_read: Sections 41 and 42 form the property-defence counterpart to the Section 38/39 body-defence binary — classify the offence against Section 41's list first; lethal force is permitted only on a match, otherwise Section 42 caps the response below death.

sections.title: Commencement and continuance of right of private defence of property
key_terms: temporal window of private defence of property

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 43 fixes separate start-and-end windows for the right of private defence of property depending on which specific offence is being resisted: it always starts once a reasonable apprehension of danger to the property arises, but how long it lasts differs for theft (until the thief escapes with the property, help arrives, or the property is recovered), robbery (as long as danger or fear of instant death/hurt/restraint continues), criminal trespass/mischief (as long as the trespass/mischief continues), and night house-breaking (as long as the resulting house-trespass continues).
essential_elements: A single commencement rule (clause (a)) applies across all property offences.
Four distinct continuance rules (clauses (b)-(e)) are each tailored to a specific offence category — theft, robbery, criminal trespass/mischief, and night house-breaking.
Clause (b)'s theft rule gives three independent endpoints: successful retreat with the property, arrival of public-authority assistance, or recovery of the property.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Using force after the relevant continuance window has closed (e.g. after a thief has successfully retreated and escaped, under clause (b)) converts the response from defence into unlawful retaliation.
breakdown.how_to_read: Identify which specific property offence is in play first, then apply the matching clause ((b)-(e)) to determine exactly when the defender's right of private defence of property legally ends — the end-point differs meaningfully across the four offence types.

sections.title: Right of private defence against deadly assault when there is risk of harm to innocent person
sections.raw_text:
If in the exercise of the right of private defence against an assault which reasonably causes the apprehension of death, the defender be so situated that he cannot effectually exercise that right without risk of harm to an innocent person, his right of private defence extends to the running of that risk.

Illustration.
A is attacked by a mob who attempt to murder him. He cannot effectually exercise his right of private defence without firing on the mob, and he cannot fire without risk of harming young children who are mingled with the mob. A commits no offence if by so firing he harms any of the children.
key_terms: private defence with incidental risk to bystanders

breakdown.plain_summary: The final provision in the private-defence scheme addresses a hard case: if a defender facing an assault that reasonably threatens death cannot effectively exercise the right of private defence without risking incidental harm to an innocent bystander, the right extends to running that risk — as illustrated by a person forced to fire into a threatening mob that includes children, without committing an offence even if a child is incidentally harmed.
essential_elements: Applies only where the underlying assault reasonably causes apprehension of death — the highest tier of threat.
Requires genuine impossibility of exercising the defence effectively without risking the innocent third party.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This does not license indifference to bystander safety generally — it applies narrowly to situations of genuine necessity where no safer means of effective defence exists.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as the closing safety-valve of the private-defence scheme, applicable only in the most extreme (apprehension-of-death) cases and only where effective defence is genuinely impossible without incidental risk to an innocent person — not a general license to disregard bystanders.

sections.title: Abetment of a thing
sections.raw_text: A person abets the doing of a thing, who— (a) instigates any person to do that thing; or (b) engages with one or more other person or persons in any conspiracy for the doing of that thing, if an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing; or (c) intentionally aids, by any act or illegal omission, the doing of that thing. Explanation 1.—A person who, by wilful misrepresentation, or by wilful concealment of a material fact which he is bound to disclose, voluntarily causes or procures, or attempts to cause or procure, a thing to be done, is said to instigate the doing of that thing. Illustration.—A, a public officer, is authorised by a warrant from a Court to apprehend Z. B, knowing that fact and also that C is not Z, wilfully represents to A that C is Z, and thereby intentionally causes A to apprehend C. Here B abets by instigation the apprehension of C. Explanation 2.—Whoever, either prior to or at the time of the commission of an act, does anything in order to facilitate the commission of that act, and thereby facilitates the commission thereof, is said to aid the doing of that act.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 45 opens Chapter IV by defining the three distinct routes by which a person can 'abet' the doing of a thing — instigating someone to do it, conspiring with others toward it where some act or illegal omission follows in pursuance of the conspiracy, or intentionally aiding its doing by act or illegal omission. The two Explanations widen 'instigation' to cover wilful misrepresentation or wilful concealment of a fact one is bound to disclose, and define 'aiding' as facilitating an act's commission, whether the facilitation happens before or during the act.
essential_elements: Three independent modes of abetment: instigation, conspiracy-with-overt-act, or intentional aiding.
For the conspiracy mode, an act or illegal omission must actually take place in pursuance of the conspiracy.
Instigation extends to wilful misrepresentation or wilful concealment of a fact the person was bound to disclose.
Aiding requires the facilitating act to actually facilitate the commission of the principal act.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Mere passive knowledge of another's intention, without instigation, conspiracy, or active aid, does not amount to abetment.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Section 45 as the master definition clause for the whole of Chapter IV — every abetment offence in Sections 46-60 presupposes conduct falling within one of this section's three limbs.

sections.title: Abettor
sections.raw_text: A person abets an offence, who abets either the commission of an offence, or the commission of an act which would be an offence, if committed by a person capable by law of committing an offence with the same intention or knowledge as that of the abettor. Explanation 1.—The abetment of the illegal omission of an act may amount to an offence although the abettor may not himself be bound to do that act. Explanation 2.—To constitute the offence of abetment it is not necessary that the act abetted should be committed, or that the effect requisite to constitute the offence should be caused. Illustrations.—(a) A instigates B to murder C. B refuses to do so. A is guilty of abetting B to commit murder. (b) A instigates B to murder D. B in pursuance of the instigation stabs D. D recovers from the wound. A is guilty of instigating B to commit murder. Explanation 3.—It is not necessary that the person abetted should be capable by law of committing an offence, or that he should have the same guilty intention or knowledge as that of the abettor, or any guilty intention or knowledge. Illustrations.—(a) A, with a guilty intention, abets a child or a person of unsound mind to commit an act which would be an offence, if committed by a person capable by law of committing an offence, and having the same intention as A. Here A, whether the act be committed or not, is guilty of abetting an offence. (b) A, with the intention of murdering Z, instigates B, a child under seven years of age, to do an act which causes Z's death. B, in consequence of the abetment, does the act in the absence of A and thereby causes Z's death. Here, though B was not capable by law of committing an offence, A is liable to be punished in the same manner as if B had been capable by law of committing an offence, and had committed murder, and he is therefore subject to the punishment of death. (c) A instigates B to set fire to a dwelling-house. B, in consequence of his unsoundness of mind, being incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is wrong or contrary to law, sets fire to the house in consequence of A's instigation. B has committed no offence, but A is guilty of abetting the offence of setting fire to a dwelling-house, and is liable to the punishment provided for that offence. (d) A, intending to cause a theft to be committed, instigates B to take property belonging to Z out of Z's possession. A induces B to believe that the property belongs to A. B takes the property out of Z's possession, in good faith, believing it to be A's property. B, acting under this misconception, does not take dishonestly, and therefore does not commit theft. But A is guilty of abetting theft, and is liable to the same punishment as if B had committed theft. Explanation 4.—The abetment of an offence being an offence, the abetment of such an abetment is also an offence. Illustration.—A instigates B to instigate C to murder Z. B accordingly instigates C to murder Z, and C commits that offence in consequence of B's instigation. B is liable to be punished for his offence with the punishment for murder; and, as A instigated B to commit the offence, A is also liable to the same punishment. Explanation 5.—It is not necessary to the commission of the offence of abetment by conspiracy that the abettor should concert the offence with the person who commits it. It is sufficient if he engages in the conspiracy in pursuance of which the offence is committed. Illustration.—A concerts with B a plan for poisoning Z. It is agreed that A shall administer the poison. B then explains the plan to C mentioning that a third person is to administer the poison, but without mentioning A's name. C agrees to procure the poison, and procures and delivers it to B for the purpose of its being used in the manner explained. A administers the poison; Z dies in consequence. Here, though A and C have not conspired together, yet C has been engaged in the conspiracy in pursuance of which Z has been murdered. C has therefore committed the offence defined in this section and is liable to the punishment for murder.
key_terms: engaging in a conspiracy without concert

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 46 completes the abetment framework by defining who counts as an 'abettor' and, through five Explanations, strips away several possible escape routes: it does not matter whether the principal offence is actually committed (Explanation 2), whether the person abetted is legally capable of committing the offence at all — e.g. a child or a person of unsound mind (Explanation 3) — whether the abettor is bound to do the act whose omission is abetted (Explanation 1), whether the chain of instigation is one level or several (Explanation 4, abetting an abetment), or whether the conspirators ever met each other directly, so long as each engaged in the pursuit of the same conspiracy (Explanation 5).
essential_elements: Abetment liability attaches regardless of whether the offence abetted is ultimately committed.
An abettor remains liable even where the person abetted lacks legal capacity (a child, a person of unsound mind) or lacks the same guilty state of mind.
Abetment of an abetment is itself a punishable abetment (chained instigation).
Conspirators need not have directly concerted with one another, only have engaged in the same pursued conspiracy.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Where the person actually abetted is incapable by law of committing the offence, the abettor is punished as though that person had committed it with the abettor's own intention or knowledge.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Section 46 together with Section 45: Section 45 defines the conduct that amounts to abetment, while Section 46 defines who is treated as an 'abettor' of an 'offence' and forecloses defences based on the principal's incapacity, the chain's length, or the offence's non-commission.

sections.title: Abetment in India of offences outside India
sections.raw_text: A person abets an offence within the meaning of this Sanhita who, in India, abets the commission of any act without and beyond India which would constitute an offence if committed in India. Illustration.—A, in India, instigates B, a foreigner in country X, to commit a murder in that country, A is guilty of abetting murder.
key_terms: abetment in India of offences outside India

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 47 extends abetment liability extraterritorially in one direction: a person physically present in India who abets an act committed outside India is guilty of abetment under the Sanhita, provided that act — had it been committed in India — would itself be an offence under the Sanhita. The nationality of the person actually committing the act abroad is irrelevant.
essential_elements: The abetting conduct (instigation, conspiracy, or aiding) must occur in India.
The act abetted occurs outside India.
That act must be one which would constitute an offence under the Sanhita if committed in India.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair with Section 48, which covers the mirror-image scenario (abetment from outside India of an act committed in India) — together they close the jurisdictional gap for abetment that crosses India's borders in either direction.

sections.title: Abetment outside India for offence in India
sections.raw_text: A person abets an offence within the meaning of this Sanhita who, without and beyond India, abets the commission of any act in India which would constitute an offence if committed in India. Illustration.—A, in country X, instigates B, to commit a murder in India, A is guilty of abetting murder.
key_terms: abetment outside India for offence in India

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 48 is the reverse of Section 47: a person physically outside India who abets the commission of an act within India is guilty of abetment under the Sanhita, so long as that act would be an offence if committed in India.
essential_elements: The abetting conduct occurs outside India.
The act abetted is committed, or is to be committed, in India.
That act must constitute an offence under the Sanhita.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Section 47 and the extraterritorial-jurisdiction scheme of Section 1(4)-(5): abetment that crosses India's border, in either direction, is captured by one of these two mirror provisions.

sections.title: Punishment of abetment if act abetted is committed in consequence and where no express provision is made for its punishment
sections.raw_text: Whoever abets any offence shall, if the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made by this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence. Explanation.—An act or offence is said to be committed in consequence of abetment, when it is committed in consequence of the instigation, or in pursuance of the conspiracy, or with the aid which constitutes the abetment. Illustrations.—(a) A instigates B to give false evidence. B, in consequence of the instigation, commits that offence. A is guilty of abetting that offence, and is liable to the same punishment as B. (b) A and B conspire to poison Z. A, in pursuance of the conspiracy, procures the poison and delivers it to B in order that he may administer it to Z. B, in pursuance of the conspiracy, administers the poison to Z in A's absence and thereby causes Z's death. Here B is guilty of murder. A is guilty of abetting that offence by conspiracy, and is liable to the punishment for murder.
key_terms: punishment of abetment where offence is committed in consequence

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 49 lays down the default punishment rule for abetment: where the abetted offence is actually committed as a result of the abetment and no other section of the Sanhita specially fixes a punishment for that particular abetment, the abettor is liable to exactly the same punishment as that provided for the completed offence itself.
essential_elements: The offence abetted must actually be committed, and 'in consequence of' the abetment (instigation, conspiracy, or aid).
No other express provision of the Sanhita fixes a specific punishment for that abetment.
The abettor is then punished with the same punishment as for the substantive offence.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a residual/default rule — it yields wherever a more specific abetment-punishment provision (e.g. Sections 55, 56, 57) applies instead.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 49 is the general 'same punishment as the completed offence' default; Sections 50-53 then modify this default for scenarios where the act done diverges from what was actually abetted.

sections.title: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor
sections.raw_text: Whoever abets the commission of an offence shall, if the person abetted does the act with a different intention or knowledge from that of the abettor, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence which would have been committed if the act had been done with the intention or knowledge of the abettor and with no other.
key_terms: abetment with differing intention between abettor and person abetted

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 50 fixes the abettor's punishment by reference to the abettor's own state of mind, not that of the person who physically does the act — if the person abetted acts with a different intention or knowledge than the abettor had, the abettor is punished as though the offence that the abettor intended had actually been committed.
essential_elements: The person abetted commits the act, but with an intention or knowledge differing from the abettor's.
The abettor's punishment tracks the offence that would correspond to the abettor's own intention or knowledge, not the executor's.
breakdown.how_to_read: Contrast with Section 46's general principle that the abettor need not share the executor's state of mind — Section 50 supplies the specific punishment consequence when the two states of mind actually diverge.

sections.title: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done
sections.raw_text: When an act is abetted and a different act is done, the abettor is liable for the act done, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had directly abetted it: Provided that the act done was a probable consequence of the abetment, and was committed under the influence of the instigation, or with the aid or in pursuance of the conspiracy which constituted the abetment. Illustrations.—(a) A instigates a child to put poison into the food of Z, and gives him poison for that purpose. The child, in consequence of the instigation, by mistake puts the poison into the food of Y, which is by the side of that of Z. Here, if the child was acting under the influence of A's instigation, and the act done was under the circumstances a probable consequence of the abetment, A is liable in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had instigated the child to put the poison into the food of Y. (b) A instigates B to burn Z's house, B sets fire to the house and at the same time commits theft of property there. A, though guilty of abetting the burning of the house, is not guilty of abetting the theft; for the theft was a distinct act, and not a probable consequence of the burning. (c) A instigates B and C to break into an inhabited house at midnight for the purpose of robbery, and provides them with arms for that purpose. B and C break into the house, and being resisted by Z, one of the inmates, murder Z. Here, if that murder was the probable consequence of the abetment, A is liable to the punishment provided for murder.
key_terms: probable-consequence liability for a different act done

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 51 extends an abettor's liability beyond the exact act abetted to a different act actually done, but only where that different act was a probable consequence of the abetment and was committed under the influence of the instigation, aid, or conspiracy. The three illustrations mark the line: a mistaken-target poisoning remains within probable consequence, but an opportunistic theft committed alongside an abetted arson is a distinct, unconnected act outside the abettor's liability.
essential_elements: A different act (not the one literally abetted) is actually done by the person abetted.
That different act must be a probable consequence of the abetment.
The different act must be committed under the influence of the instigation, or with the aid, or in pursuance of the conspiracy constituting the abetment.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A distinct, independently-motivated act (such as opportunistic theft during an abetted arson) falls outside this extended liability.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 51 is the 'probable consequence' extension of abetment liability — read its three illustrations together, since they are the clearest guide to where courts draw the probable-versus-distinct-act line.

sections.title: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done
sections.raw_text: If the act for which the abettor is liable under section 51 is committed in addition to the act abetted, and constitute a distinct offence, the abettor is liable to punishment for each of the offences. Illustration.—A instigates B to resist by force a distress made by a public servant. B, in consequence, resists that distress. In offering the resistance, B voluntarily causes grievous hurt to the officer executing the distress. As B has committed both the offence of resisting the distress, and the offence of voluntarily causing grievous hurt, B is liable to punishment for both these offences; and, if A knew that B was likely voluntarily to cause grievous hurt in resisting the distress, A will also be liable to punishment for each of the offences.
key_terms: cumulative punishment for act abetted and act done

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 52 addresses the case where the act done under Section 51 is committed in addition to (not instead of) the act actually abetted, and the two constitute separate, distinct offences — in that situation the abettor, like the principal, is liable to be punished separately for each offence, not just once.
essential_elements: The additional act done under Section 51 is committed in addition to the act abetted.
The act abetted and the act done each independently constitute a distinct offence.
The abettor is then punished for both offences cumulatively.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 52 is a narrow extension of Section 51 for the 'both acts happened' scenario — it does not create a new form of abetment, only a cumulative-punishment consequence when two distinct offences both flow from the same episode of abetment.

sections.title: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor
sections.raw_text: When an act is abetted with the intention on the part of the abettor of causing a particular effect, and an act for which the abettor is liable in consequence of the abetment, causes a different effect from that intended by the abettor, the abettor is liable for the effect caused, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had abetted the act with the intention of causing that effect, provided he knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect. Illustration.—A instigates B to cause grievous hurt to Z. B, in consequence of the instigation, causes grievous hurt to Z. Z dies in consequence. Here, if A knew that the grievous hurt abetted was likely to cause death, A is liable to be punished with the punishment provided for murder.
key_terms: liability for an unintended effect known to be likely

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 53 fixes the abettor's liability where the act actually abetted is carried out as intended, but produces a graver or different effect than the abettor meant — the abettor is liable for that actual effect (as though it had been intended) provided the abettor knew the abetted act was likely to cause that effect. The grievous-hurt-escalating-to-death illustration shows the abettor becoming liable for murder, not merely for abetting grievous hurt.
essential_elements: The act abetted is carried out, but causes an effect different from (typically graver than) the one the abettor intended.
The abettor knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that different effect.
The abettor is then liable as though they had abetted the act with intent to cause that actual effect.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Without the abettor's knowledge that the graver effect was a likely consequence, liability does not escalate to match the actual outcome.
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish Section 53 (same act, unintended effect) from Section 51 (a different act altogether that was a probable consequence) — both extend abettor liability beyond the literal scope of the abetment, but on different triggers.

sections.title: Abettor present when offence is committed
sections.raw_text: Whenever any person, who is absent would be liable to be punished as an abettor, is present when the act or offence for which he would be punishable in consequence of the abetment is committed, he shall be deemed to have committed such act or offence.
key_terms: presence at the scene deeming abettor a principal

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 54 deems an abettor who is physically present when the abetted offence is actually committed to have committed the offence itself, not merely abetted it — collapsing the abetment/principal-offender distinction in cases of presence at the scene.
essential_elements: The person would, if absent, be liable only as an abettor.
That person is instead present when the abetted act or offence is actually committed.
Presence deems them to have committed the act or offence itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 54 is a short but powerful deeming provision — it converts what would otherwise be mere abetment liability into principal-offender liability purely on the fact of presence at the scene of commission.

sections.title: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life
sections.raw_text: Whoever abets the commission of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, shall, if that offence be not committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made under this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if any act for which the abettor is liable in consequence of the abetment, and which causes hurt to any person, is done, the abettor shall be liable to imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to fourteen years, and shall also be liable to fine. Illustration.—A instigates B to murder Z. The offence is not committed. If B had murdered Z, he would have been subject to the punishment of death or imprisonment for life. Therefore, A is liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and also to a fine; and if any hurt be done to Z in consequence of the abetment, he will be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to fourteen years, and to fine.
key_terms: abetment of an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment, uncommitted

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 55 fixes punishment for abetting an offence that itself carries death or life imprisonment, where that offence is not actually committed in consequence of the abetment: up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, rising to up to fourteen years plus fine if the abetted act, though not completing the main offence, causes hurt to any person.
essential_elements: The offence abetted must itself be punishable with death or imprisonment for life.
That offence must not actually be committed in consequence of the abetment.
No other express Sanhita provision fixes the punishment for that specific abetment.
Base punishment: up to seven years' imprisonment (either description) plus fine; enhanced to up to fourteen years plus fine if hurt is caused to any person by an act for which the abettor is liable.
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare Section 55 (offence not committed) against Section 49 (offence committed in consequence of abetment, attracting the full substantive punishment) — Section 55 is specifically the attempted-but-uncompleted abetment scenario for the gravest category of offences.

sections.title: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment
sections.raw_text: Whoever abets an offence punishable with imprisonment shall, if that offence be not committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made under this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term provided for that offence; or with such fine as is provided for that offence, or with both; and if the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant, whose duty it is to prevent the commission of such offence, the abettor shall be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the longest term provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both. Illustrations.—(a) A instigates B to give false evidence. Here, if B does not give false evidence, A has nevertheless committed the offence defined in this section, and is punishable accordingly. (b) A, a police officer, whose duty it is to prevent robbery, abets the commission of robbery. Here, though the robbery be not committed, A is liable to one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for that offence, and also to fine. (c) B abets the commission of a robbery by A, a police officer, whose duty it is to prevent that offence. Here, though the robbery be not committed, B is liable to one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for the offence of robbery, and also to fine.
key_terms: abetment of an imprisonment-only offence, uncommitted

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 56 is the parallel provision to Section 55 for offences punishable with imprisonment (not death or life imprisonment): if not committed in consequence of the abetment, the abettor is liable to up to one-fourth of the longest imprisonment term for that offence (or fine, or both) — doubled to up to one-half where either the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant whose duty was to prevent that very offence.
essential_elements: The offence abetted is punishable with imprisonment (any description) and is not death/life-imprisonment punishable.
That offence is not actually committed in consequence of the abetment.
Base punishment: up to one-fourth of the longest term provided for the offence, or fine, or both.
Enhanced to up to one-half of the longest term where the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant duty-bound to prevent that offence.
breakdown.how_to_read: Sections 55 and 56 form a matched pair graded by the gravity of the offence abetted — always check first whether the abetted offence carries death/life imprisonment (Section 55) or only imprisonment (Section 56) before computing the abettor's exposure.

sections.title: Abetting commission of offence by the public or by more than ten persons
sections.raw_text: Whoever abets the commission of an offence by the public generally or by any number or class of persons exceeding ten, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years and with fine. Illustration.—A affixes in a public place a placard instigating a sect consisting of more than ten members to meet at a certain time and place, for the purpose of attacking the members of an adverse sect, while engaged in a procession. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
key_terms: abetment directed at the public or a class exceeding ten persons

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 57 specifically criminalises abetment aimed not at a single identifiable person but at the public generally or at any group exceeding ten persons, fixing a flat punishment of up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine regardless of whether the mass-abetted offence is actually committed.
essential_elements: The abetment must be directed at the public generally, or at any number or class of persons exceeding ten.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to seven years, and fine (both mandatory, not alternative).
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 57 is a specialised, scale-driven abetment offence — useful for mass-instigation scenarios like inflammatory placards or broadcast calls to violence, independent of the general Sections 55-56 scheme.

sections.title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life
sections.raw_text: Whoever intending to facilitate or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby facilitate the commission of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, voluntarily conceals by any act or omission, or by the use of encryption or any other information hiding tool, the existence of a design to commit such offence or makes any representation which he knows to be false respecting such design shall,–– (a) if that offence be committed, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years; or (b) if the offence be not committed, with imprisonment of either description, for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine. Illustration.—A, knowing that dacoity is about to be committed at B, falsely informs the Magistrate that a dacoity is about to be committed at C, a place in an opposite direction, and thereby misleads the Magistrate with intent to facilitate the commission of the offence. The dacoity is committed at B in pursuance of the design. A is punishable under this section.
key_terms: concealment of design to commit a death/life-imprisonment offence

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 58 criminalises voluntarily concealing, or giving false information about, a known design to commit an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment, where the concealment or false representation is intended or known to be likely to facilitate that offence — a distinct wrong from abetment itself, punishing complicity through silence or misdirection. The Sanhita explicitly extends 'concealment' to cover use of encryption or any other information-hiding tool, addressing digital-age concealment methods the IPC's 1860 text could not contemplate.
essential_elements: The offence whose design is concealed must be punishable with death or imprisonment for life.
Concealment must be voluntary, by act, omission, encryption, or any other information-hiding tool — or a knowingly false representation about the design.
The accused must intend to facilitate, or know it likely to facilitate, the offence's commission.
Punishment graded by outcome: up to seven years if the offence is committed, up to three years if not, plus fine in either case.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 58's express mention of 'encryption or any other information hiding tool' is a notable BNS modernisation absent from the old IPC Section 118 — flag it when discussing what is genuinely new in the Sanhita versus carried over from the IPC.

sections.title: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant, intending to facilitate or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby facilitate the commission of an offence which it is his duty as such public servant to prevent, voluntarily conceals, by any act or omission or by the use of encryption or any other information hiding tool, the existence of a design to commit such offence, or makes any representation which he knows to be false respecting such design shall,–– (a) if the offence be committed, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the longest term of such imprisonment, or with such fine as is provided for that offence, or with both; or (b) if the offence be punishable with death or imprisonment for life, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years; or (c) if the offence be not committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term of such imprisonment or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both. Illustration.—A, an officer of police, being legally bound to give information of all designs to commit robbery which may come to his knowledge, and knowing that B designs to commit robbery, omits to give such information, with intent to so facilitate the commission of that offence. Here A has by an illegal omission concealed the existence of B's design, and is liable to punishment according to the provision of this section.
key_terms: public servant's heightened duty to disclose a known design

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 59 is a specially aggravated version of Section 58, applying only to a public servant who conceals a design to commit an offence that it was specifically that public servant's duty to prevent — the punishment is graded more severely than Section 58's general version, scaling up to one-half of the longest term for the offence, or up to ten years flat where the concealed offence itself carries death or life imprisonment.
essential_elements: The accused must be a public servant whose official duty was to prevent the very offence concealed.
Concealment by act, omission, encryption, or other information-hiding tool, or a knowingly false representation about the design.

Punishment grading: up to one-half of the longest term for the offence if committed; a flat up to ten years if the concealed offence carries death/life imprisonment; up to one-fourth if the offence is not committed.
breakdown.how_to_read: Sections 58 and 59 form a matched pair: Section 58 is the general concealment offence applicable to anyone; Section 59 raises the stakes specifically where the concealer is a public servant who had an official duty to prevent that very offence.

sections.title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment
sections.raw_text: Whoever, intending to facilitate or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby facilitate the commission of an offence punishable with imprisonment, voluntarily conceals, by any act or illegal omission, the existence of a design to commit such offence, or makes any representation which he knows to be false respecting such design shall,–– (a) if the offence be committed, be punished with imprisonment of the description provided for the offence, for a term which may extend to one-fourth; and (b) if the offence be not committed, to one-eighth, of the longest term of such imprisonment, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both.
key_terms: concealment of design to commit an imprisonment-only offence

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 60 is the residual concealment offence covering designs to commit offences that carry only imprisonment (not death or life imprisonment), scaled down from Sections 58-59: up to one-fourth of the longest imprisonment term if the offence is committed, and only up to one-eighth if it is not.
essential_elements: The concealed design relates to an offence punishable with imprisonment (not death/life imprisonment).
Concealment must be by act or illegal omission, or a knowingly false representation about the design.
Punishment: up to one-fourth of the longest term if the offence is committed, up to one-eighth if not, or fine, or both.
breakdown.how_to_read: Sections 58, 59, and 60 together form a three-tier concealment-of-design scheme graded purely by the gravity of the underlying offence: death/life imprisonment (58), the same but by a duty-bound public servant (59), and mere-imprisonment offences (60).

sections.title: Criminal conspiracy
sections.raw_text: (1) When two or more persons agree with the common object to do, or cause to be done–– (a) an illegal act; or (b) an act which is not illegal by illegal means, such an agreement is designated a criminal conspiracy: Provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof. Explanation.—It is immaterial whether the illegal act is the ultimate object of such agreement, or is merely incidental to that object. (2) Whoever is a party to a criminal conspiracy,–– (a) to commit an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a term of two years or upwards, shall, where no express provision is made in this Sanhita for the punishment of such a conspiracy, be punished in the same manner as if he had abetted such offence; (b) other than a criminal conspiracy to commit an offence punishable as aforesaid shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding six months, or with fine or with both.
key_terms: agreement as the gist of conspiracy

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 61 defines 'criminal conspiracy' as an agreement between two or more persons with the common object of doing (or causing to be done) either an illegal act, or a lawful act by illegal means. Crucially, where the agreement is itself to commit an offence, the agreement alone is enough to constitute the conspiracy; for any other kind of agreement within the definition, some overt act beyond the bare agreement must also be done by at least one party in pursuance of it. Sub-section (2) grades punishment by the gravity of the object offence: conspiracy to commit an offence carrying death, life imprisonment, or two-plus years' rigorous imprisonment is punished as though the conspirator had abetted that offence; all other criminal conspiracies draw a flat cap of six months' imprisonment, fine, or both.
essential_elements: An agreement between two or more persons with a common object.
The object is either (a) an illegal act, or (b) a legal act accomplished by illegal means.
Where the agreement itself is to commit an offence, the agreement alone suffices for liability.
For any other agreement within the definition, an overt act beyond the bare agreement, done by at least one party in pursuance of it, is required.
Punishment is graded: same as abetment of the object offence where that offence carries death/life/2+ years' rigorous imprisonment; otherwise capped at six months plus/or fine.
exceptions_and_qualifications: It is immaterial under the Explanation whether the illegal act was the agreement's ultimate object or merely incidental to it.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 61 is the BNS's codification of criminal conspiracy as a distinct substantive offence (not merely a mode of abetment under Section 45(b)) — note carefully the proviso's overt-act requirement, which applies to all conspiracies except those aimed directly at committing an offence.

sections.title: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment
sections.raw_text: Whoever attempts to commit an offence punishable by this Sanhita with imprisonment for life or imprisonment, or to cause such an offence to be committed, and in such attempt does any act towards the commission of the offence, shall, where no express provision is made by this Sanhita for the punishment of such attempt, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the imprisonment for life or, as the case may be, one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both. Illustrations.—(a) A makes an attempt to steal some jewels by breaking open a box, and finds after so opening the box, that there is no jewel in it. He has done an act towards the commission of theft, and therefore is guilty under this section. (b) A makes an attempt to pick the pocket of Z by thrusting his hand into Z's pocket. A fails in the attempt in consequence of Z's having nothing in his pocket. A is guilty under this section.
key_terms: act towards the commission of the offence

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 62 is the Sanhita's general, residual provision punishing attempts: where a person attempts to commit an offence punishable with life imprisonment or any other imprisonment, and in that attempt does some act towards the offence's commission, and no other provision fixes a specific attempt punishment, the attempt draws up to one-half of the maximum punishment for the completed offence (plus or instead, fine). Both illustrations confirm that an attempt is punishable even where it was factually impossible to succeed (an empty box, an empty pocket) — what matters is the act done towards commission, not the possibility of completion.
essential_elements: An attempt to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment for life or any imprisonment.
Some act must actually be done towards the commission of that offence (mere preparation is insufficient).
No other express Sanhita provision fixes a specific punishment for attempting that particular offence.
Punishment: up to one-half of the life-imprisonment-or-longest-term maximum for the completed offence, or fine as provided for the offence, or both.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Factual impossibility of completing the offence (e.g. an empty box or pocket) does not bar conviction for attempt, so long as an act towards commission was done.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 62 closes Chapter IV as the general attempt provision — always check first whether a specific offence elsewhere in the Sanhita already prescribes its own attempt punishment (the section's 'no express provision' qualifier) before falling back on this residual one-half-of-maximum rule.

sections.title: Rape
sections.raw_text: A man is said to commit “rape” if he— (a) penetrates his penis, to any extent, into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or (b) inserts, to any extent, any object or a part of the body, not being the penis, into the vagina, the urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or (c) manipulates any part of the body of a woman so as to cause penetration into the vagina, urethra, anus or any part of body of such woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or (d) applies his mouth to the vagina, anus, urethra of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person, under the circumstances falling under any of the following seven descriptions:— (i) against her will; (ii) without her consent; (iii) with her consent, when her consent has been obtained by putting her or any person in whom she is interested, in fear of death or of hurt; (iv) with her consent, when the man knows that he is not her husband and that her consent is given because she believes that he is another man to whom she is or believes herself to be lawfully married; (v) with her consent when, at the time of giving such consent, by reason of unsoundness of mind or intoxication or the administration by him personally or through another of any stupefying or unwholesome substance, she is unable to understand the nature and consequences of that to which she gives consent; (vi) with or without her consent, when she is under eighteen years of age; (vii) when she is unable to communicate consent. Explanation 1.—For the purposes of this section, “vagina” shall also include labia majora. Explanation 2.—Consent means an unequivocal voluntary agreement when the woman by words, gestures or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication, communicates willingness to participate in the specific sexual act: Provided that a woman who does not physically resist to the act of penetration shall not by the reason only of that fact, be regarded as consenting to the sexual activity. Exception 1.—A medical procedure or intervention shall not constitute rape. Exception 2.—Sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under eighteen years of age, is not rape.
key_terms: consent obtained by impersonation of husband

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 63 defines rape through four alternative acts of penetration or sexual contact (listed in clauses (a)-(d)) combined with any one of seven circumstances (listed (i)-(vii)) that vitiate true consent — absence of will, absence of consent, consent obtained by fear, consent obtained through impersonation of the husband, incapacity to understand the act's nature due to unsoundness of mind/intoxication, the victim being under eighteen regardless of purported consent, or inability to communicate consent at all. Explanation 2's proviso clarifies that physical non-resistance alone does not amount to consent. Two Exceptions carve out genuine medical procedures and (with the wife not being under eighteen) marital sexual relations from the definition.
essential_elements: One of the four acts in clauses (a)-(d) — various forms of penetration or oral contact.
Combined with at least one of the seven vitiating circumstances in clauses (i)-(vii).
Consent requires an unequivocal, voluntary, communicated agreement (Explanation 2) — mere physical non-resistance is not consent.
A woman under eighteen years of age cannot in law give effective consent to the act (clause (vi)).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Exception 1: a genuine medical procedure or intervention does not constitute rape.
Exception 2: sexual intercourse or acts by a man with his own wife, provided she is not under eighteen, is excluded from the definition.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 63 is the gateway definitional provision for the whole sexual-offences sub-chapter — Sections 64-66 then supply the graded punishments for rape as here defined, so always check the two Exceptions before assuming a given act falls within the definition.

sections.title: Punishment for rape
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever, except in the cases provided for in sub-section (2), commits rape, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than ten years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. (2) Whoever,— (a) being a police officer, commits rape,— (i) within the limits of the police station to which such police officer is appointed; or (ii) in the premises of any station house; or (iii) on a woman in such police officer's custody or in the custody of a police officer subordinate to such police officer; or (b) being a public servant, commits rape on a woman in such public servant's custody or in the custody of a public servant subordinate to such public servant; or (c) being a member of the armed forces deployed in an area by the Central Government or a State Government commits rape in such area; or (d) being on the management or on the staff of a jail, remand home or other place of custody established by or under any law for the time being in force or of a women's or children's institution, commits rape on any inmate of such jail, remand home, place or institution; or (e) being on the management or on the staff of a hospital, commits rape on a woman in that hospital; or (f) being a relative, guardian or teacher of, or a person in a position of trust or authority towards the woman, commits rape on such woman; or (g) commits rape during communal or sectarian violence; or (h) commits rape on a woman knowing her to be pregnant; or (i) commits rape, on a woman incapable of giving consent; or (j) being in a position of control or dominance over a woman, commits rape on such woman; or (k) commits rape on a woman suffering from mental or physical disability; or (l) while committing rape causes grievous bodily harm or maims or disfigures or endangers the life of a woman; or (m) commits rape repeatedly on the same woman, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section,— (a) “armed forces” means the naval, army and air forces and includes any member of the Armed Forces constituted under any law for the time being in force, including the paramilitary forces and any auxiliary forces that are under the control of the Central Government or the State Government; (b) “hospital” means the precincts of the hospital and includes the precincts of any institution for the reception and treatment of persons during convalescence or of persons requiring medical attention or rehabilitation; (c) “police officer” shall have the same meaning as assigned to the expression “police” under the Police Act, 1861; (d) “women's or children's institution” means an institution, whether called an orphanage or a home for neglected women or children or a widow's home or an institution called by any other name, which is established and maintained for the reception and care of women or children.
key_terms: aggravated rape by persons in custodial or institutional authority

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 64 fixes the punishment for rape as defined in Section 63: a non-negotiable minimum of ten years' rigorous imprisonment, extendable to life imprisonment, plus fine, for ordinary rape under sub-section (1); and the same minimum-to-life range but with 'life imprisonment' expressly meaning imprisonment for the remainder of the offender's natural life, for a long enumerated list of aggravated circumstances under sub-section (2) — rape by police officers, other public servants, armed-forces personnel, custodial/institutional staff, relatives/guardians/teachers/persons of trust, during communal violence, of a pregnant or consent-incapable or disabled woman, with grievous injury, or repeated rape of the same woman.
essential_elements: Base offence (sub-section (1)): minimum ten years' rigorous imprisonment, up to life imprisonment, plus fine.
Aggravated offence (sub-section (2), clauses (a)-(m)): same minimum-to-life range but 'life imprisonment' is defined to mean the remainder of the offender's natural life.
The aggravating circumstances turn principally on an abuse of custodial, institutional, professional, or positional authority, or on the vulnerability of the victim or severity of the resulting harm.
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the critical distinction in how 'imprisonment for life' is defined between sub-section (1) (ordinary life-imprisonment meaning, open to remission per general sentencing law) and sub-section (2) (expressly fixed at the remainder of natural life) — this distinction recurs throughout the chapter wherever the phrase appears.

sections.title: Punishment for rape in certain cases
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever, commits rape on a woman under sixteen years of age shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than twenty years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, and shall also be liable to fine: Provided that such fine shall be just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses and rehabilitation of the victim: Provided further that any fine imposed under this sub-section shall be paid to the victim. (2) Whoever, commits rape on a woman under twelve years of age shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than twenty years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, and with fine or with death: Provided that such fine shall be just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses and rehabilitation of the victim: Provided further that any fine imposed under this sub-section shall be paid to the victim.
key_terms: rape of a minor under sixteen
rape of a minor under twelve
capital punishment for rape of a child under twelve

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 65 further escalates punishment for rape where the victim is a minor: rape of a woman under sixteen draws a minimum of twenty years' rigorous imprisonment up to life imprisonment (meaning the remainder of natural life) plus a fine reserved for the victim's medical and rehabilitation needs; rape of a girl under twelve carries the same minimum-twenty-years-to-life range but opens the possibility of a death sentence, with the fine again directed to the victim's benefit, not the State.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): victim under sixteen years — minimum twenty years' rigorous imprisonment up to life imprisonment (full natural life), plus fine.
Sub-section (2): victim under twelve years — minimum twenty years up to life imprisonment (full natural life), with fine or with death.
In both sub-sections, the fine must be just and reasonable to cover the victim's medical expenses and rehabilitation, and is payable to the victim, not the State treasury.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Sections 64 and 65 together as a three-tier severity ladder by victim age/circumstance: ordinary/aggravated rape (64) → rape of a victim under sixteen (65(1)) → rape of a victim under twelve, which alone opens the death penalty (65(2)).

sections.title: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim
sections.raw_text: Whoever, commits an offence punishable under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) of section 64 and in the course of such commission inflicts an injury which causes the death of the woman or causes the woman to be in a persistent vegetative state, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than twenty years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, or with death.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 66 escalates punishment further still where an injury inflicted in the course of committing rape under Section 64 causes the victim's death or leaves her in a persistent vegetative state — the offender faces a minimum of twenty years' rigorous imprisonment, up to life imprisonment (full natural life), or death.
essential_elements: The underlying offence must be rape punishable under Section 64(1) or (2).
In the course of committing that offence, an injury is inflicted that causes either the victim's death or a persistent vegetative state.
Punishment: minimum twenty years' rigorous imprisonment, up to life imprisonment (full natural life), or death.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 66 is causation-driven — it does not require an intention to kill, only that the death or persistent vegetative state resulted from an injury inflicted during the commission of the rape.

sections.title: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation
sections.raw_text: Whoever has sexual intercourse with his own wife, who is living separately, whether under a decree of separation or otherwise, without her consent, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than two years but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation.—In this section, “sexual intercourse” shall mean any of the acts mentioned in clauses (a) to (d) of section 63.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 67 criminalises non-consensual sexual intercourse by a husband with his wife during a period of separation (whether formalised by a decree or otherwise), fixing a distinct, lower punishment band (two to seven years plus fine) than ordinary rape under Section 64 — this remains a narrower offence than rape itself, operative only during the separation.
essential_elements: The parties must be husband and wife, living separately (formally decreed or otherwise).
Sexual intercourse (as defined by cross-reference to Section 63's clauses (a)-(d)) occurs without the wife's consent.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description for two to seven years, plus fine.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 67 fills a narrow gap left by Section 63 Exception 2 (which excludes ordinary marital intercourse from rape) — it applies specifically to the separation scenario, with its own distinct, lesser punishment scale.

sections.title: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being— (a) in a position of authority or in a fiduciary relationship; or (b) a public servant; or (c) superintendent or manager of a jail, remand home or other place of custody established by or under any law for the time being in force, or a women's or children's institution; or (d) on the management of a hospital or being on the staff of a hospital, abuses such position or fiduciary relationship to induce or seduce any woman either in his custody or under his charge or present in the premises to have sexual intercourse with him, such sexual intercourse not amounting to the offence of rape, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than five years, but which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation 1.—In this section, “sexual intercourse” shall mean any of the acts mentioned in clauses (a) to (d) of section 63. Explanation 2.—For the purposes of this section, Explanation 1 to section 63 shall also be applicable. Explanation 3.—“Superintendent”, in relation to a jail, remand home or other place of custody or a women's or children's institution, includes a person holding any other office in such jail, remand home, place or institution by virtue of which such person can exercise any authority or control over its inmates.
