exceptions_and_qualifications: The lower two-year punishment ceiling applies only to registered medical practitioners (as statutorily defined by reference to the National Medical Commission Act, 2019) acting within a medical procedure — not to unregistered practitioners or acts outside a medical procedure
breakdown.how_to_read: Sub-section (2) is a deliberate, significant departure from the former IPC's Section 304A (which had no hit-and-run enhancement) — it was a major point of public controversy when first proposed, since it roughly doubles exposure for drivers who flee an accident scene instead of reporting it.

sections.title: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind
sections.raw_text: If any child, any person of unsound mind, any delirious person or any person in a state of intoxication, commits suicide, whoever abets the commission of such suicide, shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: abetment of suicide of a vulnerable person

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 107 BNS imposes a severe, murder-adjacent punishment band (death, life imprisonment, or up to ten years, plus fine) on anyone who abets the suicide of a victim drawn from four vulnerable categories — a child, a person of unsound mind, a delirious person, or an intoxicated person — reflecting the law's view that such victims cannot meaningfully exercise free will in taking their own lives, making the abettor's culpability closer to that of a killer than an ordinary abettor of suicide.
essential_elements: The victim falls within one of four categories: a child, a person of unsound mind, a delirious person, or a person in a state of intoxication
That victim commits suicide
The accused abetted (instigated, conspired in, or intentionally aided) that suicide
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare directly with Section 101's Exception 5 illustration: instigating a child's suicide is treated as abetment of murder in that illustration, while Section 107 provides the companion, more specifically-targeted standalone offence covering the same vulnerable-victim rationale across all four incapacity categories, not just children.

sections.title: Abetment of suicide
sections.raw_text: If any person commits suicide, whoever abets the commission of such suicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 108 BNS is the general abetment-of-suicide offence, applicable whenever any person (not limited to the vulnerable categories in Section 107) commits suicide and another person abetted that act — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine, without the death-penalty/life-imprisonment exposure that Section 107 carries for vulnerable victims.
essential_elements: The victim (of any age or mental capacity) commits suicide
The accused abetted that suicide through instigation, conspiracy, or intentional aid
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Sections 107 and 108 as a matched pair graded purely by victim vulnerability: identical conduct (abetting a suicide) draws a dramatically harsher punishment band under Section 107 if the victim was a child, of unsound mind, delirious, or intoxicated, and the ordinary Section 108 band otherwise.

sections.title: Attempt to murder
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge, and under such circumstances that, if he by that act caused death, he would be guilty of murder, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if hurt is caused to any person by such act, the offender shall be liable either to imprisonment for life, or to such punishment as is hereinbefore mentioned.
(2) When any person offending under sub-section (1) is under sentence of imprisonment for life, he may, if hurt is caused, be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person's natural life.
Illustrations.
(a) A shoots at Z with intention to kill him, under such circumstances that, if death ensued, A would be guilty of murder. A is liable to punishment under this section.
(b) A, with the intention of causing the death of a child of tender years, exposes it in a desert place. A has committed the offence defined by this section, though the death of the child does not ensue.
(c) A, intending to murder Z, buys a gun and loads it. A has not yet committed the offence. A fires the gun at Z. He has committed the offence defined in this section, and, if by such firing he wounds Z, he is liable to the punishment provided by the latter part of sub-section (1).
(d) A, intending to murder Z by poison, purchases poison and mixes the same with food which remains in A's keeping; A has not yet committed the offence defined in this section. A places the food on Z's table or delivers it to Z's servants to place it on Z's table. A has committed the offence defined in this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 109 BNS punishes attempted murder — doing an act with the intention/knowledge and in circumstances that would make the offender guilty of murder had death actually resulted — with up to ten years, rising to life imprisonment if the attempt causes hurt. Sub-section (2) layers on a life-convict enhancement mirroring Section 104: a life-convict who attempts murder and causes hurt may face death or whole-life imprisonment.
essential_elements: An act done with the intention or knowledge, and under circumstances, that would constitute murder if death resulted
Death does not actually result (otherwise Section 101/103 would apply instead)
Enhanced punishment (life imprisonment) if the act causes hurt to any person
Sub-section (2): offender was already under a life sentence when the attempt (causing hurt) occurred
breakdown.how_to_read: Illustrations (c) and (d) are the classic attempt-threshold teaching examples — mere preparation (buying/loading a gun, mixing poison and keeping it) is not yet an attempt, but the moment the offender fires or actually delivers the poisoned food towards the victim, the Section 62 'act towards commission' threshold is crossed and Section 109 is complete.

sections.title: Attempt to commit culpable homicide
sections.raw_text:
Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge and under such circumstances that, if he by that act caused death, he would be guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both; and, if hurt is caused to any person by such act, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both.
Illustration.
A, on grave and sudden provocation, fires a pistol at Z, under such circumstances that if he thereby caused death, he would be guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
key_terms: attempt to commit culpable homicide not amounting to murder

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 110 BNS is the attempt-level mirror of Section 105: where an act, had it caused death, would have amounted only to culpable homicide not amounting to murder (e.g. because a Section 101 Exception like grave-and-sudden-provocation would have applied), the attempt itself draws a much lighter punishment band — up to three years, rising to seven if hurt actually results — than attempted murder under Section 109.
essential_elements: An act done with the intention/knowledge, and under circumstances, that would amount to culpable homicide not amounting to murder if death resulted
Death does not actually result
Enhanced punishment (up to seven years) if hurt is caused
breakdown.how_to_read: Grading logic travels downward in lockstep across the homicide-attempt scheme: Section 101 Exceptions reduce a completed killing from murder to Section 105 culpable homicide; the same Exception-driven facts, applied to an unsuccessful attempt, pull the attempt down from Section 109 to this lighter Section 110 band.

sections.title: Organised crime
sections.raw_text:
(1) Any continuing unlawful activity including kidnapping, robbery, vehicle theft, extortion, land grabbing, contract killing, economic offence, cyber-crimes, trafficking of persons, drugs, weapons or illicit goods or services, human trafficking for prostitution or ransom, by any person or a group of persons acting in concert, singly or jointly, either as a member of an organised crime syndicate or on behalf of such syndicate, by use of violence, threat of violence, intimidation, coercion, or by any other unlawful means to obtain direct or indirect material benefit including a financial benefit, shall constitute organised crime.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section,––
(i) "organised crime syndicate" means a group of two or more persons who, acting either singly or jointly, as a syndicate or gang indulge in any continuing unlawful activity;
(ii) "continuing unlawful activity" means an activity prohibited by law which is a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment of three years or more, undertaken by any person, either singly or jointly, as a member of an organised crime syndicate or on behalf of such syndicate in respect of which more than one charge-sheets have been filed before a competent Court within the preceding period of ten years and that Court has taken cognizance of such offence, and includes economic offence;
(iii) "economic offence" includes criminal breach of trust, forgery, counterfeiting of currency-notes, bank-notes and Government stamps, hawala transaction, mass-marketing fraud or running any scheme to defraud several persons or doing any act in any manner with a view to defraud any bank or financial institution or any other institution or organisation for obtaining monetary benefits in any form.
(2) Whoever commits organised crime shall,—
(a) if such offence has resulted in the death of any person, be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than ten lakh rupees;
(b) in any other case, be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than five lakh rupees.
(3) Whoever abets, attempts, conspires or knowingly facilitates the commission of an organised crime, or otherwise engages in any act preparatory to an organised crime, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than five lakh rupees.
(4) Any person who is a member of an organised crime syndicate shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than five lakh rupees.
(5) Whoever, intentionally, harbours or conceals any person who has committed the offence of an organised crime shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than five lakh rupees:
Provided that this sub-section shall not apply to any case in which the harbour or concealment is by the spouse of the offender.
(6) Whoever possesses any property derived or obtained from the commission of an organised crime or proceeds of any organised crime or which has been acquired through the organised crime, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than two lakh rupees.
(7) If any person on behalf of a member of an organised crime syndicate is, or at any time has been in possession of movable or immovable property which he cannot satisfactorily account for, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to imprisonment for ten years and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than one lakh rupees.
key_terms: membership of an organised crime syndicate
unaccounted property linked to organised crime

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 111 BNS is an entirely new, MCOCA/state-organised-crime-Act-style provision — the first time general central criminal law has directly codified organised crime as a standalone Sanhita offence. It defines organised crime through a 'continuing unlawful activity' threshold requiring multiple charge-sheets over ten years against a syndicate, lists a wide range of predicate activities (kidnapping, extortion, trafficking, land grabbing, cyber-crime, economic offences), and then separately punishes commission (2), abetment/conspiracy/facilitation (3), mere membership (4), harbouring an offender (5, with a spousal carve-out), possession of crime proceeds (6), and unaccounted property held on a syndicate member's behalf (7).
essential_elements: A 'continuing unlawful activity' as statutorily defined — a cognizable offence punishable with three-plus years' imprisonment, pursued by/on behalf of a syndicate, with more than one charge-sheet filed and cognizance taken within the preceding ten years
Committed by a person or group acting in concert, as or on behalf of an organised crime syndicate (two or more persons acting as a syndicate or gang)
Through violence, threat of violence, intimidation, coercion, or other unlawful means
To obtain direct or indirect material/financial benefit
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-section (5)'s harbouring/concealment offence does not apply where the harbourer or concealer is the offender's spouse
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat sub-section (1)'s Explanation as the real gatekeeper: unless the 'continuing unlawful activity' and 'organised crime syndicate' definitional thresholds (especially the multiple-charge-sheet, ten-year window) are satisfied, a string of predicate offences — however serious individually — does not elevate into 'organised crime' under this section; sub-sections (2)-(7) then layer distinct, independently chargeable offences onto that base definition.

sections.title: Petty organised crime
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever, being a member of a group or gang, either singly or jointly, commits any act of theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorised selling of tickets, unauthorised betting or gambling, selling of public examination question papers or any other similar criminal act, is said to commit petty organised crime.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section "theft" includes trick theft, theft from vehicle, dwelling house or business premises, cargo theft, pick pocketing, theft through card skimming, shoplifting and theft of Automated Teller Machine.
(2) Whoever commits any petty organised crime shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 112 BNS creates a lesser, lower-threshold sibling to Section 111: 'petty organised crime' covers group or gang members committing lower-level property and fraud offences — theft in its many modern forms (card skimming, ATM theft, cargo theft), snatching, cheating, ticket touting, illegal betting, or exam-paper leaks — without Section 111's demanding 'continuing unlawful activity' threshold, punishable with one to seven years plus fine.
essential_elements: The offender is a member of a group or gang
Acting singly or jointly as such a member

Commits theft (in any of the Explanation's listed modern forms), snatching, cheating, unauthorised ticket selling, unauthorised betting/gambling, selling of public examination question papers, or any other similar criminal act
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 112 was added specifically to address organised street-level and small-gang crime (pickpocket rings, ATM-skimming gangs, exam-paper-leak rackets) that falls well short of Section 111's syndicate-level organised crime threshold but still warrants gang-based aggravated punishment beyond the ordinary individual theft/cheating offences.

sections.title: Terrorist act
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever does any act with the intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India or with the intent to strike terror or likely to strike terror in the people or any section of the people in India or in any foreign country,––
(a) by using bombs, dynamite or other explosive substance or inflammable substance or firearms or other lethal weapons or poisonous or noxious gases or other chemicals or by any other substance (whether biological, radioactive, nuclear or otherwise) of a hazardous nature or by any other means of whatever nature to cause or likely to cause,—
(i) death of, or injury to, any person or persons; or
(ii) loss of, or damage to, or destruction of, property; or
(iii) disruption of any supplies or services essential to the life of the community in India or in any foreign country; or
(iv) damage to, the monetary stability of India by way of production or smuggling or circulation of counterfeit Indian paper currency, coin or of any other material; or
(v) damage or destruction of any property in India or in a foreign country used or intended to be used for the defence of India or in connection with any other purposes of the Government of India, any State Government or any of their agencies; or
(b) overawes by means of criminal force or the show of criminal force or attempts to do so or causes death of any public functionary or attempts to cause death of any public functionary; or
(c) detains, kidnaps or abducts any person and threatening to kill or injure such person or does any other act in order to compel the Government of India, any State Government or the Government of a foreign country or an international or inter-governmental organisation or any other person to do or abstain from doing any act,
commit a terrorist act.
Explanation.—For the purpose of this sub-section,—
(a) "public functionary" means the constitutional authorities or any other functionary notified in the Official Gazette by the Central Government as public functionary;
(b) "counterfeit Indian currency" means the counterfeit currency as may be declared after examination by an authorised or notified forensic authority that such currency imitates or compromises with the key security features of Indian currency.
(2) Whoever commits a terrorist act shall,—
(a) if such offence has resulted in the death of any person, be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine;
(b) in any other case, be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
(3) Whoever conspires or attempts to commit, or advocates, abets, advises or incites, directly or knowingly facilitates the commission of a terrorist act or any act preparatory to the commission of a terrorist act, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
(4) Whoever organises or causes to be organised any camp or camps for imparting training in terrorist act, or recruits or causes to be recruited any person or persons for commission of a terrorist act, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
(5) Any person who is a member of an organisation which is involved in terrorist act, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
(6) Whoever voluntarily harbours or conceals, or attempts to harbour or conceal any person knowing that such person has committed a terrorist act shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine:
Provided that this sub-section shall not apply to any case in which the harbour or concealment is by the spouse of the offender.
(7) Whoever knowingly possesses any property derived or obtained from commission of any terrorist act or acquired through the commission of any terrorist act shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
Explanation.—For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that the officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police shall decide whether to register the case under this section or under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 113 BNS is another entirely new provision bringing a UAPA-style terrorist-act offence directly into general criminal law for the first time. Sub-section (1) defines 'terrorist act' through an intent-to-threaten-India's-sovereignty/security-or-strike-terror threshold combined with any of three means: using explosive/hazardous substances to cause death, property damage, essential-supply disruption, or currency destabilisation (clause (a)); overawing or killing a public functionary by criminal force (clause (b)); or hostage-taking/kidnapping to compel government or international action (clause (c)). Sub-sections (2)-(7) separately punish commission, conspiracy/abetment/facilitation, running training camps or recruiting, mere membership of a terrorist organisation, harbouring (with a spousal carve-out), and possession of terrorism-linked property. A final Explanation requires a Superintendent-of-Police-or-above officer to decide whether to register under this section or the separate Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.
essential_elements: An act done with intent (or likely) to threaten India's unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security, or to strike terror in people in India or a foreign country

Carried out through one of clauses (a)-(c): hazardous-substance attacks causing/likely to cause death, property damage, essential-service disruption, or currency destabilisation; overawing or killing a public functionary; or detention/kidnapping/abduction to compel government or international action
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-section (6)'s harbouring/concealment offence does not apply where the harbourer or concealer is the offender's spouse
The final Explanation leaves registration choice (this section vs. the UAPA, 1967) to an officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police, rather than mandating one statute over the other
breakdown.how_to_read: Because this duplicates ground long covered by the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, practitioners should always check which statute a given prosecution is actually brought under — the final Explanation makes that an executive charging decision, not an automatic rule, and the two regimes carry materially different procedural safeguards (e.g. bail standards, designated courts).

sections.title: Hurt
sections.raw_text: Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 114 BNS supplies the foundational, deliberately broad definition of 'hurt' — any bodily pain, disease, or infirmity caused to another person — which anchors the entire hurt/grievous-hurt offence ladder that follows in Sections 115-125.
essential_elements: Causing bodily pain, disease, or infirmity
To any person
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a pure definitional section with no punishment of its own — every operative hurt offence (Sections 115 onward) borrows this definition and then adds its own mental-element and aggravating-circumstance requirements.

sections.title: Voluntarily causing hurt
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever does any act with the intention of thereby causing hurt to any person, or with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause hurt to any person, and does thereby cause hurt to any person, is said "voluntarily to cause hurt".
(2) Whoever, except in the case provided for by sub-section (1) of section 122 voluntarily causes hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 115 BNS defines and punishes the base offence of voluntarily causing hurt — intentionally or knowingly causing bodily pain, disease, or infirmity (as defined in Section 114) — with up to one year's imprisonment, a fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both, subject to the lower provocation-based punishment in Section 122(1) where applicable.
essential_elements: An act done with the intention of causing hurt, or with knowledge that hurt is a likely consequence
Hurt is actually caused to a person as a result
exceptions_and_qualifications: Section 122(1)'s lighter, provocation-based punishment applies instead where the hurt was caused on grave and sudden provocation without intent/knowledge of harming anyone beyond the provoker
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the baseline against which every aggravated hurt offence in the Chapter (by dangerous weapons, for extortion, against public servants, by acid, etc.) adds a specific aggravating circumstance or purpose to increase the punishment well beyond this one-year ceiling.

sections.title: Grievous hurt

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 116 BNS supplies a closed, exhaustive list of eight specific categories of hurt that qualify as 'grievous' — ranging from permanent physical losses (sight, hearing, a limb or joint) to fractures and life-endangering or fifteen-day-disabling injuries. Only hurt falling within one of these eight categories counts as grievous for the purposes of every grievous-hurt offence elsewhere in the Sanhita; the list is not illustrative, it is exhaustive.
essential_elements: The hurt caused must fall within one of the eight named categories (a)-(h)
breakdown.how_to_read: Category (h) is the most frequently contested in practice — the fifteen-day severe-pain/inability-to-pursue-ordinary-activities threshold is a question of medical and factual evidence, usually proven through the treating doctor's testimony and medical records.

sections.title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt, if the hurt which he intends to cause or knows himself to be likely to cause is grievous hurt, and if the hurt which he causes is grievous hurt, is said "voluntarily to cause grievous hurt".
Explanation.—A person is not said voluntarily to cause grievous hurt except when he both causes grievous hurt and intends or knows himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt. But he is said voluntarily to cause grievous hurt, if intending or knowing himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt of one kind, he actually causes grievous hurt of another kind.
Illustration.
A, intending of knowing himself to be likely permanently to disfigure Z's face, gives Z a blow which does not permanently disfigure Z's face, but which causes Z to suffer severe bodily pain for the space of fifteen days. A has voluntarily caused grievous hurt.
(2) Whoever, except in the case provided for by sub-section (2) of section 122, voluntarily causes grievous hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
(3) Whoever commits an offence under sub-section (1) and in the course of such commission causes any hurt to a person which causes that person to be in permanent disability or in persistent vegetative state, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life.
(4) When a group of five or more persons acting in concert, causes grievous hurt to a person on the ground of his race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be guilty of the offence of causing grievous hurt, and shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: grievous hurt of a different kind than intended
permanent disability or persistent vegetative state from grievous hurt

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 117 BNS defines and punishes voluntarily causing grievous hurt: both intent/knowledge of likely grievous hurt and actual grievous hurt (as defined in Section 116) must be present, though the Explanation clarifies that the kind of grievous hurt intended need not match the kind actually caused. The base punishment is up to seven years. Sub-section (3) escalates sharply — ten years to life — where the act results in permanent disability or persistent vegetative state. Sub-section (4) mirrors Section 103(2)'s mob-violence provision, extending group liability for discriminatory-ground grievous hurt to every member of a five-or-more group acting in concert.
essential_elements: An act causing grievous hurt (as defined in Section 116)
Done with intention or knowledge of likely grievous hurt (of any kind — not necessarily the specific kind actually caused)
Sub-section (3): the grievous hurt results in permanent disability or persistent vegetative state
Sub-section (4): caused by a five-or-more-person group acting in concert on a discriminatory ground
exceptions_and_qualifications: Section 122(2)'s lighter, provocation-based punishment applies instead where the grievous hurt was caused on grave and sudden provocation
breakdown.how_to_read: The Explanation's 'different kind of grievous hurt' rule is a frequent examination and courtroom point — liability does not fail merely because the actual injury (e.g. fifteen-day severe pain) differs from the originally intended injury (e.g. permanent disfigurement), so long as both qualify as grievous hurt under Section 116.

sections.title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever, except in the case provided for by sub-section (1) of section 122, voluntarily causes hurt by means of any instrument for shooting, stabbing or cutting, or any instrument which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, or by means of fire or any heated substance, or by means of any poison or any corrosive substance, or by means of any explosive substance, or by means of any substance which it is deleterious to the human body to inhale, to swallow, or to receive into the blood, or by means of any animal, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to twenty thousand rupees, or with both.
(2) Whoever, except in the case provided for by sub-section (2) of section 122, voluntarily causes grievous hurt by any means referred to in sub–section (1), shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons or means

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 118 BNS escalates the ordinary hurt/grievous-hurt punishment bands wherever the means used are inherently dangerous — shooting/stabbing/cutting instruments, any weapon likely to cause death, fire, heated substances, poison, corrosive substances, explosives, substances deleterious to inhale/swallow/inject, or animals. Simple hurt by such means draws up to three years (versus one year under the base Section 115), while grievous hurt by such means draws a minimum one year extendable to life (versus a flat seven-year ceiling under the base Section 117).
essential_elements: Hurt or grievous hurt is caused voluntarily

By one of the specifically listed dangerous means: cutting/stabbing/shooting instruments, a death-likely weapon, fire/heat, poison/corrosive substances, explosives, inhalation/injection-deleterious substances, or animals
exceptions_and_qualifications: Section 122's provocation-based lighter punishments apply instead where the relevant conditions are met
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is the standard charge wherever a knife, acid (though acid has its own dedicated Section 124), firearm, or poison is the instrument of hurt — the weapon/means itself is the aggravating factor here, independent of any extortion, provocation, or public-servant-targeting purpose covered by the surrounding sections.

sections.title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal act
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt for the purpose of extorting from the sufferer, or from any person interested in the sufferer, any property or valuable security, or of constraining the sufferer or any person interested in such sufferer to do anything which is illegal or which may facilitate the commission of an offence, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
(2) Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt for any purpose referred to in sub-section (1), shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 119 BNS punishes hurt or grievous hurt inflicted for the specific purpose of extorting property/valuable security, or constraining the victim to do something illegal or offence-facilitating — up to ten years for simple hurt, rising to life imprisonment (or up to ten years) for grievous hurt, reflecting the extortionate purpose as the core aggravating element rather than the means used.
essential_elements: Hurt or grievous hurt caused voluntarily

For the specific purpose of extorting property/valuable security from the sufferer or a person interested in the sufferer, OR constraining the sufferer/interested person to do an illegal act or one facilitating an offence
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish this purpose-driven offence from the means-driven Section 118 — the same violent act can attract both provisions where the offender both uses a dangerous weapon and acts for an extortionate purpose, but each section independently supplies its own complete offence and punishment band.

sections.title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of property
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt for the purpose of extorting from the sufferer or from any person interested in the sufferer, any confession or any information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or for the purpose of constraining the sufferer or any person interested in the sufferer to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security or to satisfy any claim or demand, or to give information which may lead to the restoration of any property or valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
Illustrations.
(a) A, a police officer, tortures Z in order to induce Z to confess that he committed a crime. A is guilty of an offence under this section.
(b) A, a police officer, tortures B to induce him to point out where certain stolen property is deposited. A is guilty of an offence under this section.
(c) A, a revenue officer, tortures Z in order to compel him to pay certain arrears of revenue due from Z. A is guilty of an offence under this section.
(2) Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt for any purpose referred to in sub-section (1), shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 120 BNS is the Sanhita's principal custodial-torture provision — it punishes hurt or grievous hurt inflicted to extort a confession, offence-detecting information, or restoration of property/satisfaction of a claim. The illustrations expressly target police and revenue officers torturing suspects, underscoring its use against custodial abuse of power, with up to seven years for simple hurt and up to ten years for grievous hurt.
essential_elements: Hurt or grievous hurt caused voluntarily

For the purpose of extorting a confession or offence/misconduct-detecting information, OR constraining restoration of property/valuable security, satisfaction of a claim/demand, or information leading to such restoration
breakdown.how_to_read: The illustrations make this the default charge for custodial violence by police or revenue officials — practitioners should plead this section specifically (rather than the generic Section 115/117) whenever the hurt was inflicted to extract a confession or compel restitution, since the purpose element is what unlocks this section's distinct, higher punishment band.

sections.title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt to any person being a public servant in the discharge of his duty as such public servant, or with intent to prevent or deter that person or any other public servant from discharging his duty as such public servant or in consequence of anything done or attempted to be done by that person in the lawful discharge of his duty as such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both.
(2) Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt to any person being a public servant in the discharge of his duty as such public servant, or with intent to prevent or deter that person or any other public servant from discharging his duty as such public servant or in consequence of anything done or attempted to be done by that person in the lawful discharge of his duty as such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter a public servant

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 121 BNS specifically protects public servants performing their official duties — causing hurt to a public servant in the discharge of duty, or to deter/prevent them (or any other public servant) from discharging duty, or in consequence of their lawful official acts, draws up to five years; causing grievous hurt in the same circumstances draws a minimum one year extendable to ten.
essential_elements: Hurt or grievous hurt caused voluntarily to a person who is a public servant

Either while that public servant is in the discharge of duty, OR with intent to prevent/deter that public servant or any other public servant from discharging duty, OR in consequence of something done/attempted in lawful discharge of duty
breakdown.how_to_read: The three alternative triggers (during discharge of duty, to deter future discharge, or in reprisal for past discharge) mean this section covers attacks on public servants before, during, or after the official act in question — not merely contemporaneous assaults.

sections.title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt on grave and sudden provocation, if he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause hurt to any person other than the person who gave the provocation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
(2) Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt on grave and sudden provocation, if he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt to any person other than the person who gave the provocation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.
Explanation.—This section is subject to the same proviso as Exception 1 of section 101.
key_terms: voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 122 BNS is the hurt-offence counterpart to Section 101's murder-reducing provocation Exception: hurt or grievous hurt caused on grave and sudden provocation, directed only at the provoker (not at an innocent bystander by mistake), draws dramatically lighter punishment — up to one month for simple hurt, up to five years for grievous hurt — than the ordinary Sections 115/117 bands, provided the same three-part proviso from Section 101 Exception 1 (no self-seeking provocation, no provocation by lawful public-servant action, no provocation by lawful private defence) is satisfied.
essential_elements: Hurt or grievous hurt caused voluntarily on grave and sudden provocation
Directed at the person who actually gave the provocation (not a different, uninvolved person)
The Section 101 Exception 1 proviso conditions are met (provocation not self-sought, not given by lawful public-servant act, not given by lawful private defence)
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the provision every Section 115/117/118 punishment clause expressly excepts ('except in the case provided for by section 122') — always check whether grave and sudden provocation is in play before defaulting to the higher general hurt/grievous-hurt punishment bands.

sections.title: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence
sections.raw_text: Whoever administers to or causes to be taken by any person any poison or any stupefying, intoxicating or unwholesome drug, or other thing with intent to cause hurt to such person, or with intent to commit or to facilitate the commission of an offence or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: causing hurt by poison to facilitate an offence

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 123 BNS specifically targets administering poison, stupefying drugs, intoxicants, or other harmful substances — whether to directly cause hurt or to facilitate the commission of some other offence (e.g. robbery after drugging a victim) — punishable with up to ten years plus fine, independent of whether hurt in the Section 114 sense actually results, so long as the requisite intent or knowledge is present.
essential_elements: Administering, or causing to be taken, poison, a stupefying/intoxicating/unwholesome drug, or other thing
With intent to cause hurt, OR intent to commit/facilitate an offence, OR knowledge that hurt is a likely consequence
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the standard charge in 'drink-spiking' and 'drug-and-rob' fact patterns — the intent to facilitate a separate offence (robbery, sexual assault, etc.) is independently sufficient, so the prosecution need not always prove intent to cause hurt as such.

sections.title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever causes permanent or partial damage or deformity to, or burns or maims or disfigures or disables, any part or parts of the body of a person or causes grievous hurt by throwing acid on or by administering acid to that person, or by using any other means with the intention of causing or with the knowledge that he is likely to cause such injury or hurt or causes a person to be in a permanent vegetative state shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than ten years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and with fine:
Provided that such fine shall be just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses of the treatment of the victim:
Provided further that any fine imposed under this sub-section shall be paid to the victim.
(2) Whoever throws or attempts to throw acid on any person or attempts to administer acid to any person, or attempts to use any other means, with the intention of causing permanent or partial damage or deformity or burns or maiming or disfigurement or disability or grievous hurt to that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
Explanation 1.—For the purposes of this section, "acid" includes any substance which has acidic or corrosive character or burning nature, that is capable of causing bodily injury leading to scars or disfigurement or temporary or permanent disability.
Explanation 2.—For the purposes of this section, permanent or partial damage or deformity or permanent vegetative state shall not be required to be irreversible.
key_terms: attempt to throw or administer acid
irreversibility not required for acid-attack injury

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 124 BNS is the Sanhita's dedicated acid-attack provision, carrying one of the heaviest non-homicide punishment bands in the Chapter — a minimum of ten years rising to life imprisonment for a completed acid attack causing damage, disfigurement, disability, or permanent vegetative state, with fine specifically directed to the victim's medical expenses. Sub-section (2) separately punishes attempted acid attacks (throwing or administering, or attempting to) with five to seven years, even where the attempt fails to cause the intended injury.
essential_elements: Causing permanent/partial damage, deformity, burns, maiming, disfigurement, disability, grievous hurt, or permanent vegetative state
By throwing or administering acid, or any other means
With intention of causing, or knowledge of likelihood of causing, such injury
Sub-section (2): attempting (rather than completing) such an acid attack
exceptions_and_qualifications: Explanation 2 clarifies that the injury need not be irreversible to qualify — temporary damage/deformity/vegetative state still satisfies the section
breakdown.how_to_read: The two mandatory fine provisos (medical-expense adequacy and direct payment to the victim) make this section's sentencing structure explicitly victim-centred/restorative, distinct from the general fine-to-State-treasury default seen elsewhere in the Sanhita.

sections.title: Act endangering life or personal safety of others
key_terms: act endangering life or personal safety of others

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 125 BNS punishes rash or negligent acts that merely endanger human life or personal safety — even where no hurt at all results — with a modest base punishment of up to three months, scaling up to six months where hurt is caused and three years where grievous hurt results, forming a graduated ladder tied directly to actual outcome.
essential_elements: An act done rashly or negligently
That endangers human life or the personal safety of others
Punishment escalates based on actual outcome: no injury (base band), hurt caused (clause (a)), or grievous hurt caused (clause (b))
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the Sanhita's general rash-endangerment offence and is frequently charged alongside Section 106 (causing death by negligence) or the hurt provisions where the rash act's actual consequences vary — it supplies the baseline liability even when, fortunately, no one is actually hurt.

sections.title: Wrongful restraint
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever voluntarily obstructs any person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed, is said wrongfully to restrain that person.
Exception.—The obstruction of a private way over land or water which a person in good faith believes himself to have a lawful right to obstruct, is not an offence within the meaning of this section.
Illustration.
A obstructs a path along which Z has a right to pass, A not believing in good faith that he has a right to stop the path. Z is thereby prevented from passing. A wrongfully restrains Z.
(2) Whoever wrongfully restrains any person shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: good-faith claim of right to obstruct a private way

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 126 BNS defines and punishes wrongful restraint — voluntarily obstructing a person's right to proceed in a direction they are entitled to go — with a modest penalty of up to one month's simple imprisonment. The built-in Exception protects a person who, in good faith, genuinely believes they have a lawful right to obstruct a private way, even if that belief later turns out to be mistaken.
essential_elements: Voluntary obstruction of a person
Preventing that person from proceeding in a direction they have a legal right to proceed in
exceptions_and_qualifications: Good-faith obstruction of a private way by someone who genuinely believes they have a lawful right to obstruct it is not an offence under this section
breakdown.how_to_read: Wrongful restraint is the lesser, 'blocking' offence; Section 127 (wrongful confinement) is its aggravated sibling where the obstruction goes further and actually encloses the victim within circumscribed limits — always check which of the two actually occurred on the facts.

sections.title: Wrongful confinement
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whoever wrongfully restrains any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceedings beyond certain circumscribing limits, is said "wrongfully to confine" that person.
Illustrations.
(a) A causes Z to go within a walled space, and locks Z in. Z is thus prevented from proceeding in any direction beyond the circumscribing line of wall. A wrongfully confines Z.
(b) A places men with firearms at the outlets of a building, and tells Z that they will fire at Z if Z attempts to leave the building. A wrongfully confines Z.
(2) Whoever wrongfully confines any person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
(3) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for three days, or more, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.
(4) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for ten days or more, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees.
(5) Whoever keeps any person in wrongful confinement, knowing that a writ for the liberation of that person has been duly issued, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years in addition to any term of imprisonment to which he may be liable under any other section of this Chapter and shall also be liable to fine.
(6) Whoever wrongfully confines any person in such manner as to indicate an intention that the confinement of such person may not be known to any person interested in the person so confined, or to any public servant, or that the place of such confinement may not be known to or discovered by any such person or public servant as hereinbefore mentioned, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years in addition to any other punishment to which he may be liable for such wrongful confinement and shall also be liable to fine.
(7) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for the purpose of extorting from the person confined, or from any person interested in the person confined, any property or valuable security or of constraining the person confined or any person interested in such person to do anything illegal or to give any information which may facilitate the commission of an offence, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.
(8) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for the purpose of extorting from the person confined or any person interested in the person confined any confession or any information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or for the purpose of constraining the person confined or any person interested in the person confined to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security or to satisfy any claim or demand, or to give information which may lead to the restoration of any property or valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: confinement defying a writ of liberation

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 127 BNS defines wrongful confinement as restraint within circumscribing limits (as opposed to mere directional obstruction under Section 126) and then builds a detailed, duration- and purpose-based punishment ladder across eight sub-sections: a base one-year offence (2), escalating to three years for three-plus days' confinement (3) and five years for ten-plus days (4), a distinct offence for defying a liberation writ (5), concealment-of-whereabouts aggravation (6), and purpose-based extortion-of-property (7) and extortion-of-confession (8) variants mirroring the hurt-offence structure in Sections 119-120.
essential_elements: Wrongful restraint (Section 126) within circumscribing limits preventing the victim from proceeding beyond them
Duration-based escalation: three-plus days (sub-section (3)), ten-plus days (sub-section (4))
Sub-section (5): confinement continued with knowledge that a liberation writ has been issued
Sub-section (6): confinement carried out to conceal it from interested persons or public servants
Sub-sections (7)-(8): confinement for the purpose of extorting property/valuable security, or a confession/offence-detecting information
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat sub-sections (3)-(8) as independently chargeable aggravations layered on top of the base sub-section (2) offence — a single confinement lasting, say, twelve days and carried out to extort a confession could in principle attract sub-sections (4) and (8) together, so plead and prove each aggravating fact (duration, purpose, concealment, writ-defiance) separately.

sections.title: Force
sections.raw_text: A person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other's body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other's sense of feeling: Provided that the person causing the motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion, causes that motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion in one of the following three ways, namely:-- (a) by his own bodily power; (b) by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person; (c) by inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 128 opens the 'Of criminal force and assault' sub-chapter by defining the neutral physical concept of 'force' before Section 129 narrows it to 'criminal' force. Force is causing motion, a change of motion, or a stopping of motion to another person or to a substance that then touches that person's body, clothes, or anything they're carrying, or anything positioned so the contact affects their sense of feeling. It only counts if brought about in one of three ways: by the actor's own bodily power, by arranging a substance so the motion happens without any further act, or by inducing an animal to move.
essential_elements: Causing motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to another person or to a substance
The motion causes contact with the other person's body, clothing, or carried items, or affects their sense of feeling
The motion is brought about by the actor's own bodily power, by disposing a substance, or by inducing an animal
breakdown.how_to_read: A purely definitional section, mirrored by near-identical illustrations to the historic IPC Section 349 -- read it before Section 129 to understand that 'force' itself is morally neutral; criminality is added only by the absence of consent and the actor's intent or knowledge under Section 129.

sections.title: Criminal force
sections.raw_text: Whoever intentionally uses force to any person, without that person's consent, in order to the committing of any offence, or intending by the use of such force to cause, or knowing it to be likely that by the use of such force he will cause injury, fear or annoyance to the person to whom the force is used, is said to use criminal force to that other. Illustrations. (a) Z is sitting in a moored boat on a river. A unfastens the moorings, and thus intentionally causes the boat to drift down the stream. Here A intentionally causes motion to Z, and he does this by disposing substances in such a manner that the motion is produced without any other action on any person's part. A has therefore intentionally used force to Z; and if he has done so without Z's consent, in order to the committing of any offence, or intending or knowing it to be likely that this use of force will cause injury, fear or annoyance to Z, A has used criminal force to Z. (b) Z is riding in a chariot. A lashes Z's horses, and thereby causes them to quicken their pace. Here A has caused change of motion to Z by inducing the animals to change their motion. A has therefore used force to Z; and if A has done this without Z's consent, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby injure, frighten or annoy Z, A has used criminal force to Z. (c) Z is riding in a palanquin. A, intending to rob Z, seizes the pole and stops the palanquin. Here A has caused cessation of motion to Z, and he has done this by his own bodily power. A has therefore used force to Z; and as A has acted thus intentionally, without Z's consent, in order to the commission of an offence. A has used criminal force to Z. (d) A intentionally pushes against Z in the street. Here A has by his own bodily power moved his own person so as to bring it into contact with Z. He has therefore intentionally used force to Z; and if he has done so without Z's consent, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby injure, frighten or annoy Z, he has used criminal force to Z. (e) A throws a stone, intending or knowing it to be likely that the stone will be thus brought into contact with Z, or with Z's clothes, or with something carried by Z, or that it will strike water and dash up the water against Z's clothes or something carried by Z. Here, if the throwing of the stone produce the effect of causing any substance to come into contact with Z, or Z's clothes, A has used force to Z, and if he did so without Z's consent, intending thereby to injure, frighten or annoy Z, he has used criminal force to Z. (f) A intentionally pulls up a woman's veil. Here A intentionally uses force to her, and if he does so without her consent intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby injure, frighten or annoy her, he has used criminal force to her. (g) Z is bathing. A pours into the bath water which he knows to be boiling. Here A intentionally by his own bodily power causes such motion in the boiling water as brings that water into contact with Z, or with other water so situated that such contact must affect Z's sense of feeling; A has therefore intentionally used force to Z; and if he has done this without Z's consent intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause injury, fear or annoyance to Z, A has used criminal force. (h) A incites a dog to spring upon Z, without Z's consent. Here, if A intends to cause injury, fear or annoyance to Z, he uses criminal force to Z.

breakdown.plain_summary: Criminal force is Section 128's plain 'force' plus two further conditions: it must be used without the other person's consent, and it must either be in order to commit an offence, or be intended (or known likely) to cause that person injury, fear, or annoyance. The eight illustrations -- cutting a boat's moorings, whipping a chariot's horses, stopping a palanquin to rob its occupant, jostling someone in the street, throwing a stone, pulling up a woman's veil, pouring boiling water into someone's bath, and siccing a dog on someone -- walk through each of the three force-causing methods from Section 128 combined with the non-consent and intent/knowledge requirements.
essential_elements: Intentional use of force (as defined in Section 128) to any person
The force is used without that person's consent
Either the force is used in order to commit an offence, or the actor intends or knows it likely to cause injury, fear, or annoyance to that person
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as the bridge definition between plain 'force' (Section 128) and the specific assault/criminal-force offences in Sections 131-136 -- Section 129 itself prescribes no punishment; it only defines the conduct that those later sections criminalise.

sections.title: Assault
sections.raw_text: Whoever makes any gesture, or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person, is said to commit an assault. Explanation.--Mere words do not amount to an assault. But the words which a person uses may give to his gestures or preparation such a meaning as may make those gestures or preparations amount to an assault. Illustrations. (a) A shakes his fist at Z, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause Z to believe that A is about to strike Z. A has committed an assault. (b) A begins to unloose the muzzle of a ferocious dog, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause Z to believe that he is about to cause the dog to attack Z. A has committed an assault upon Z. (c) A takes up a stick, saying to Z, 'I will give you a beating'. Here, though the words used by A could in no case amount to an assault, and though the mere gesture, unaccompanied by any other circumstances, might not amount to an assault, the gesture explained by the words may amount to an assault.
key_terms: mere words not amounting to assault

breakdown.plain_summary: Assault is an anticipatory offence: it is committed by a gesture or preparation -- not actual contact -- that is intended or known likely to make a person present apprehend that criminal force is about to be used on them. Mere words alone never amount to an assault, but words can colour an otherwise ambiguous gesture (like picking up a stick) into one that does.
essential_elements: A gesture or preparation (not actual force) by the accused
Intention or knowledge that it is likely to cause apprehension in a person present
The apprehension must be of imminent criminal force being used against that person
exceptions_and_qualifications: Mere words, standing alone, never amount to an assault
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the deliberate sequencing: Section 128 defines force, 129 narrows it to criminal force, and 130 defines assault as the anticipatory, gesture-based cousin of criminal force -- the three illustrations show words either being irrelevant (shaking a fist), bolstering a gesture (unloosing a dog's muzzle), or transforming an otherwise-insufficient gesture into an assault (picking up a stick while threatening a beating).

sections.title: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation
sections.raw_text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both. Explanation 1.--Grave and sudden provocation will not mitigate the punishment for an offence under this section,-- (a) if the provocation is sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse for the offence; or (b) if the provocation is given by anything done in obedience to the law, or by a public servant, in the lawful exercise of the powers of such public servant; or (c) if the provocation is given by anything done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. Explanation 2.--Whether the provocation was grave and sudden enough to mitigate the offence, is a question of fact.
key_terms: punishment for base assault or criminal force
grave and sudden provocation defence to assault

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the base punishment provision for simple assault or criminal force: up to three months' imprisonment, fine up to one thousand rupees, or both -- but only where the act was not done on grave and sudden provocation by the victim (that scenario is punished more lightly under Section 136). The two Explanations borrow the same three provocation-disqualifying circumstances used elsewhere in the Sanhita (sought/self-provoked, lawful official conduct, lawful private defence) and confirm that whether provocation was grave and sudden enough is always a question of fact for the court.
essential_elements: Assault or use of criminal force to any person
The act was not committed on grave and sudden provocation given by that person
exceptions_and_qualifications: Grave and sudden provocation is excluded as a mitigating factor where it was sought or self-provoked by the offender as an excuse
Grave and sudden provocation is excluded where given by lawful official conduct
Grave and sudden provocation is excluded where given by lawful exercise of the right of private defence
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the residual/default assault punishment section -- always check first whether Sections 132-135 apply (public-servant, dishonour, theft, or wrongful-confinement contexts), since those carry heavier punishment; Section 131 catches everything else, and Section 136 is its own lighter-punishment mirror for genuinely provoked assaults.

sections.title: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty
sections.raw_text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person being a public servant in the execution of his duty as such public servant, or with intent to prevent or deter that person from discharging his duty as such public servant, or in consequence of anything done or attempted to be done by such person in the lawful discharge of his duty as such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: assault or criminal force to deter a public servant

breakdown.plain_summary: An aggravated assault offence protecting public servants in three overlapping scenarios: being assaulted while actually executing official duty, being assaulted with intent to prevent or deter that duty, or being assaulted in consequence of having lawfully discharged that duty -- punishable up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
essential_elements: Assault or use of criminal force to a public servant
Either (a) the public servant was in the execution of duty, or (b) the act was intended to prevent/deter duty, or (c) the act was in consequence of duty lawfully discharged
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare with the hurt-level equivalent, Section 121 (causing hurt to deter a public servant) -- Section 132 is the lighter, assault/force-only counterpart that doesn't require actual hurt to be caused.

sections.title: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave provocation
sections.raw_text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, intending thereby to dishonour that person, otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour

breakdown.plain_summary: A dignity-protecting offence: assaulting or using criminal force with the specific intention of dishonouring the victim, where that was not provoked by grave and sudden provocation from the victim, draws up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- heavier than the base Section 131 offence because of the added dishonouring intent.
essential_elements: Assault or use of criminal force to any person
Intention to thereby dishonour that person
The act was not committed on grave and sudden provocation given by that person
breakdown.how_to_read: The dishonouring-intent element is what separates this from plain Section 131 assault -- in practice this is pleaded where the assault is accompanied by a public, humiliating element (e.g. slapping or striking someone in front of others specifically to humiliate them).

sections.title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person
sections.raw_text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, in attempting to commit theft on any property which that person is then wearing or carrying, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of carried property

breakdown.plain_summary: A theft-related aggravation: assaulting or using criminal force on a person while attempting to steal property they are currently wearing or carrying (e.g. snatching a chain, grabbing a bag) is punishable up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
essential_elements: Assault or use of criminal force to a person
Done in the course of attempting to commit theft on property that person is then wearing or carrying
breakdown.how_to_read: A common charge in chain-snatching and bag-snatching cases where the theft attempt involves direct physical contact with the victim -- if actual force sufficient to overcome resistance is used to carry the property away, consider whether robbery (which builds on theft plus force) is the more apt charge instead.

sections.title: Assault or criminal force in attempt wrongfully to confine a person
sections.raw_text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, in attempting wrongfully to confine that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: assault or criminal force in attempt wrongfully to confine

breakdown.plain_summary: Assaulting or using criminal force on someone while attempting to wrongfully confine them is punishable up to one year's imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both -- the attempt-stage counterpart that precedes a completed wrongful confinement under Section 127.
essential_elements: Assault or use of criminal force to a person
Done in attempting to wrongfully confine that person
breakdown.how_to_read: If the confinement is actually completed (not merely attempted), charge under Section 127 instead (or in addition, depending on the facts) -- Section 135 specifically targets the attempt stage where force or assault was used but confinement didn't fully succeed.

sections.title: Assault or criminal force on grave and sudden provocation
sections.raw_text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both. Explanation.--This section is subject to the same Explanation as section 131.
key_terms: assault or criminal force on grave and sudden provocation

breakdown.plain_summary: The mitigated mirror of Section 131: where the assault or criminal force was genuinely provoked by grave and sudden provocation from the victim (and none of Section 131's three disqualifying circumstances apply), punishment is capped much lower -- simple imprisonment up to one month, fine up to one thousand rupees, or both.
essential_elements: Assault or use of criminal force to any person
The act was committed on grave and sudden provocation given by that person
exceptions_and_qualifications: Subject to the same three disqualifying circumstances as Section 131's Explanation 1 (self-sought provocation, lawful official conduct, lawful private defence)
breakdown.how_to_read: Always read together with Section 131 -- the two sections are mirror images keyed to the single fact of whether grave and sudden provocation triggered the assault, with 136 as the lenient outcome and 131 as the default.

sections.title: Kidnapping
sections.raw_text: (1) Kidnapping is of two kinds: kidnapping from India, and kidnapping from lawful guardianship-- (a) whoever conveys any person beyond the limits of India without the consent of that person, or of some person legally authorised to consent on behalf of that person, is said to kidnap that person from India; (b) whoever takes or entices any child or any person of unsound mind, out of the keeping of the lawful guardian of such child or person of unsound mind, without the consent of such guardian, is said to kidnap such child or person from lawful guardianship. Explanation.--The words 'lawful guardian' in this clause include any person lawfully entrusted with the care or custody of such child or other person. Exception.--This clause does not extend to the act of any person who in good faith believes himself to be the father of an illegitimate child, or who in good faith believes himself to be entitled to the lawful custody of such child, unless such act is committed for an immoral or unlawful purpose. (2) Whoever kidnaps any person from India or from lawful guardianship shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 137 opens the 'Of kidnapping, abduction, slavery and forced labour' sub-chapter by defining kidnapping in two distinct forms: kidnapping from India (conveying any person beyond India's limits without their own or their lawful guardian's consent), and kidnapping from lawful guardianship (taking or enticing a child or person of unsound mind out of their lawful guardian's keeping without that guardian's consent). Both forms are punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine. A targeted exception protects a person who in good faith believes himself the father of an illegitimate child, or believes he is entitled to lawful custody, unless the act is for an immoral or unlawful purpose.
essential_elements: Either: conveying any person beyond India's limits without consent of that person or their legally authorised consenter
Or: taking or enticing a child or person of unsound mind out of the keeping of their lawful guardian, without the guardian's consent
exceptions_and_qualifications: A good-faith belief of being the illegitimate child's father, or of being entitled to lawful custody of the child, is a defence -- unless the act was for an immoral or unlawful purpose
breakdown.how_to_read: Note that the victim's own consent is irrelevant for the lawful-guardianship form if the victim is a child or person of unsound mind -- it is the guardian's consent that matters, reflecting that such victims are deemed incapable of consenting to being taken away.

sections.title: Abduction
sections.raw_text: Whoever by force compels, or by any deceitful means induces, any person to go from any place, is said to abduct that person.

breakdown.plain_summary: Abduction is defined separately from kidnapping: it is compelling a person by force, or inducing them by deceitful means, to go from any place. Unlike kidnapping, abduction by itself is not an independent offence under the Sanhita -- it only becomes punishable when combined with a specific wrongful purpose set out in later sections (e.g. Sections 140, 142).
essential_elements: Compelling a person to go from a place by force, or inducing them to go by deceitful means
breakdown.how_to_read: Unlike kidnapping (independently punishable under Section 137(2)), abduction is merely an ingredient -- always check which later section (140, 142, etc.) attaches a punishable purpose to the abduction before charging it as an offence.

sections.title: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever kidnaps any child or, not being the lawful guardian of such child, obtains the custody of the child, in order that such child may be employed or used for the purposes of begging shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. (2) Whoever maims any child in order that such child may be employed or used for the purposes of begging shall be punishable with imprisonment which shall not be less than twenty years, but which may extend to life which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, and with fine. (3) Where any person, not being the lawful guardian of a child employs or uses such child for the purposes of begging, it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that he kidnapped or otherwise obtained the custody of such child in order that such child might be employed or used for the purposes of begging. (4) In this section 'begging' means-- (i) soliciting or receiving alms in a public place, whether under the pretence of singing, dancing, fortune telling, performing tricks or selling articles or otherwise; (ii) entering on any private premises for the purpose of soliciting or receiving alms; (iii) exposing or exhibiting, with the object of obtaining or extorting alms, any sore, wound, injury, deformity or disease, whether of himself or of any other person or of an animal; (iv) using such child as an exhibit for the purpose of soliciting or receiving alms.

breakdown.plain_summary: A severe child-protection provision targeting organised begging rackets: kidnapping or wrongfully obtaining custody of a child to use them for begging draws rigorous imprisonment of ten years to life, while actually maiming a child for that purpose draws a minimum twenty years up to life meaning the remainder of natural life.
