Sub-section (3) creates a reverse presumption -- anyone other than the lawful guardian found using a child for begging is presumed to have kidnapped or obtained custody of that child for that very purpose, unless they prove otherwise. 'Begging' itself is broadly defined to include soliciting alms in public under any pretence, entering private premises to solicit alms, exhibiting injuries or deformities to extort alms, or using a child as a prop for alms-seeking.
essential_elements: Kidnapping a child, or obtaining custody without being the lawful guardian
The purpose of such kidnapping or custody is that the child may be employed or used for begging
(For sub-section (2)) maiming a child, with the purpose that the child may be used for begging
breakdown.how_to_read: Sub-section (3)'s reversed burden of proof is the practically decisive feature -- prosecutors need only show a non-guardian using a child to beg; the accused must then affirmatively disprove the kidnapping/wrongful-custody purpose, a significant departure from the ordinary presumption of innocence.

sections.title: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever kidnaps or abducts any person in order that such person may be murdered or may be so disposed of as to be put in danger of being murdered, shall be punished with imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Illustrations. (a) A kidnaps Z from India, intending or knowing it to be likely that Z may be sacrificed to an idol. A has committed the offence defined in this section. (b) A forcibly carries or entices B away from his home in order that B may be murdered. A has committed the offence defined in this section. (2) Whoever kidnaps or abducts any person or keeps a person in detention after such kidnapping or abduction, and threatens to cause death or hurt to such person, or by his conduct gives rise to a reasonable apprehension that such person may be put to death or hurt, or causes hurt or death to such person in order to compel the Government or any foreign State or international inter-governmental organisation or any other person to do or abstain from doing any act or to pay a ransom, shall be punishable with death, or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. (3) Whoever kidnaps or abducts any person with intent to cause that person to be secretly and wrongfully confined, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. (4) Whoever kidnaps or abducts any person in order that such person may be subjected, or may be so disposed of as to be put in danger of being subjected to grievous hurt, or slavery, or to the unnatural lust of any person, or knowing it to be likely that such person will be so subjected or disposed of, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: kidnapping or abducting for secret wrongful confinement
kidnapping or abducting to subject to grievous hurt or slavery

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 140 graduates kidnapping/abduction punishment by the wrongful purpose behind it. Sub-section (1): kidnapping/abducting to murder or expose to danger of murder draws life imprisonment or up to ten years' rigorous imprisonment. Sub-section (2), the ransom/hostage-taking provision: kidnapping/abducting and threatening death or hurt, or actually causing hurt or death, to compel a government, foreign state, international organisation, or any person to act or pay ransom, draws death or life imprisonment -- the most severe band in this section. Sub-section (3): kidnapping/abducting to secretly and wrongfully confine someone draws up to seven years. Sub-section (4): kidnapping/abducting to subject someone to grievous hurt, slavery, or unnatural lust draws up to ten years.
essential_elements: Kidnapping or abduction of a person

Coupled with one of the specific wrongful purposes in sub-sections (1)-(4): murder/danger of murder; ransom/compelling an act via threat or infliction of death or hurt; secret wrongful confinement; or grievous hurt/slavery/unnatural lust
breakdown.how_to_read: A multi-tier section -- always identify which specific sub-section's purpose matches the facts, since the punishment ladder ranges enormously, from seven years (secret confinement) up to death (ransom/hostage-taking with threatened or actual harm).

sections.title: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country
sections.raw_text: Whoever imports into India from any country outside India any girl under the age of twenty-one years or any boy under the age of eighteen years with intent that girl or boy may be, or knowing it to be likely that girl or boy will be, forced or seduced to illicit intercourse with another person, shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to ten years and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: importation of girl or boy for illicit intercourse

breakdown.plain_summary: A cross-border trafficking-adjacent offence: importing a girl under twenty-one or a boy under eighteen into India from abroad, with intent or knowledge that they will be forced or seduced into illicit intercourse with another, is punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine -- notable for its asymmetric age thresholds (twenty-one for girls, eighteen for boys).
essential_elements: Importing into India from a foreign country a girl under twenty-one or a boy under eighteen
Intent that the girl or boy will be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse, or knowledge it is likely
breakdown.how_to_read: Note this offence is keyed specifically to cross-border importation, distinguishing it from the general trafficking offence (Section 143) which has no such territorial-crossing requirement.

sections.title: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person
sections.raw_text: Whoever, knowing that any person has been kidnapped or has been abducted, wrongfully conceals or confines such person, shall be punished in the same manner as if he had kidnapped or abducted such person with the same intention or knowledge, or for the same purpose as that with or for which he conceals or detains such person in confinement.
key_terms: wrongfully concealing a kidnapped or abducted person
derivative liability for concealment matching original purpose

breakdown.plain_summary: A derivative-liability provision: a person who, knowing that someone has been kidnapped or abducted, wrongfully conceals or confines that person is punished exactly as if they themselves had kidnapped or abducted that person with the same intention, knowledge, or purpose that underlies the concealment or confinement -- effectively equating the concealer's liability to Section 140's graduated purpose-based scheme.
essential_elements: Knowledge that the person has been kidnapped or abducted
Wrongfully concealing or confining that person
breakdown.how_to_read: The punishment is not fixed independently -- it borrows whatever punishment would apply under the kidnapping/abduction provisions (chiefly Section 140) matching the concealer's own intention or purpose in concealing/confining, so always trace back to which purpose-specific tier applies.

sections.title: Trafficking of person
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever, for the purpose of exploitation recruits, transports, harbours, transfers, or receives a person or persons, by-- (a) using threats; or (b) using force, or any other form of coercion; or (c) by abduction; or (d) by practising fraud, or deception; or (e) by abuse of power; or (f) by inducement, including the giving or receiving of payments or benefits, in order to achieve the consent of any person having control over the person recruited, transported, harboured, transferred or received, commits the offence of trafficking. Explanation 1.--The expression 'exploitation' shall include any act of physical exploitation or any form of sexual exploitation, slavery or practices similar to slavery, servitude, beggary or forced removal of organs. Explanation 2.--The consent of the victim is immaterial in determination of the offence of trafficking. (2) Whoever commits the offence of trafficking shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years, but which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. (3) Where the offence involves the trafficking of more than one person, it shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. (4) Where the offence involves the trafficking of a child, it shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. (5) Where the offence involves the trafficking of more than one child, it shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than fourteen years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. (6) If a person is convicted of the offence of trafficking of a child on more than one occasion, then such person shall be punished with imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, and shall also be liable to fine. (7) When a public servant or a police officer is involved in the trafficking of any person then, such public servant or police officer shall be punished with imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: public servant or police officer trafficking

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 143 is the Sanhita's comprehensive anti-trafficking provision. Sub-section (1) defines trafficking broadly: recruiting, transporting, harbouring, transferring, or receiving a person for exploitation, using any of six listed means (threats, force/coercion, abduction, fraud/deception, abuse of power, or inducement including payments to whoever controls the victim). 'Exploitation' is defined expansively to cover physical or sexual exploitation, slavery-like practices, servitude, beggary, or forced organ removal, and -- critically -- the victim's consent is expressly made immaterial. The punishment ladder then escalates sharply: seven to ten years as the base (2); ten years to life for trafficking more than one person (3); ten years to life for trafficking a child (4); fourteen years to life for trafficking more than one child (5); mandatory life (remainder of natural life) for a repeat child-trafficking conviction (6); and mandatory life for any public servant or police officer involved in trafficking (7).
essential_elements: Recruiting, transporting, harbouring, transferring, or receiving a person or persons
For the purpose of exploitation
By one of the six specified means: threats, force/coercion, abduction, fraud/deception, abuse of power, or inducement
breakdown.how_to_read: Explanation 2's abolition of victim consent as a defence is the single most important interpretive point -- unlike many other Sanhita offences, a trafficking victim's apparent agreement to be recruited, transported, or transferred is legally irrelevant once the exploitation purpose and one of the six means is shown.

sections.title: Exploitation of a trafficked person
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever, knowingly or having reason to believe that a child has been trafficked, engages such child for sexual exploitation in any manner, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years, but which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. (2) Whoever, knowingly or having reason to believe that a person has been trafficked, engages such person for sexual exploitation in any manner, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years, but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

breakdown.plain_summary: A demand-side offence distinct from Section 143's supply-side trafficking offence: knowingly or having reason to believe a person has been trafficked, and then engaging that person for sexual exploitation, is independently punishable -- five to ten years where the victim is a child, three to seven years where the victim is an adult.
essential_elements: Knowledge or reason to believe that the person has been trafficked
Engaging that person for sexual exploitation in any manner
breakdown.how_to_read: This section targets the end-user/exploiter of a trafficking chain, complementing Section 143's focus on the recruiter/transporter/harbourer -- both can be separately charged on the same facts where a trafficked person is subsequently sexually exploited by a different person.

sections.title: Habitual dealing in slaves
sections.raw_text: Whoever habitually imports, exports, removes, buys, sells, traffics or deals in slaves, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

breakdown.plain_summary: A standalone anti-slavery offence targeting habitual conduct -- repeatedly importing, exporting, removing, buying, selling, trafficking, or otherwise dealing in slaves is punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years' imprisonment, plus fine.
essential_elements: Habitual conduct (not a single isolated act) of importing, exporting, removing, buying, selling, trafficking, or dealing in slaves
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'habitually' requirement distinguishes this from a single, isolated transaction -- a pattern of repeated dealing is the gravamen of this offence, carried forward largely unchanged from the former IPC's equivalent provision.

sections.title: Unlawful compulsory labour
sections.raw_text: Whoever unlawfully compels any person to labour against the will of that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.

breakdown.plain_summary: The final provision of Chapter VI: unlawfully compelling any person to labour against their will is punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both -- a general forced-labour offence catching situations not otherwise covered by the more specific slavery or trafficking provisions.
essential_elements: Compelling a person to labour
Against the will of that person
The compulsion is unlawful
breakdown.how_to_read: A residual, comparatively lightly punished offence -- where the forced labour arises from or forms part of a trafficking or exploitation scheme, consider the heavier Sections 143-144 instead; Section 146 is better suited to standalone forced-labour situations outside an organised trafficking context.

sections.title: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India
sections.raw_text: Whoever wages war against the Government of India, or attempts to wage such war, or abets the waging of such war, shall be punished with death, or imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fine. Illustration. A joins an insurrection against the Government of India. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
key_terms: waging war against the Government of India

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 147 opens Chapter VII ('Of Offences Against the State') with the gravest offence against the State: waging war, attempting to wage war, or abetting the waging of war against the Government of India, punishable with death or life imprisonment plus fine -- one of the few offences in the Sanhita carrying a flat death-or-life punishment band with no lesser alternative.
essential_elements: Waging war against the Government of India, or attempting to wage such war, or abetting its waging
breakdown.how_to_read: The single illustration -- simply joining an insurrection -- shows how low the threshold for 'waging war' is set; mere participation, not organising or leading, suffices. Read alongside Section 148 (conspiracy) and Sections 149-150 (preparatory/concealment offences) which punish earlier stages of the same underlying conduct.

sections.title: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147
sections.raw_text: Whoever within or without and beyond India conspires to commit any of the offences punishable by section 147, or conspires to overawe, by means of criminal force or the show of criminal force, the Central Government or any State Government, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation.--To constitute a conspiracy under this section, it is not necessary that any act or illegal omission shall take place in pursuance thereof.
key_terms: conspiracy to overawe the Government by criminal force

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 148 criminalises the conspiracy stage of waging war (and the related act of conspiring to overawe the Central or State Government through criminal force or its show), punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine, and expressly applies whether the conspiracy is hatched within or outside India. The Explanation makes clear that, unlike the general criminal-conspiracy offence under Section 61 (which usually requires an overt act for non-offence agreements), no overt act is needed here -- the bare agreement to wage war or overawe Government suffices.
essential_elements: A conspiracy (agreement) to commit an offence under Section 147, or to overawe the Central or State Government by criminal force or its show
The conspiracy may be formed within India, outside India, or spanning both
exceptions_and_qualifications: No act or illegal omission in pursuance of the conspiracy is required -- the bare agreement itself is sufficient
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a notable, express carve-out from the general conspiracy rule (Section 61's proviso) that otherwise usually requires an overt act for non-offence agreements -- here Parliament has made the bare agreement itself punishable given the gravity of the subject matter (waging war / overawing Government).

sections.title: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India
sections.raw_text: Whoever collects men, arms or ammunition or otherwise prepares to wage war with the intention of either waging or being prepared to wage war against the Government of India, shall be punished with imprisonment for life or imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: collecting arms or men to wage war
preparation to wage war against the Government

breakdown.plain_summary: A preparatory offence sitting below the full waging-war offence in Section 147: collecting men, arms, or ammunition, or otherwise preparing to wage war, with the intention of either actually waging war or merely being prepared to do so, is punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine.
essential_elements: Collecting men, arms, or ammunition, or otherwise preparing to wage war
Intention of either waging war, or merely being prepared to wage war, against the Government of India
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the intention element is satisfied even by mere readiness ('being prepared to wage war') -- the offender need not have settled on an actual plan or timeline to attack; stockpiling arms with a contingent intention to be ready is enough.

sections.title: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war
sections.raw_text: Whoever by any act, or by any illegal omission, conceals the existence of a design to wage war against the Government of India, intending by such concealment to facilitate, or knowing it to be likely that such concealment will facilitate, the waging of such war, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: concealment of a design to wage war

breakdown.plain_summary: A concealment offence paralleling the general concealment-of-design provisions in Sections 58-60: concealing, by act or illegal omission, the existence of a known design to wage war against the Government of India, intending or knowing likely that the concealment will facilitate that war, is punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine.
essential_elements: Concealment, by act or illegal omission, of the existence of a design to wage war against the Government of India
Intention that the concealment will facilitate the waging of such war, or knowledge that it is likely to do so
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare with the general-purpose concealment-of-design offences in Sections 58-60 -- Section 150 is the State-security-specific counterpart, applicable only where the concealed design is specifically to wage war against the Government of India.

sections.title: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power
sections.raw_text: Whoever, with the intention of inducing or compelling the President of India, or Governor of any State, to exercise or refrain from exercising in any manner any of the lawful powers of such President or Governor, assaults or wrongfully restrains, or attempts wrongfully to restrain, or overawes, by means of criminal force or the show of criminal force, or attempts so to overawe, such President or Governor, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: assaulting the President or a Governor to compel exercise of power

breakdown.plain_summary: A specific offence protecting the President of India and State Governors from coercion: assaulting, wrongfully restraining (or attempting to), or overawing (or attempting to overawe) by criminal force or its show, with the intention of inducing or compelling them to exercise or refrain from exercising any lawful power, is punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine.
essential_elements: Assault, wrongful restraint (or attempt), or overawing by criminal force or its show (or attempt), directed at the President of India or a State Governor
Intention of inducing or compelling that President or Governor to exercise, or refrain from exercising, any lawful power
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish this from the general assault/criminal force offences (Sections 131-136) -- the elevated seven-year punishment here flows from the specific constitutional-office status of the victim and the coercive purpose of compelling or restraining an exercise of lawful power.

sections.title: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
sections.raw_text: Whoever, purposely or knowingly, by words, either spoken or written, or by signs, or by visible representation, or by electronic communication or by use of financial mean, or otherwise, excites or attempts to excite, secession or armed rebellion or subversive activities, or encourages feelings of separatist activities or endangers sovereignty or unity and integrity of India; or indulges in or commits any such act shall be punished with imprisonment for life or with imprisonment which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation.--Comments expressing disapprobation of the measures, or administrative or other action of the Government with a view to obtain their alteration by lawful means without exciting or attempting to excite the activities referred to in this section do not constitute an offence under this section.
key_terms: act endangering sovereignty unity and integrity of India

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 152 is the Sanhita's replacement for the former IPC's colonial-era sedition provision (Section 124A), recast around the protection of India's sovereignty, unity, and integrity rather than disaffection towards Government. It punishes purposely or knowingly exciting (or attempting to excite) secession, armed rebellion, or subversive activities, or encouraging separatist feelings, or otherwise endangering India's sovereignty or unity and integrity, by words (spoken or written), signs, visible representation, electronic communication, or financial means -- with imprisonment for life or up to seven years plus fine. The Explanation expressly protects lawful dissent: comments disapproving of Government measures or actions, made with a view to obtaining their alteration by lawful means, are not an offence so long as they don't excite the listed activities.
essential_elements: Purposely or knowingly acting by words, signs, visible representation, electronic communication, or financial means
Exciting or attempting to excite secession, armed rebellion, or subversive activities, or encouraging separatist feelings, or endangering sovereignty/unity/integrity of India
exceptions_and_qualifications: Comments expressing disapproval of Government measures or administrative action, made with a view to obtaining their lawful alteration, do not constitute an offence under this section, provided they do not excite or attempt to excite the listed activities
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the modern, narrower successor to sedition -- the explicit lawful-dissent Explanation is the key textual safeguard to plead for critical political speech; the offence is centred on exciting secession/rebellion/subversion and endangering sovereignty/unity/integrity, not mere criticism of the Government as such.

sections.title: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India
sections.raw_text: Whoever wages war against the Government of any foreign State at peace with the Government of India or attempts to wage such war, or abets the waging of such war, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, to which fine may be added, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, to which fine may be added, or with fine.
key_terms: waging war against a friendly foreign State

breakdown.plain_summary: Protects India's diplomatic relations by criminalising waging war, attempting to wage war, or abetting the waging of war, against the government of any foreign State that is at peace with India -- punishable with life imprisonment plus optional fine, or up to seven years plus optional fine, or fine alone.
essential_elements: Waging war, attempting to wage war, or abetting the waging of war, against the Government of a foreign State
That foreign State must be at peace with the Government of India at the relevant time
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'at peace with Government of India' qualifier is the operative limiting condition -- this section does not touch conduct directed against a foreign State that is itself hostile to or at war with India.

sections.title: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India
sections.raw_text: Whoever commits depredation, or makes preparations to commit depredation, on the territories of any foreign State at peace with the Government of India, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine and to forfeiture of any property used or intended to be used in committing such depredation, or acquired by such depredation.
key_terms: depredation on a friendly foreign State's territory

breakdown.plain_summary: Criminalises committing, or merely preparing to commit, depredation (plundering or raiding) on the territory of a foreign State at peace with India, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, plus forfeiture of any property used, intended to be used, or acquired by such depredation -- the forfeiture limb directly strips the offender of the raid's instruments and proceeds.
essential_elements: Committing depredation, or making preparations to commit depredation
On the territories of a foreign State at peace with the Government of India
breakdown.how_to_read: Notice this offence is complete even at the mere-preparation stage, unlike many offences that require an actual attempt -- the forfeiture consequence (property used, intended to be used, or acquired by the depredation) is a distinctive additional punishment beyond imprisonment and fine.

sections.title: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154
sections.raw_text: Whoever receives any property knowing the same to have been taken in the commission of any of the offences mentioned in sections 153 and 154, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine and to forfeiture of the property so received.
key_terms: receiving property taken by war or depredation

breakdown.plain_summary: A receiving-stolen-property-style offence specific to the proceeds of Sections 153-154: knowingly receiving property taken through waging war on, or depredation against, a friendly foreign State, is punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, plus forfeiture of the property received.
essential_elements: Receiving property
Knowledge that the property was taken in the commission of an offence under Section 153 or Section 154
breakdown.how_to_read: The knowledge requirement is key -- a person who receives such property without knowing its tainted origin is not caught; this mirrors the general structure of property-offence 'receiving' provisions elsewhere in the Sanhita, adapted here to the war/depredation context.

sections.title: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant and having the custody of any State prisoner or prisoner of war, voluntarily allows such prisoner to escape from any place in which such prisoner is confined, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: public servant voluntarily allowing a State prisoner or prisoner of war to escape

breakdown.plain_summary: A public-servant breach-of-custody offence: a public servant who has custody of a State prisoner or prisoner of war and voluntarily allows that prisoner to escape is punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine -- the voluntary, deliberate nature of the lapse is what draws this severe punishment, contrasted with the merely negligent version in Section 157.
essential_elements: The accused is a public servant having custody of a State prisoner or prisoner of war
Voluntarily allowing that prisoner to escape from the place of confinement
breakdown.how_to_read: Always compare with Section 157 (negligent, not voluntary, escape) -- the punishment gap between the two (life/ten years here versus three years' simple imprisonment there) turns entirely on whether the public servant's conduct was deliberate or merely careless.

sections.title: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant and having the custody of any State prisoner or prisoner of war, negligently suffers such prisoner to escape from any place of confinement in which such prisoner is confined, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: public servant negligently suffering escape of a State prisoner or prisoner of war

breakdown.plain_summary: The negligence-based mirror of Section 156: a public servant who, through mere negligence rather than voluntary conduct, allows a State prisoner or prisoner of war in their custody to escape is punishable with simple imprisonment up to three years plus fine -- a much lighter punishment than the voluntary-escape offence.
essential_elements: The accused is a public servant having custody of a State prisoner or prisoner of war
Negligently (not voluntarily) suffering that prisoner to escape from the place of confinement
breakdown.how_to_read: The word 'negligently' is the entire distinction from Section 156 -- establishing carelessness rather than deliberate facilitation is what keeps this offence in the lighter, simple-imprisonment band.

sections.title: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner
sections.raw_text: Whoever knowingly aids or assists any State prisoner or prisoner of war in escaping from lawful custody, or rescues or attempts to rescue any such prisoner, or harbours or conceals any such prisoner who has escaped from lawful custody, or offers or attempts to offer any resistance to the recapture of such prisoner, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation.--A State prisoner or prisoner of war, who is permitted to be at large on his parole within certain limits in India, is said to escape from lawful custody if he goes beyond the limits within which he is allowed to be at large.
key_terms: aiding escape of a State prisoner or prisoner of war
harbouring an escaped State prisoner or prisoner of war
resisting recapture of an escaped prisoner
parole limits as custody under Section 158

breakdown.plain_summary: A broad outsider-liability offence covering four distinct ways a person (not necessarily a public servant) can interfere with the custody of a State prisoner or prisoner of war: knowingly aiding or assisting their escape, rescuing or attempting to rescue them, harbouring or concealing an already-escaped prisoner, or resisting (or attempting to resist) their recapture -- all punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine. The Explanation extends 'escape' to a parolee who strays beyond the geographic limits of their permitted parole.
essential_elements: Any one of: knowingly aiding/assisting escape, rescuing/attempting to rescue, harbouring/concealing an escaped prisoner, or resisting/attempting to resist recapture
The person concerned must be a State prisoner or prisoner of war in lawful custody (or, per the Explanation, a parolee who has gone beyond permitted limits)
breakdown.how_to_read: The parole Explanation is the subtle but important point -- custody is not limited to physical confinement behind walls; a paroled State prisoner or prisoner of war who simply wanders beyond their permitted parole limits is deemed to have 'escaped,' and anyone who then harbours them falls within this section.

sections.title: Abetting mutiny, or attempting to seduce a soldier, sailor or airman from his duty
sections.raw_text: Whoever abets the committing of mutiny by an officer, soldier, sailor or airman, in the Army, Navy or Air Force of the Government of India or attempts to seduce any such officer, soldier, sailor or airman from his allegiance or his duty, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: seducing a soldier sailor or airman from duty

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter VIII ('Of Offences Relating to the Army, Navy and Air Force') by punishing two related acts: abetting the committing of mutiny by a member of the Armed Forces, or attempting to seduce any such member from their allegiance or duty -- both drawing life imprisonment or up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine, regardless of whether the mutiny or desertion actually follows.
essential_elements: Abetting the committing of mutiny by an officer, soldier, sailor, or airman of the Army, Navy, or Air Force of the Government of India, or
Attempting to seduce any such person from their allegiance or duty
breakdown.how_to_read: This punishes the abetment/seduction itself, irrespective of outcome -- contrast with Section 160, which applies the far more severe death-or-life punishment specifically where mutiny actually results in consequence of the abetment.

sections.title: Abetment of mutiny, if mutiny is committed in consequence thereof
sections.raw_text: Whoever abets the committing of mutiny by an officer, soldier, sailor or airman, in the Army, Navy or Air Force of the Government of India, shall, if mutiny be committed in consequence of that abetment, be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: abetment of mutiny resulting in actual mutiny

breakdown.plain_summary: An aggravated, outcome-based escalation of Section 159: where the abetted mutiny is actually committed in consequence of the abetment, the abettor becomes liable to death or life imprisonment, or up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine -- the same consequence-triggered-escalation structure used throughout the Sanhita's abetment scheme (compare Section 49).
essential_elements: Abetting the committing of mutiny by an officer, soldier, sailor, or airman of the Army, Navy, or Air Force of the Government of India
Mutiny must actually be committed in consequence of that abetment
breakdown.how_to_read: The outcome -- mutiny actually occurring in consequence of the abetment -- is what separates this section's death-or-life-imprisonment exposure from Section 159's lesser, outcome-independent punishment for the bare abetment; always check whether the mutiny in fact materialised before charging under Section 160 rather than Section 159.

sections.title: Abetment of assault by soldier, sailor or airman on his superior officer, when in execution of his office
sections.raw_text: Whoever abets an assault by an officer, soldier, sailor or airman, in the Army, Navy or Air Force of the Government of India, on any superior officer being in the execution of his office, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: abetment of assault on a superior officer

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes abetting an assault by a member of the Armed Forces on their superior officer while that superior is in the execution of office, with up to three years' imprisonment plus fine -- the base, outcome-independent version, escalated by Section 162 if the assault actually occurs.
essential_elements: Abetting an assault by an officer, soldier, sailor, or airman on a superior officer
The superior officer must be in the execution of his office at the time
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Section 162 -- the identical fact pattern draws a heavier punishment (up to seven years) where the abetted assault is actually committed.

sections.title: Abetment of such assault, if assault committed
sections.raw_text: Whoever abets an assault by an officer, soldier, sailor or airman, in the Army, Navy or Air Force of the Government of India, on any superior officer being in the execution of his office, shall, if such assault be committed in consequence of that abetment be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: abetment of assault on superior officer resulting in actual assault

breakdown.plain_summary: The consequence-triggered escalation of Section 161: where the abetted assault on a superior officer is actually committed, the abettor's maximum punishment rises from three years to up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine.
essential_elements: Abetting an assault by a member of the Armed Forces on a superior officer in execution of office
The assault must actually be committed in consequence of the abetment
breakdown.how_to_read: Mirrors the Section 159/160 structure for mutiny -- the Sanhita consistently doubles or more-than-doubles the abettor's maximum exposure once the abetted military offence actually materialises.

sections.title: Abetment of desertion of soldier, sailor or airman
sections.raw_text: Whoever abets the desertion of any officer, soldier, sailor or airman, in the Army, Navy or Air Force of the Government of India, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes abetting the desertion of any member of the Armed Forces, with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- a lighter punishment band than mutiny or assault-on-superior abetment, reflecting desertion's comparatively lower gravity.
essential_elements: Abetting the desertion of an officer, soldier, sailor, or airman of the Army, Navy, or Air Force of the Government of India
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare the punishment ladder across Sections 159-163: mutiny abetment draws the heaviest punishment (life/ten years), assault-on-superior abetment is intermediate (three to seven years), and desertion abetment is the lightest (two years) -- reflecting the Sanhita's graduated view of military-discipline offences by severity.

sections.title: Harbouring deserter
sections.raw_text: Whoever, except as hereinafter excepted, knowing or having reason to believe that an officer, soldier, sailor or airman, in the Army, Navy or Air Force of the Government of India, has deserted, harbours such officer, soldier, sailor or airman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine or with both. Exception.--This provision does not extend to the case in which the harbour is given by the spouse of the deserter.
key_terms: spousal exception to harbouring a deserter

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes knowingly harbouring a deserter from the Armed Forces with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both -- but an express Exception entirely removes liability where the person giving harbour is the deserter's own spouse, recognising the practical reality of spousal cohabitation.
essential_elements: Knowledge or reason to believe that the person harboured has deserted from the Army, Navy, or Air Force
Harbouring that deserter
exceptions_and_qualifications: The provision does not extend to harbour given by the spouse of the deserter
breakdown.how_to_read: The spousal exception recurs throughout the Sanhita's harbouring-type offences (compare the organised-crime and terrorist-act harbouring provisions in Sections 111 and 113) -- always check whether the harbourer is the offender's spouse before concluding liability attaches.

sections.title: Deserter concealed on board merchant vessel through negligence of master
sections.raw_text: The master or person in charge of a merchant vessel, on board of which any deserter from the Army, Navy or Air Force of the Government of India is concealed, shall, though ignorant of such concealment, be liable to a penalty not exceeding three thousand rupees, if he might have known of such concealment but for some neglect of his duty as such master or person in charge, or but for some want of discipline on board of the vessel.
key_terms: negligent concealment of a deserter on a merchant vessel

breakdown.plain_summary: A strict, negligence-based penalty (not a conventional imprisonment offence) on the master or person in charge of a merchant vessel: even if genuinely ignorant that a deserter is concealed aboard, they face a penalty up to three thousand rupees if their own neglect of duty, or a want of discipline on the vessel, is what allowed the concealment to go undetected.
essential_elements: A deserter from the Army, Navy, or Air Force is concealed on board a merchant vessel
The master or person in charge, though actually ignorant of the concealment, might have known of it but for neglect of duty or want of discipline on board
breakdown.how_to_read: Unusual among Sanhita provisions for imposing only a monetary penalty (no imprisonment) and for attaching liability despite the master's actual ignorance -- the test is constructive knowledge via neglect of duty or a lack of shipboard discipline, not actual awareness.

sections.title: Abetment of act of insubordination by soldier, sailor or airman
sections.raw_text: Whoever abets what he knows to be an act of insubordination by an officer, soldier, sailor or airman, in the Army, Navy or Air Force, of the Government of India, shall, if such act of insubordination be committed in consequence of that abetment, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes knowingly abetting an act of insubordination by a member of the Armed Forces, but only where that insubordination is actually committed in consequence of the abetment -- up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
essential_elements: Abetting what the accused knows to be an act of insubordination by a member of the Army, Navy, or Air Force
The act of insubordination must actually be committed in consequence of that abetment
breakdown.how_to_read: Unlike the mutiny and assault-on-superior provisions (which punish the bare abetment under Sections 159 and 161 even without the underlying act occurring), Section 166 requires the insubordination to have actually resulted -- there is no lesser outcome-independent counterpart for insubordination.

sections.title: Persons subject to certain Acts
sections.raw_text: No person subject to the Air Force Act, 1950, the Army Act, 1950 and the Navy Act, 1957, or shall be subject to punishment under this Sanhita for any of the offences defined in this Chapter.
key_terms: savings clause for the special military Acts

breakdown.plain_summary: A jurisdiction-clearing savings clause: persons already subject to the Air Force Act 1950, the Army Act 1950, or the Navy Act 1957 are not liable to punishment under the Sanhita for any offence defined in Chapter VIII -- preventing double jeopardy between the Sanhita's general military-offence provisions and the special service-specific military codes, mirroring the mutiny/desertion savings clause already found in Section 1(6).
essential_elements: The accused is a person subject to the Air Force Act 1950, the Army Act 1950, or the Navy Act 1957
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Section 1(6)'s general savings clause for mutiny and desertion -- Section 167 is the Chapter-specific reinforcement ensuring Chapter VIII's offences never duplicate liability already covered by the special military statutes for persons actually subject to them.

sections.title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman
sections.raw_text: Whoever, not being a soldier, sailor or airman in the Army, Naval or Air service of the Government of India, wears any garb or carries any token resembling any garb or token used by such a soldier, sailor or airman with the intention that it may be believed that he is such a soldier, sailor or airman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: impersonating a soldier sailor or airman by garb or token

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Chapter VIII with a modest impersonation offence: a civilian who wears a garb or carries a token resembling that used by a soldier, sailor, or airman, intending to be believed to actually be one, is punishable with up to three months' imprisonment, fine up to two thousand rupees, or both.
essential_elements: The accused is not actually a soldier, sailor, or airman in the Army, Naval, or Air service of the Government of India
Wearing a garb, or carrying a token, resembling that used by such a person
Intention that it be believed the accused is such a soldier, sailor, or airman
breakdown.how_to_read: The deliberate intent-to-be-believed element distinguishes this from innocent costume-wearing (e.g. theatrical or fancy-dress use of military-style clothing) -- liability turns on the specific intention to deceive observers into believing genuine service status.

sections.title: Candidate, electoral right defined
sections.raw_text: For the purposes of this Chapter-- (a) "candidate" means a person who has been nominated as a candidate at any election; (b) "electoral right" means the right of a person to stand, or not to stand as, or to withdraw from being, a candidate or to vote or refrain from voting at an election.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter IX ('Of Offences Relating to Elections') with the two foundational definitions the rest of the Chapter depends on: a 'candidate' is anyone nominated at an election, and 'electoral right' covers the full bundle of choices around standing, withdrawing, voting, and abstaining.
essential_elements: Candidate: a person nominated as a candidate at any election
Electoral right: the right to stand, not stand, withdraw from being a candidate, vote, or refrain from voting at an election
breakdown.how_to_read: Every other Chapter IX offence (bribery, undue influence, personation) is built around interference with, or reward for exercising, one of these two defined terms -- read them first before applying any later section in this Chapter.

sections.title: Bribery
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever-- (i) gives a gratification to any person with the object of inducing him or any other person to exercise any electoral right or of rewarding any person for having exercised any such right; or (ii) accepts either for himself or for any other person any gratification as a reward for exercising any such right or for inducing or attempting to induce any other person to exercise any such right, commits the offence of bribery: Provided that a declaration of public policy or a promise of public action shall not be an offence under this section. (2) A person who offers, or agrees to give, or offers or attempts to procure, a gratification shall be deemed to give a gratification. (3) A person who obtains or agrees to accept or attempts to obtain a gratification shall be deemed to accept a gratification, and a person who accepts a gratification as a motive for doing what he does not intend to do, or as a reward for doing what he has not done, shall be deemed to have accepted the gratification as a reward.

breakdown.plain_summary: Defines the offence of election bribery from both sides: giving a gratification to induce or reward the exercise of an electoral right, and accepting a gratification as a reward for exercising or inducing the exercise of such a right -- with deeming provisions that sweep in mere offers, agreements, and attempts, and an express proviso protecting genuine public-policy declarations or promises of public action from being mistaken for bribery.
essential_elements: Giving a gratification to induce or reward the exercise of an electoral right, or
Accepting (or agreeing or attempting to accept) a gratification as a reward for exercising, or for inducing another to exercise, an electoral right
exceptions_and_qualifications: A declaration of public policy or a promise of public action is not an offence under this section
breakdown.how_to_read: The deeming sub-sections (2) and (3) matter in practice: bribery is complete at the offer/attempt stage on the giving side, and at the agreement/attempt-to-obtain stage on the receiving side -- actual exchange of the gratification is not required for either half of the offence.

sections.title: Undue influence at elections
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever voluntarily interferes or attempts to interfere with the free exercise of any electoral right commits the offence of undue influence at an election. (2) Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions of sub-section (1), whoever-- (a) threatens any candidate or voter, or any person in whom a candidate or voter is interested, with injury of any kind; or (b) induces or attempts to induce a candidate or voter to believe that he or any person in whom he is interested will become or will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure or of spiritual censure, shall be deemed to interfere with the free exercise of the electoral right of such candidate or voter, within the meaning of sub-section (1). (3) A declaration of public policy or a promise of public action or the mere exercise of a legal right without intent to interfere with an electoral right, shall not be deemed to be interference within the meaning of this section.
key_terms: threat of injury to a candidate or voter
spiritual or divine-displeasure threats at elections

breakdown.plain_summary: Criminalises voluntarily interfering, or attempting to interfere, with anyone's free exercise of an electoral right, with two illustrative (non-exhaustive) deemed forms of interference: threatening injury to a candidate, voter, or someone they care about, and threats of Divine displeasure or spiritual censure -- while expressly excluding genuine public-policy statements and the mere exercise of a legal right made without any intent to interfere.
essential_elements: Voluntary interference, or attempted interference, with the free exercise of any electoral right
exceptions_and_qualifications: A declaration of public policy or a promise of public action is not interference
The mere exercise of a legal right, without intent to interfere with an electoral right, is not interference
breakdown.how_to_read: Sub-section (2)'s threat and spiritual-censure examples are deeming provisions, not an exhaustive list -- sub-section (1)'s general 'voluntary interference' language can still catch other forms of coercion not spelt out in (2)(a) or (b).

sections.title: Personation at elections
sections.raw_text: Whoever at an election applies for a voting paper on votes in the name of any other person, whether living or dead, or in a fictitious name, or who having voted once at such election applies at the same election for a voting paper in his own name, and whoever abets, procures or attempts to procure the voting by any person in any such way, commits the offence of personation at an election: Provided that nothing in this section shall apply to a person who has been authorised to vote as proxy for an elector under any law for the time being in force in so far as he votes as a proxy for such elector.

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes three overlapping ways of personation at an election: voting in the name of another living or dead person or in a fictitious name, voting a second time in one's own name after already voting once, and abetting or procuring any such fraudulent voting by another -- with an express exception for lawfully authorised proxy voters acting strictly within their proxy authority.
essential_elements: Applying for a voting paper in the name of another (living or dead) or in a fictitious name, or
Applying for a voting paper in one's own name after having already voted once at the same election, or
Abetting, procuring, or attempting to procure voting by any person in either of the above ways
exceptions_and_qualifications: Does not apply to a person authorised to vote as proxy for an elector under any law in force, so far as he votes as that elector's proxy
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the abetment/procurement limb folds a third party's liability directly into the same section, rather than relying on the Sanhita's general abetment provisions (Sections 45 onward) -- personation abettors are liable under Section 172 itself.

sections.title: Punishment for bribery
sections.raw_text: Whoever commits the offence of bribery shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both: Provided that bribery by treating shall be punished with fine only. Explanation.--"Treating" means that form of bribery where the gratification consists in food, drink, entertainment, or provision.
key_terms: punishment for bribery at an election

breakdown.plain_summary: Fixes the punishment for Section 170 bribery at up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both -- but carves out 'treating' (bribery where the gratification is food, drink, entertainment, or provision) for a lighter fine-only punishment, reflecting its comparatively lower gravity among forms of electoral bribery.
essential_elements: Commission of the offence of bribery as defined in Section 170
exceptions_and_qualifications: Bribery by treating (gratification consisting of food, drink, entertainment, or provision) is punished with fine only, not imprisonment
breakdown.how_to_read: Always classify the bribery first: if the gratification was food, drink, entertainment, or provision, the treating proviso caps the punishment at fine alone, regardless of how egregious the surrounding conduct otherwise appears.

sections.title: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election
sections.raw_text: Whoever commits the offence of undue influence or personation at an election shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: punishment for undue influence or personation

breakdown.plain_summary: Fixes an identical punishment band -- up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both -- for both undue influence (Section 171) and personation (Section 172) at an election, treating the two distinct offences as equally grave for sentencing purposes.
essential_elements: Commission of the offence of undue influence (Section 171) or personation (Section 172) at an election
breakdown.how_to_read: Unlike bribery, which splits into a lighter treating-only band under Section 173, undue influence and personation share a single flat punishment ceiling regardless of the particular form the interference or personation took.

sections.title: False statement in connection with an election
sections.raw_text: Whoever with intent to affect the result of an election makes or publishes any statement purporting to be a statement of fact which is false and which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true, in relation to the personal character or conduct of any candidate shall be punished with fine.
key_terms: false statement about a candidate's personal character or conduct

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes, with fine only, making or publishing a statement of fact about a candidate's personal character or conduct that the maker knows or believes to be false, or does not believe to be true, done with intent to affect the election's result -- a narrow, intent-and-falsity-specific defamation-adjacent offence confined to the electoral context.
essential_elements: Making or publishing a statement purporting to be a statement of fact
The statement is false, and the accused knows or believes it to be false, or does not believe it to be true
The statement relates to the personal character or conduct of a candidate
Intent to affect the result of the election
breakdown.how_to_read: The mental element is deliberately broad on the falsity side (knowledge, belief of falsity, or mere absence of belief in its truth all suffice) but narrow on the targeting side (must concern a candidate's personal character or conduct, and be made with intent to affect the election result) -- genuine policy criticism of a candidate falls outside this section.

sections.title: Illegal payments in connection with an election
sections.raw_text: Whoever without the general or special authority in writing of a candidate incurs or authorises expenses on account of the holding of any public meeting, or upon any advertisement, circular or publication, or in any other way whatsoever for the purpose of promoting or procuring the election of such candidate, shall be punished with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees: Provided that if any person having incurred any such expenses not exceeding the amount of ten rupees without authority obtains within ten days from the date on which such expenses were incurred the approval in writing of the candidate, he shall be deemed to have incurred such expenses with the authority of the candidate.
key_terms: illegal election expenses without candidate's written authority
retrospective approval of small election expenses

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes, with a fine up to ten thousand rupees, incurring or authorising election-promotion expenses (public meetings, advertisements, circulars, publications, or any other means) without the candidate's general or special written authority -- but a proviso lets expenses of ten rupees or less be retrospectively legitimised if the candidate gives written approval within ten days.
essential_elements: Incurring or authorising expenses for the purpose of promoting or procuring a candidate's election
Absence of the candidate's general or special authority in writing for those expenses
exceptions_and_qualifications: Expenses not exceeding ten rupees, incurred without authority, are deemed authorised if the candidate gives written approval within ten days of the expense being incurred
breakdown.how_to_read: The ten-rupee/ten-day proviso is a narrow safety valve for small, good-faith campaign spending by supporters -- it does not extend to larger unauthorised expenditure, which remains punishable regardless of any later ratification by the candidate.

sections.title: Failure to keep election accounts
sections.raw_text: Whoever being required by any law for the time being in force or any rule having the force of law to keep accounts of expenses incurred at or in connection with an election fails to keep such accounts shall be punished with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees.
key_terms: failure to keep election expense accounts

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Chapter IX with a straightforward compliance offence: failing to keep accounts of election-related expenses, where some law or statutory rule requires such accounts to be kept, is punishable with a fine up to five thousand rupees.
essential_elements: The accused is required by law or a rule having the force of law to keep accounts of election-related expenses
Failure to keep such accounts
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a pure recordkeeping offence tied to an external legal duty (typically arising under election law, e.g. the Representation of the People Act) -- the Sanhita itself does not prescribe what accounts must be kept, only punishes the failure once such a duty exists elsewhere in law.

sections.title: Counterfeiting coin, Government stamps, currency-notes or bank-notes
sections.raw_text: Whoever counterfeits, or knowingly performs any part of the process of counterfeiting, any coin, stamp issued by Government for the purpose of revenue, currency-note or bank-note, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation.--For the purposes of this Chapter-- (1) the expression "bank-note" means a promissory note or engagement for the payment of money to bearer on demand issued by any person carrying on the business of banking in any part of the world, or issued by or under the authority of any State or Sovereign Power, and intended to be used as equivalent to, or as a substitute for money; (2) "coin" shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in section 2 of the Coinage Act, 2011 and includes metal used for the time being as money and is stamped and issued by or under the authority of any State or Sovereign Power intended to be so used; (3) a person commits the offence of "counterfeiting Government stamp" who counterfeits by causing a genuine stamp of one denomination to appear like a genuine stamp of a different denomination; (4) a person commits the offence of counterfeiting coin who intending to practise deception, or knowing it to be likely that deception will thereby be practised, causes a genuine coin to appear like a different coin; and (5) the offence of "counterfeiting coin" includes diminishing the weight or alteration of the composition, or alteration of the appearance of the coin.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter X ('Of Offences Relating to Coin, Currency-notes, Bank-notes, and Government Stamps') with the core counterfeiting offence -- counterfeiting, or knowingly performing any part of the process of counterfeiting, a coin, revenue stamp, currency-note, or bank-note, punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine -- followed by a five-part Explanation defining bank-note, cross-referencing coin to the Coinage Act 2011, and specifying what counts as counterfeiting a Government stamp versus counterfeiting a coin (including weight-diminishing and appearance alteration).
essential_elements: Counterfeiting, or knowingly performing any part of the process of counterfeiting
The subject-matter is a coin, a Government revenue stamp, a currency-note, or a bank-note
breakdown.how_to_read: The five-limb Explanation does heavy definitional lifting for the whole Chapter X -- in particular, note that 'counterfeiting coin' extends beyond outright fakes to include diminishing a genuine coin's weight or altering its composition or appearance, so even tampering with a real coin can qualify.

sections.title: Using as genuine, forged or counterfeit coin, Government stamp, currency-notes or bank-notes
sections.raw_text: Whoever imports or exports, or sells or delivers to, or buys or receives from, any other person, or otherwise traffics or uses as genuine, any forged or counterfeit coin, stamp, currency-note or bank-note, knowing or having reason to believe the same to be forged or counterfeit, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: using forged or counterfeit currency as genuine
trafficking in forged or counterfeit coin or notes

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes, with the same life-imprisonment-or-ten-years band as counterfeiting itself, the downstream conduct of importing, exporting, buying, selling, delivering, receiving, trafficking, or otherwise using as genuine any forged or counterfeit coin, stamp, currency-note, or bank-note -- provided the accused knew or had reason to believe it was forged or counterfeit.
essential_elements: Importing, exporting, selling, delivering, buying, receiving, trafficking in, or using as genuine, any forged or counterfeit coin, stamp, currency-note, or bank-note
Knowledge or reason to believe that the item is forged or counterfeit
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 179 punishes dealing with already-counterfeit items just as severely as Section 178 punishes the act of counterfeiting itself -- the knowledge/reason-to-believe element is what separates an innocent recipient from a punishable trafficker.

sections.title: Possession of forged or counterfeit coin, Government stamp, currency-notes or bank-notes
sections.raw_text: Whoever has in his possession any forged or counterfeit coin, stamp, currency-note or bank-note, knowing or having reason to believe the same to be forged or counterfeit and intending to use the same as genuine or that it may be used as genuine, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both. Explanation.--If a person establishes the possession of the forged or counterfeit coin, stamp, currency-note or bank-note to be from a lawful source, it shall not constitute an offence under this section.
key_terms: possession of forged or counterfeit currency with intent to use as genuine
lawful-source defence to possession of counterfeit currency

breakdown.plain_summary: A lighter-punishment (up to seven years) possession offence sitting below Sections 178 and 179: mere possession of forged or counterfeit coin, stamp, currency-note, or bank-note, with knowledge or reason to believe it is forged, coupled with intent to use or allow its use as genuine -- but the Explanation gives a complete defence where the possessor establishes the item came from a lawful source.
essential_elements: Possession of a forged or counterfeit coin, stamp, currency-note, or bank-note
Knowledge or reason to believe that it is forged or counterfeit
Intention to use it as genuine, or that it may be used as genuine
exceptions_and_qualifications: No offence is constituted if the person establishes that possession of the forged or counterfeit item is from a lawful source
breakdown.how_to_read: The lawful-source Explanation places a burden on the possessor to affirmatively establish the item's origin once possession and the forged/counterfeit character are shown -- compare the similarly structured reverse-onus provisions elsewhere in the Sanhita (e.g. Section 139's begging presumption).

sections.title: Making or possessing instruments or materials for forging or counterfeiting coin, Government stamp, currency-notes or bank-notes
sections.raw_text: Whoever makes or mends, or performs any part of the process of making or mending, or buys or sells or disposes of, or has in his possession, any machinery, die, or instrument or material for the purpose of being used, or knowing or having reason to believe that it is intended to be used, for forging or counterfeiting any coin, stamp issued by Government for the purpose of revenue, currency-note or bank-note, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: making or possessing counterfeiting instruments or materials

breakdown.plain_summary: Extends the heaviest counterfeiting-level punishment (life imprisonment or up to ten years plus fine) to the preparatory conduct of making, mending, buying, selling, disposing of, or possessing any machinery, die, instrument, or material intended (or known/believed to be intended) for forging or counterfeiting coin, revenue stamps, currency-notes, or bank-notes.
essential_elements: Making, mending, buying, selling, disposing of, or possessing machinery, a die, an instrument, or material
Purpose of its being used, or knowledge/reason to believe it is intended to be used, for forging or counterfeiting coin, a Government revenue stamp, a currency-note, or a bank-note
breakdown.how_to_read: Equipment-and-materials liability under Section 181 carries the identical maximum punishment as actual counterfeiting under Section 178 -- the Sanhita treats readying the means of counterfeiting as gravely as the completed act itself.

sections.title: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever makes, or causes to be made, or uses for any purpose whatsoever, or delivers to any person, any document purporting to be, or in any way resembling, or so nearly resembling as to be calculated to deceive, any currency-note or bank-note shall be punished with fine which may extend to three hundred rupees. (2) If any person, whose name appears on a document the making of which is an offence under sub-section (1), refuses, without lawful excuse, to disclose to a police officer on being so required the name and address of the person by whom it was printed or otherwise made, he shall be punished with fine which may extend to six hundred rupees. (3) Where the name of any person appears on any document in respect of which any person is charged with an offence under sub-section (1) or on any other document used or distributed in connection with that document it may, until the contrary is proved, be presumed that the person caused the document to be made.
key_terms: document resembling a currency-note or bank-note
refusal to disclose maker of a currency-resembling document
presumption of causing a currency-resembling document to be made

breakdown.plain_summary: A deception-adjacent offence distinct from outright counterfeiting: making, using, or delivering a document that purports to be, resembles, or is so nearly resembling a currency-note or bank-note as to be calculated to deceive, punishable by fine up to three hundred rupees -- with escalating fines for refusing to disclose the document's maker to police, and a presumption (rebuttable) that anyone whose name appears on such a document caused it to be made.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): making, causing to be made, using, or delivering any document purporting to be, resembling, or so nearly resembling as to be calculated to deceive, a currency-note or bank-note
Sub-section (2): the named maker's refusal, without lawful excuse, to disclose the printer's/maker's name and address to a police officer on demand
breakdown.how_to_read: This section covers deceptively currency-like documents (e.g. novelty or prop notes crafted to pass as real) that fall short of true counterfeiting under Section 178 -- note the comparatively modest fine-only punishment reflects its lesser gravity, and the sub-section (3) presumption shifts a practical evidentiary burden onto anyone named on such a document.

sections.title: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government
sections.raw_text: Whoever, fraudulently or with intent to cause loss to the Government, removes or effaces from any substance, bearing any stamp issued by Government for the purpose of revenue, any writing or document for which such stamp has been used, or removes from any writing or document a stamp which has been used for such writing or document, in order that such stamp may be used for a different writing or document, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: effacing writing from a Government-stamped substance
removing a used Government stamp to reuse it

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes, with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both, two fraudulent-intent revenue-evasion manoeuvres: effacing the writing or document for which a Government revenue stamp was used, or removing a used stamp from a document, in either case done to enable the same stamp to be reused on a different writing or document and thereby cause loss to Government revenue.
essential_elements: Fraudulent intent or intent to cause loss to the Government
Removing or effacing writing/a document for which a Government revenue stamp has been used, or removing the stamp itself from the document
Purpose that the stamp may be used for a different writing or document
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a revenue-protection offence, not a counterfeiting offence -- the stamp itself may be entirely genuine; the wrong lies in fraudulently extending its use beyond the single transaction for which the revenue was paid.

sections.title: Using Government stamp known to have been before used
sections.raw_text: Whoever, fraudulently or with intent to cause loss to the Government, uses for any purpose a stamp issued by Government for the purpose of revenue, which he knows to have been before used, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: using a previously used Government revenue stamp

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes, with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both, fraudulently or loss-intending use of a Government revenue stamp the user knows has already been used once before -- the natural completion offence to Section 183's stamp-removal conduct, catching the actual reuse of a detached stamp.
essential_elements: Fraudulent intent or intent to cause loss to the Government
Using a Government revenue stamp for any purpose
Knowledge that the stamp has been used before
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Section 183: 183 criminalises detaching a used stamp to enable its reuse, while 184 criminalises the actual act of reusing a stamp already known to be used -- the two sections typically apply to successive stages of the same revenue-evasion scheme.

sections.title: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used
sections.raw_text: Whoever, fraudulently or with intent to cause loss to Government, erases or removes from a stamp issued by Government for the purpose of revenue, any mark, put or impressed upon such stamp for the purpose of denoting that the same has been used, or knowingly has in his possession or sells or disposes of any such stamp from which such mark has been erased or removed, or sells or disposes of any such stamp which he knows to have been used, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: erasing the used-mark from a Government revenue stamp
possessing or dealing in a stamp with its used-mark erased

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes out the stamp-reuse offence cluster (Sections 183-185) by punishing, with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both, erasing or removing the mark that denotes a Government revenue stamp has already been used, as well as knowingly possessing, selling, or disposing of such a cleaned stamp, or selling/disposing of a stamp known to have been used at all.
essential_elements: Fraudulent intent or intent to cause loss to Government, and erasing/removing the used-denoting mark from a Government revenue stamp, or
Knowingly possessing, selling, or disposing of a stamp from which such a mark has been erased or removed, or
Selling or disposing of a stamp known to have been used
breakdown.how_to_read: Sections 183-185 together form a complete chain covering the stamp-reuse fraud lifecycle: detaching the stamp (183), reusing it knowing it was used (184), and erasing the physical evidence that it was ever used plus dealing in such doctored stamps (185).

sections.title: Prohibition of fictitious stamps
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever-- (a) makes, knowingly utters, deals in or sells any fictitious stamp, or knowingly uses for any postal purpose any fictitious stamp; or (b) has in his possession, without lawful excuse, any fictitious stamp; or (c) makes or, without lawful excuse, has in his possession any die, plate, instrument or materials for making any fictitious stamp, shall be punished with fine which may extend to two hundred rupees. (2) Any such stamp, die, plate, instrument or materials in the possession of any person for making any fictitious stamp may be seized and, if seized shall be forfeited. (3) In this section "fictitious stamp" means any stamp falsely purporting to be issued by Government for the purpose of denoting a rate of postage, or any facsimile or imitation or representation, whether on paper or otherwise, of any stamp issued by Government for that purpose. (4) In this section and also in sections 178 to 181 (both inclusive), and sections 183 to 185 (both inclusive) the word "Government", when used in connection with, or in reference to any stamp issued for the purpose of denoting a rate of postage, shall, notwithstanding anything in clause (12) of section 2, be deemed to include the person or persons authorised by law to administer executive Government in any part of India or in any foreign country.
key_terms: extended meaning of Government for postage stamps
