breakdown.plain_summary: A lighter, fine-only (up to two hundred rupees) postal-stamp-specific offence: making, uttering, dealing in, selling, or postally using a 'fictitious stamp' (a fake or imitation postage stamp falsely purporting to be Government-issued), possessing one without lawful excuse, or making or possessing without lawful excuse the means to make one -- with mandatory seizure and forfeiture of any such stamp or stamp-making equipment found in a person's possession, and a deeming sub-section extending 'Government' to foreign postal authorities for this purpose.
essential_elements: Making, knowingly uttering, dealing in, or selling a fictitious stamp, or knowingly using one for a postal purpose, or
Possessing a fictitious stamp without lawful excuse, or
Making, or possessing without lawful excuse, a die, plate, instrument, or material for making a fictitious stamp
exceptions_and_qualifications: Possession of a fictitious stamp, die, plate, instrument, or material is not an offence if the person has lawful excuse
breakdown.how_to_read: Sub-section (4)'s extended definition of 'Government' matters for cross-border postal fraud -- for postage-stamp purposes across Sections 178-181 and 183-185, 'Government' includes whoever administers executive government anywhere, not just India, recognising that postal stamp fraud often has an international dimension.

sections.title: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being employed in any mint lawfully established in India, does any act, or omits what he is legally bound to do, with the intention of causing any coin issued from that mint to be of a different weight or composition from the weight or composition fixed by law, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: mint employee causing coin of wrongful weight or composition

breakdown.plain_summary: A specific insider offence for persons employed in a lawfully established Indian mint: doing any act, or omitting a legally required act, with the intention of causing coin issued from that mint to deviate from its legally fixed weight or composition, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine.
essential_elements: The accused is employed in a mint lawfully established in India
Doing an act, or omitting an act the accused is legally bound to do
Intention of causing coin issued from that mint to be of a different weight or composition from that fixed by law
breakdown.how_to_read: This is an intent-based insider-sabotage offence aimed at mint employees specifically -- distinct from the general counterfeiting offences in Sections 178-181, which apply to anyone, this section targets the institutional integrity of lawful coin production itself.

sections.title: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint
sections.raw_text: Whoever, without lawful authority, takes out of any mint, lawfully established in India, any coining tool or instrument, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: unlawfully taking a coining instrument from a mint

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Chapter X with a companion insider/security offence to Section 187: taking any coining tool or instrument out of a lawfully established Indian mint without lawful authority, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine, regardless of what the tool is later used for.
essential_elements: Taking a coining tool or instrument out of a mint lawfully established in India
Absence of lawful authority for doing so
breakdown.how_to_read: The offence is complete on the unauthorised removal itself -- unlike Section 181 (possessing counterfeiting instruments with forging intent), Section 188 requires no proof of any intended counterfeiting use, only that genuine mint equipment was taken out without lawful authority.

sections.title: Unlawful assembly
sections.raw_text: (1) An assembly of five or more persons is designated an "unlawful assembly", if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is-- (a) to overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force, the Central Government or any State Government or Parliament or the Legislature of any State, or any public servant in the exercise of the lawful power of such public servant; or (b) to resist the execution of any law, or of any legal process; or (c) to commit any mischief or criminal trespass, or other offence; or (d) by means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to any person, to take or obtain possession of any property, or to deprive any person of the enjoyment of a right of way, or of the use of water or other incorporeal right of which he is in possession or enjoyment, or to enforce any right or supposed right; or (e) by means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to compel any person to do what he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do what he is legally entitled to do. Explanation.--An assembly which was not unlawful when it assembled, may subsequently become an unlawful assembly. (2) Whoever, being aware of facts which render any assembly an unlawful assembly, intentionally joins that assembly, or continues in it, is said to be a member of an unlawful assembly and such member shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both. (3) Whoever joins or continues in an unlawful assembly, knowing that such unlawful assembly has been commanded in the manner prescribed by law to disperse, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. (4) Whoever, being armed with any deadly weapon, or with anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, is a member of an unlawful assembly, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. (5) Whoever knowingly joins or continues in any assembly of five or more persons likely to cause a disturbance of the public peace, after such assembly has been lawfully commanded to disperse, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both. Explanation.--If the assembly is an unlawful assembly within the meaning of sub-section (1), the offender shall be punishable under sub-section (3). (6) Whoever hires or engages, or employs, or promotes, or connives at the hiring, engagement or employment of any person to join or become a member of any unlawful assembly, shall be punishable as a member of such unlawful assembly, and for any offence which may be committed by any such person as a member of such unlawful assembly in pursuance of such hiring, engagement or employment, in the same manner as if he had been a member of such unlawful assembly, or himself had committed such offence. (7) Whoever harbours, receives or assembles, in any house or premises in his occupation or charge, or under his control any persons knowing that such persons have been hired, engaged or employed, or are about to be hired, engaged or employed, to join or become members of an unlawful assembly, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both. (8) Whoever is engaged, or hired, or offers or attempts to be hired or engaged, to do or assist in doing any of the acts specified in sub-section (1), shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both. (9) Whoever, being so engaged or hired as referred to in sub-section (8), goes armed, or engages or offers to go armed, with any deadly weapon or with anything which used as a weapon of offence is likely to cause death, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: armed member of an unlawful assembly
hiring persons to join an unlawful assembly
harbouring persons hired for an unlawful assembly

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter XI ('Of Offences Against the Public Tranquillity') with the foundational definition: an assembly of five or more persons becomes 'unlawful' if its common object falls within five listed categories (overawing government, resisting law, committing an offence, forcibly taking property or rights, or compelling illegal conduct). The section then builds a graduated liability ladder across nine sub-sections: ordinary intentional membership (six months), membership after a lawful order to disperse (two years), armed membership (two years), continuing in a disturbance-likely assembly after a dispersal order (six months), and separate offences for hiring, harbouring, or offering to join such an assembly, with an enhanced band if armed.
essential_elements: Five or more persons assembled with a common object falling within one of the five categories in sub-section (1)(a)-(e)
For membership: awareness of the facts rendering the assembly unlawful, and intentionally joining or continuing in it
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the structural foundation for the whole riot/affray cluster in Chapter XI -- Sections 190-193 all presuppose an 'unlawful assembly' as defined here. The Explanation to sub-section (1) matters practically: a gathering that starts out lawful can still become an unlawful assembly mid-way if its object shifts, and a member's liability turns on when they joined or continued relative to that shift and any dispersal order.

sections.title: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object
sections.raw_text: If an offence is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object of that assembly, or such as the members of that assembly knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object, every person who, at the time of the committing of that offence, is a member of the same assembly, is guilty of that offence.
key_terms: constructive liability of unlawful assembly members

breakdown.plain_summary: A constructive/vicarious liability rule: if any member of an unlawful assembly commits an offence in prosecution of (or known-likely in prosecution of) the assembly's common object, every person who was a member of that assembly at the time is guilty of that very offence, not merely of unlawful assembly -- membership in the group at the critical moment substitutes for individual participation in the specific act.
essential_elements: An offence is committed by a member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object, or an offence the members knew was likely in prosecution of that object
The accused was a member of the same assembly at the time the offence was committed
breakdown.how_to_read: This is one of the Sanhita's most powerful constructive-liability tools -- it does not require proof that the particular accused struck the blow or threw the stone; mere membership at the operative moment, combined with the offence falling within or being a known-likely consequence of the common object, suffices to convict every member of the completed offence.

sections.title: Rioting
sections.raw_text: (1) Whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly, or by any member thereof, in prosecution of the common object of such assembly, every member of such assembly is guilty of the offence of rioting. (2) Whoever is guilty of rioting, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. (3) Whoever is guilty of rioting, being armed with a deadly weapon or with anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: rioting armed with a deadly weapon

breakdown.plain_summary: Converts an unlawful assembly into the offence of 'rioting' the moment force or violence is used by the assembly, or by any of its members, in prosecution of the common object -- every member at that point is guilty of rioting (up to two years), escalated to up to five years if the member was armed with a deadly weapon or anything likely to cause death when used as a weapon.
essential_elements: An unlawful assembly as defined in Section 189
Use of force or violence by the assembly or any member of it, in prosecution of the common object
breakdown.how_to_read: Rioting is simply an armed-or-unarmed unlawful assembly that has turned violent -- the base/armed punishment split in sub-sections (2) and (3) mirrors the same armed-member escalation already seen in Section 189(4) for mere membership.

sections.title: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot -- if rioting be committed; if not committed
sections.raw_text: Whoever malignantly, or wantonly by doing anything which is illegal, gives provocation to any person intending or knowing it to be likely that such provocation will cause the offence of rioting to be committed, shall, if the offence of rioting be committed in consequence of such provocation, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both; and if the offence of rioting be not committed, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes malignantly or wantonly (through illegal conduct) provoking another person, intending or knowing it likely that the provocation will cause rioting -- with a consequence-triggered split: up to one year if rioting actually results from the provocation, but only up to six months if it does not, following the Sanhita's recurring pattern of escalating punishment once the provoked offence actually materialises.
essential_elements: Malignantly, or wantonly by illegal conduct, giving provocation to a person
Intention, or knowledge that it is likely, that the provocation will cause rioting
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare the consequence-triggered structure here to Sections 159/160 (mutiny abetment) and 161/162 (assault-on-superior abetment) -- the Sanhita consistently punishes the provoking/abetting conduct even if the ultimate offence never occurs, but doubles (or more) the exposure once it does.

sections.title: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes place
sections.raw_text: (1) Whenever any unlawful assembly or riot takes place, the owner or occupier of the land upon which such unlawful assembly is held, or such riot is committed, and any person having or claiming an interest in such land, shall be punishable with fine not exceeding one thousand rupees, if he or his agent or manager, knowing that such offence is being or has been committed, or having reason to believe it is likely to be committed, do not give the earliest notice thereof in his or their power to the officer in charge at the nearest police station, and do not, in the case of his or their having reason to believe that it was about to be committed, use all lawful means in his or their power to prevent it and, in the event of its taking place, do not use all lawful means in his or their power to disperse or suppress the riot or unlawful assembly. (2) Whenever a riot is committed for the benefit or on behalf of any person who is the owner or occupier of any land respecting which such riot takes place, or who claims any interest in such land, or in the subject of any dispute which gave rise to the riot, or who has accepted or derived any benefit therefrom, such person shall be punishable with fine, if he or his agent or manager, having reason to believe that such riot was likely to be committed or that the unlawful assembly by which such riot was committed was likely to be held, shall not respectively use all lawful means in his or their power to prevent such assembly or riot from taking place, and for suppressing and dispersing the same. (3) Whenever a riot is committed for the benefit or on behalf of any person who is the owner or occupier of any land respecting which such riot takes place, or who claims any interest in such land, or in the subject of any dispute which gave rise to the riot, or who has accepted or derived any benefit therefrom, the agent or manager of such person shall be punishable with fine, if such agent or manager, having reason to believe that such riot was likely to be committed, or that the unlawful assembly by which such riot was committed was likely to be held, shall not use all lawful means in his power to prevent such riot or assembly from taking place and for suppressing and dispersing the same.
key_terms: liability of landowner for unlawful assembly or riot on his land
liability of agent or manager for riot benefiting principal

breakdown.plain_summary: Imposes a fine (up to one thousand rupees under sub-section (1)) on landowners/occupiers/interest-holders who, knowing of or having reason to believe in an unlawful assembly or riot on their land, fail to give earliest notice to the nearest police station and fail to use all lawful means to prevent or suppress it; sub-sections (2) and (3) extend parallel fine liability to a person for whose benefit a riot is committed, and to that person's agent or manager, where either fails to use all lawful means to prevent or suppress a riot they had reason to believe was likely.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): ownership, occupation, or a claimed interest in land where an unlawful assembly or riot takes place, combined with knowledge or reason to believe in it, and a failure to notify police and to use lawful means to prevent/suppress it

Sub-sections (2)-(3): a riot committed for a person's benefit or on their behalf (or that of their agent/manager), combined with reason to believe it was likely and a failure to use lawful means to prevent or suppress it
breakdown.how_to_read: This is an omission-based offence -- the landowner or beneficiary is not punished for the riot itself but for failing to act (notify police, use lawful means to prevent/suppress) despite the requisite knowledge or reason to believe; passive landowners genuinely unaware of any likelihood of trouble face no liability under this section.

sections.title: Affray
sections.raw_text: (1) When two or more persons, by fighting in a public place, disturb the public peace, they are said to commit an affray. (2) Whoever commits an affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.

breakdown.plain_summary: Defines 'affray' as two or more persons fighting in a public place in a way that disturbs the public peace, punishable with a modest maximum of one month's imprisonment, fine up to one thousand rupees, or both -- the lightest public-order offence in the Chapter, distinguished from rioting by the absence of any unlawful-assembly/common-object structure.
essential_elements: Two or more persons fighting
The fighting takes place in a public place
The fighting disturbs the public peace
breakdown.how_to_read: Affray is a spontaneous, unplanned public fight -- unlike rioting (Section 191), it requires no prior unlawful assembly or common object, just two or more people fighting publicly in a way that disturbs the peace; its punishment is correspondingly far lighter.

sections.title: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc.
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever assaults or obstructs any public servant or uses criminal force on any public servant in the discharge of his duty as such public servant in endeavouring to disperse an unlawful assembly, or to suppress a riot or affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which shall not be less than twenty-five thousand rupees, or with both. (2) Whoever threatens to assault or attempts to obstruct any public servant or threatens or attempts to use criminal force to any public servant in the discharge of his duty as such public servant in endeavouring to disperse an unlawful assembly, or to suppress a riot or affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: assaulting or obstructing a public servant suppressing a riot
threatening or attempting to obstruct a public servant suppressing a riot

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes assaulting, obstructing, or using criminal force on a public servant (such as a police officer) who is discharging their duty to disperse an unlawful assembly or suppress a riot or affray, with up to three years' imprisonment plus a mandatory minimum fine of twenty-five thousand rupees; a lesser band (up to one year) applies to mere threats or attempts to assault, obstruct, or use criminal force in the same context.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): assaulting, obstructing, or using criminal force on a public servant discharging duty to disperse an unlawful assembly or suppress a riot/affray
Sub-section (2): threatening or attempting (rather than completing) the same conduct
breakdown.how_to_read: The mandatory minimum fine of twenty-five thousand rupees in sub-section (1) is notably steep and non-waivable -- a deliberate deterrent against interfering with law enforcement specifically while it is actively engaged in restoring public order.

sections.title: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever-- (a) by words, either spoken or written, or by signs or by visible representations or through electronic communication or otherwise, promotes or attempts to promote, on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, caste or community or any other ground whatsoever, disharmony or feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between different religious, racial, language or regional groups or castes or communities; or (b) commits any act which is prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony between different religious, racial, language or regional groups or castes or communities, and which disturbs or is likely to disturb the public tranquillity; or (c) organises any exercise, movement, drill or other similar activity intending that the participants in such activity shall use or be trained to use criminal force or violence or knowing it to be likely that the participants in such activity will use or be trained to use criminal force or violence, or participates in such activity intending to use or be trained to use criminal force or violence or knowing it to be likely that the participants in such activity will use or be trained to use criminal force or violence, against any religious, racial, language or regional group or caste or community and such activity for any reason whatsoever causes or is likely to cause fear or alarm or a feeling of insecurity amongst members of such religious, racial, language or regional group or caste or community, shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. (2) Whoever commits an offence specified in sub-section (1) in any place of worship or in any assembly engaged in the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies, shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to five years and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony
organising or participating in paramilitary-style activity against a group
offence committed in a place of worship (enmity-promotion enhancement)

breakdown.plain_summary: A broad, three-limbed hate-speech and communal-harmony offence: promoting or attempting to promote disharmony or enmity between groups defined by religion, race, birthplace, residence, language, caste, or community (or any other ground) through any medium; committing acts prejudicial to such harmony that disturb or risk disturbing public tranquillity; or organising or participating in paramilitary-style training/drills intended or likely to be used with criminal force or violence against such a group, causing fear or insecurity -- punishable with up to three years, escalated to up to five years plus mandatory fine if committed in a place of worship or religious assembly.
essential_elements: Limb (a): promoting or attempting to promote, through any listed medium, disharmony or feelings of enmity/hatred/ill-will between groups defined by religion, race, birthplace, residence, language, caste, community, or any other ground
Limb (b): committing an act prejudicial to harmony between such groups that disturbs or is likely to disturb public tranquillity

Limb (c): organising or participating in a drill/exercise/movement intended or known-likely to train participants in criminal force or violence against such a group, causing or likely to cause fear, alarm, or insecurity
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'any other ground whatsoever' language in limb (a) makes the listed grounds (religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, caste, community) illustrative rather than exhaustive -- and the place-of-worship aggravation under sub-section (2) applies uniformly across all three limbs of sub-section (1), not just the hate-speech limb.

sections.title: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever, by words either spoken or written or by signs or by visible representations or through electronic communication or otherwise,-- (a) makes or publishes any imputation that any class of persons cannot, by reason of their being members of any religious, racial, language or regional group or caste or community, bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established or uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India; or (b) asserts, counsels, advises, propagates or publishes that any class of persons shall, by reason of their being members of any religious, racial, language or regional group or caste or community, be denied, or deprived of their rights as citizens of India; or (c) makes or publishes any assertion, counsel, plea or appeal concerning the obligation of any class of persons, by reason of their being members of any religious, racial, language or regional group or caste or community, and such assertion, counsel, plea or appeal causes or is likely to cause disharmony or feelings of enmity or hatred or ill-will between such members and other persons; or (d) makes or publishes false or misleading information, jeopardising the sovereignty, unity and integrity or security of India, shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. (2) Whoever commits an offence specified in sub-section (1) in any place of worship or in any assembly engaged in the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies, shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to five years and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: imputation of disloyalty against a class of persons
denial of citizenship rights on group grounds
assertion of group obligation causing disharmony
false or misleading information jeopardising India's sovereignty or security

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Chapter XI with a four-limbed offence targeting speech that undermines national integration: imputing that an entire religious/racial/language/regional/caste/community class cannot be loyal to the Constitution or uphold India's sovereignty and integrity; asserting such a class should be denied citizenship rights; making group-obligation assertions likely to cause disharmony or enmity; or publishing false or misleading information jeopardising India's sovereignty, unity, integrity, or security -- punishable up to three years, escalated to up to five years plus mandatory fine if committed in a place of worship or religious assembly.
essential_elements: Limb (a): imputing disloyalty to the Constitution or to India's sovereignty/integrity against a class defined by religion, race, language, region, caste, or community
Limb (b): asserting or propagating that such a class be denied or deprived of citizenship rights
Limb (c): an assertion/counsel/plea/appeal about such a class's obligations that causes or is likely to cause disharmony, enmity, hatred, or ill-will
Limb (d): publishing false or misleading information jeopardising India's sovereignty, unity, integrity, or security
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 197's limb (d) (false/misleading information jeopardising sovereignty, unity, integrity, or security) is new territory not found in the equivalent IPC provision -- read it alongside Section 152 (the sedition-replacement offence) and note its own lawful-dissent-style boundaries are far less developed, so disinformation-type prosecutions under this limb deserve particularly careful scrutiny of the falsity and jeopardy elements.

sections.title: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant, knowingly disobeys any direction of the law as to the way in which he is to conduct himself as such public servant, intending to cause, or knowing it to be likely that he will by such disobedience, cause injury to any person, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. Illustration.--A, being an officer directed by law to take property in execution, in order to satisfy a decree pronounced in Z's favour by a Court, knowingly disobeys that direction of law, with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause injury to Z. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
key_terms: public servant knowingly disobeying a legal direction with intent to injure

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter XII ('Of Offences By or Relating to Public Servants') with a general offence: a public servant who knowingly disobeys a legal direction governing how they must conduct themselves in that role, intending to cause injury or knowing it likely that the disobedience will cause injury, is punishable with up to one year's simple imprisonment, fine, or both -- illustrated by an execution officer who knowingly flouts the legal procedure for seizing property, aware this is likely to injure the decree-holder.
essential_elements: The accused is a public servant
Knowing disobedience of a legal direction as to how they must conduct themselves as such public servant
Intention to cause injury, or knowledge that the disobedience is likely to cause injury, to any person
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the general catch-all public-servant misconduct offence; Sections 199-203 that follow carve out specific, more targeted instances of similar official misconduct (investigation-direction violations, document falsification, unlawful trading, unlawful property purchase) with their own tailored punishment bands.

sections.title: Public servant disobeying direction under law
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant,-- (a) knowingly disobeys any direction of the law which prohibits him from requiring the attendance at any place of any person for the purpose of investigation into an offence or any other matter; or (b) knowingly disobeys, to the prejudice of any person, any other direction of the law regulating the manner in which he shall conduct such investigation; or (c) fails to record any information given to him under sub-section (1) of section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 in relation to cognizable offence punishable under section 64, section 65, section 66, section 67, section 68, section 70, section 71, section 74, section 76, section 77, section 79, section 124, section 143 or section 144, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than six months but which may extend to two years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: public servant unlawfully compelling attendance for investigation
public servant violating investigation procedure to a person's prejudice
public servant failing to record cognizable-offence information (BNSS 173)

breakdown.plain_summary: A targeted investigation-misconduct offence carrying a mandatory minimum of six months' rigorous imprisonment (up to two years) plus fine: a public servant who knowingly disobeys a legal prohibition on compelling someone's attendance for investigation, who knowingly disobeys (to someone's prejudice) any other legal direction on how an investigation must be conducted, or who fails to record information given under BNSS Section 173(1) regarding specified cognizable offences (sexual offences, certain child-related and trafficking offences among others listed).
essential_elements: The accused is a public servant
Limb (a): knowing disobedience of a legal prohibition on requiring a person's attendance for investigation
Limb (b): knowing disobedience, to a person's prejudice, of any other legal direction regulating investigation conduct
Limb (c): failing to record information given under BNSS Section 173(1) for the specifically listed cognizable offences
breakdown.how_to_read: The mandatory minimum sentence (six months rigorous imprisonment) is notably strict for a public-servant offence -- limb (c)'s cross-reference to BNSS Section 173(1) and the specific list of BNS sections (largely sexual offences, acid attacks, and trafficking-related provisions) is a deliberate accountability mechanism to ensure such serious complaints are not suppressed at the police station.

sections.title: Punishment for non-treatment of victim
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being in charge of a hospital, public or private, whether run by the Central Government, the State Government, local bodies or any other person, contravenes the provisions of section 397 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: non-treatment of victim by a hospital in charge

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes, with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both, the person in charge of any hospital (public or private, regardless of which government or body runs it) who contravenes BNSS Section 397's requirement to provide immediate free treatment to victims of specified offences -- a direct penal backstop ensuring hospitals cannot lawfully refuse emergency treatment to victims on procedural or financial grounds.
essential_elements: The accused is in charge of a hospital, public or private
Contravention of the victim-treatment requirement under BNSS Section 397
breakdown.how_to_read: This section only makes sense read together with BNSS Section 397, which imposes the actual duty (immediate free first-aid/treatment to victims of acid attacks, rape, and other specified offences) -- Section 200 BNS is purely the penal consequence for breaching that cross-referenced procedural duty.

sections.title: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant, and being, as such public servant, charged with the preparation or translation of any document or electronic record, frames, prepares or translates that document or electronic record in a manner which he knows or believes to be incorrect, intending thereby to cause or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause injury to any person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: public servant framing an incorrect document or electronic record

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes, with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or both, a public servant charged with preparing or translating a document or electronic record who deliberately frames, prepares, or translates it in a manner known or believed to be incorrect, intending or knowing it likely to cause injury to any person -- a document-integrity offence targeting official drafting duties.
essential_elements: The accused is a public servant charged with preparing or translating a document or electronic record
Framing, preparing, or translating it in a manner known or believed to be incorrect
Intention to cause injury, or knowledge that injury is likely to result, to any person
breakdown.how_to_read: The offence requires both the false-framing element (knowledge/belief of incorrectness) and the injury-intent/knowledge element together -- an innocent drafting error, however careless, falls outside this section without the accompanying mental state as to injury.

sections.title: Public servant unlawfully engaging in trade
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant, and being legally bound as such public servant not to engage in trade, engages in trade, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both or with community service.
key_terms: public servant unlawfully engaging in trade

breakdown.plain_summary: A straightforward conduct-rule offence: a public servant who is legally bound by the terms of their office not to engage in trade, but does so anyway, is punishable with up to one year's simple imprisonment, fine, or both, or with community service -- notably one of relatively few BNS provisions offering community service as an express alternative sentence.
essential_elements: The accused is a public servant legally bound not to engage in trade
Engaging in trade despite that legal prohibition
breakdown.how_to_read: The community-service sentencing option reflects this offence's comparatively administrative, non-violent character -- the wrong lies purely in the conflict-of-interest created by an official trading while bound not to, not in any direct harm to a victim.

sections.title: Public servant unlawfully buying or bidding for property
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being a public servant, and being legally bound as such public servant, not to purchase or bid for certain property, purchases or bids for that property, either in his own name or in the name of another, or jointly, or in shares with others, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both; and the property, if purchased, shall be confiscated.
key_terms: public servant unlawfully purchasing or bidding for property
confiscation of property unlawfully purchased by a public servant

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes a public servant legally bound not to purchase or bid for certain property (typically property connected to their official duties, e.g. property they are auctioning or valuing) who does so anyway -- whether in their own name, another's name, jointly, or in shares -- with up to two years' simple imprisonment, fine, or both, plus mandatory confiscation of the property if actually purchased.
essential_elements: The accused is a public servant legally bound not to purchase or bid for certain property
Purchasing or bidding for that property, whether in their own name, another's name, jointly, or in shares with others
breakdown.how_to_read: The name/joint/shares language closes an obvious evasion route -- a public servant cannot escape liability by routing the purchase through a relative's name or a joint purchase; the mandatory confiscation of the property itself (not just a punishment of the person) is a notable additional consequence absent from most Chapter XII offences.

sections.title: Personating a public servant
sections.raw_text: Whoever pretends to hold any particular office as a public servant, knowing that he does not hold such office or falsely personates any other person holding such office, and in such assumed character does or attempts to do any act under colour of such office, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than six months but which may extend to three years and with fine.

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes, with a mandatory minimum of six months' imprisonment (up to three years) plus fine, falsely pretending to hold a particular public-servant office one does not hold, or falsely personating someone who genuinely holds such an office, where the impersonator goes on to do or attempt to do an act under colour of that assumed official authority.
essential_elements: Pretending to hold a particular public-servant office, knowing that is not true, or falsely personating a specific person who does hold such office
Doing, or attempting to do, an act under colour of that assumed office
breakdown.how_to_read: The offence requires an actual or attempted act under colour of the assumed office -- merely claiming a false title without acting on it falls short of Section 204, though it may still fall within Section 205's lighter garb/token offence if a uniform or insignia is also worn.

sections.title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent
sections.raw_text: Whoever, not belonging to a certain class of public servants, wears any garb or carries any token resembling any garb or token used by that class of public servants, with the intention that it may be believed, or with the knowledge that it is likely to be believed, that he belongs to that class of public servants, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: wearing garb or carrying a token of a public servant with fraudulent intent

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Chapter XII with a modest offence mirroring Section 168's military-impersonation provision: wearing a garb or carrying a token resembling that used by a particular class of public servants, with intention or knowledge that it is likely to be believed the wearer belongs to that class, punishable with up to three months' imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both.
essential_elements: The accused does not belong to the relevant class of public servants
Wearing a garb, or carrying a token, resembling that used by that class
Intention that it be believed, or knowledge that it is likely to be believed, that the accused belongs to that class
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare directly with Section 168 (impersonating military personnel by garb or token) -- Section 205 is the general public-servant counterpart, and both share the same intention-or-knowledge-of-belief structure and broadly similar (though not identical) punishment ranges.

sections.title: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding
sections.raw_text: Whoever absconds in order to avoid being served with a summons, notice or order proceeding from any public servant legally competent, as such public servant, to issue such summons, notice or order,-- (a) shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both; (b) where such summons or notice or order is to attend in person or by agent, or to produce a document or an electronic record in a Court shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: absconding to avoid service of summons

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter XIII ('Of Contempts of the Lawful Authority of Public Servants') with the offence of deliberately absconding to dodge service of a summons, notice, or order from a competent public servant -- punishable with up to one month's simple imprisonment plus fine up to five thousand rupees, escalated to up to six months plus fine up to ten thousand rupees where the dodged process specifically required attendance or document production in a Court.
essential_elements: The accused absconds (deliberately makes themselves scarce)
The purpose is to avoid being served with a summons, notice, or order
That summons, notice, or order proceeds from a public servant legally competent to issue it
Limb (b) escalation applies where the dodged process was a Court summons to attend or produce a document/electronic record
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the first of a recurring two-tier punishment pattern running through much of Chapter XIII -- a lighter general punishment band and a heavier band reserved for conduct touching a Court's own process specifically; always check which limb applies before assessing sentencing exposure.

sections.title: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof
sections.raw_text: Whoever in any manner intentionally prevents the serving on himself, or on any other person, of any summons, notice or order proceeding from any public servant legally competent, as such public servant, to issue such summons, notice or order, or intentionally prevents the lawful affixing to any place of any such summons, notice or order or intentionally removes any such summons, notice or order from any place to which it is lawfully affixed or intentionally prevents the lawful making of any proclamation, under the authority of any public servant legally competent, as such public servant, to direct such proclamation to be made,-- (a) shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both; (b) where the summons, notice, order or proclamation is to attend in person or by agent, or to produce a document or electronic record in a Court, with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: preventing service of summons notice or order
removing an affixed summons or notice

breakdown.plain_summary: Criminalises four overlapping ways of sabotaging lawful process-service: intentionally preventing service on oneself or another, preventing lawful affixing of a summons/notice/order to a place, removing one already lawfully affixed, or preventing a lawful proclamation from being made -- same one-month/six-month tiered punishment structure as Section 206, turning on whether the process concerned attendance or document production in a Court.
essential_elements: Intentional prevention of service, affixing, or proclamation (or intentional removal of an affixed summons/notice/order)
The summons, notice, order, or proclamation proceeds from, or is directed by, a public servant legally competent to issue or direct it
Limb (b) escalation applies where it concerned attendance or document/electronic-record production in a Court
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 206 punishes the person evading service of process on themselves; Section 207 is broader, reaching anyone (not just the person being served) who intentionally sabotages the service, affixing, or proclamation mechanism itself, including on behalf of a third party.

sections.title: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being legally bound to attend in person or by an agent at a certain place and time in obedience to a summons, notice, order, or proclamation proceeding from any public servant legally competent, as such public servant, to issue the same, intentionally omits to attend at that place or time or departs from the place where he is bound to attend before the time at which it is lawful for him to depart,-- (a) shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both; (b) where the summons, notice, order or proclamation is to attend in person or by agent in a Court with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both. Illustrations. (a) A, being legally bound to appear before a High Court, in obedience to a subpoena issuing from that Court, intentionally omits to appear. A has committed the offence defined in this section. (b) A, being legally bound to appear before a District Judge, as a witness, in obedience to a summons issued by that District Judge intentionally omits to appear. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
key_terms: non-attendance in obedience to a public servant's order
premature departure from a place of required attendance

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes a person legally bound to attend at a place and time per a summons/notice/order/proclamation who intentionally fails to attend, or who departs early before lawfully permitted to leave -- same tiered one-month/six-month structure, illustrated by witnesses who simply no-show before a High Court or a District Judge.
essential_elements: The accused is legally bound to attend in person or by agent at a certain place and time under a summons, notice, order, or proclamation from a competent public servant
Intentional omission to attend at that place/time, or intentional early departure before lawfully permitted to leave
Limb (b) escalation applies where the obligation was to attend in person or by agent in a Court
breakdown.how_to_read: Unlike Sections 206-207 (which punish sabotaging the process mechanism itself), Section 208 punishes simple no-shows by someone validly served -- the escalated Court-attendance limb mirrors contempt-adjacent witness/party non-appearance exposure.

sections.title: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
sections.raw_text: Whoever fails to appear at the specified place and the specified time as required by a proclamation published under sub-section (1) of section 84 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, or with community service, and where a declaration has been made under sub-section (4) of that section pronouncing him as a proclaimed offender, he shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: non-appearance under a BNSS Section 84 proclamation

breakdown.plain_summary: A much heavier, specifically cross-referenced offence: failing to appear per a proclamation issued under BNSS Section 84(1) (the proclamation-for-a-person-absconding procedure) is punishable with up to three years' imprisonment, fine, or community service -- escalating sharply to up to seven years' imprisonment plus mandatory fine where the person has additionally been declared a 'proclaimed offender' under BNSS Section 84(4).
essential_elements: A proclamation has been published under BNSS Section 84(1) requiring appearance at a specified place and time
The accused fails to appear as required by that proclamation
Enhanced punishment applies where a BNSS Section 84(4) declaration has additionally pronounced the accused a proclaimed offender
breakdown.how_to_read: This section only operates together with BNSS Section 84 -- it is the penal consequence for ignoring the proclamation procedure used against absconding accused persons, and the 'proclaimed offender' escalation is a serious standalone status with its own heavier exposure, distinct from mere non-appearance.

sections.title: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally bound to produce it
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being legally bound to produce or deliver up any document or electronic record to any public servant, as such, intentionally omits so to produce or deliver up the same,-- (a) shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both; (b) and where the document or electronic record is to be produced or delivered up to a Court with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both. Illustration. A, being legally bound to produce a document before a District Court, intentionally omits to produce the same. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
key_terms: omission to produce a document or electronic record to a public servant

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes intentional failure to produce or deliver up a document or electronic record one is legally bound to produce to a public servant -- same tiered one-month/six-month structure, escalated where the document was owed specifically to a Court, illustrated by a party who simply withholds a document a District Court required.
essential_elements: The accused is legally bound to produce or deliver up a document or electronic record to a public servant
Intentional omission to produce or deliver it up
Limb (b) escalation applies where the document/electronic record was owed to a Court
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'electronic record' language brings digital evidence/files within the same obligation as physical documents -- a deliberate modernisation choice absent from the IPC-era equivalent provision.

sections.title: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give it
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being legally bound to give any notice or to furnish information on any subject to any public servant, as such, intentionally omits to give such notice or to furnish such information in the manner and at the time required by law,-- (a) shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both; (b) where the notice or information required to be given respects the commission of an offence, or is required for the purpose of preventing the commission of an offence, or in order to the apprehension of an offender, with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both; (c) where the notice or information required to be given is required by an order passed under section 394 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: omission to give notice or information to a public servant

breakdown.plain_summary: A three-tier offence: intentionally failing to give a legally required notice or information, in the manner and time required, to a public servant -- base punishment up to one month, escalated to up to six months where the withheld information concerned an offence's commission, prevention, or an offender's apprehension, and a separate up-to-six-months tier where the information was specifically required by a BNSS Section 394 order.
essential_elements: The accused is legally bound to give notice or furnish information on a subject to a public servant
Intentional omission to do so in the manner and at the time required by law
Limb (b) escalation applies where the information concerns offence commission, prevention, or offender apprehension
Limb (c) applies where the information was specifically required by a BNSS Section 394 order
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Section 212's Explanation (shared with this section) extending 'offence' and 'offender' to specified extraterritorial acts -- the information-withholding duty under limb (b) therefore also covers knowledge of certain offences committed abroad.

sections.title: Furnishing false information
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being legally bound to furnish information on any subject to any public servant, as such, furnishes, as true, information on the subject which he knows or has reason to believe to be false,-- (a) shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both; (b) where the information which he is legally bound to give respects the commission of an offence, or is required for the purpose of preventing the commission of an offence, or in order to the apprehension of an offender, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. Illustrations. (a) A, a landholder, knowing of the commission of a murder within the limits of his estate, wilfully misinforms the Magistrate of the district that the death has occurred by accident in consequence of the bite of a snake. A is guilty of the offence defined in this section. (b) A, a village watchman, knowing that a considerable body of strangers has passed through his village in order to commit a dacoity in the house of Z, a wealthy merchant residing in a neighbouring place, and being legally bound to give early and punctual information of the above fact to the officer of the nearest police station, wilfully misinforms the police officer that a body of suspicious characters passed through the village with a view to commit dacoity in a certain distant place in a different direction. Here A is guilty of the offence defined in this section. Explanation.--In section 211 and in this section the word "offence" include any act committed at any place out of India, which, if committed in India, would be punishable under any of the following sections, namely, 103, 105, 307, sub-sections (2), (3) and (4) of section 309, sub-sections (2), (3), (4) and (5) of section 310, 311, 312, clauses (f) and (g) of section 326, sub-sections (4), (6), (7) and (8) of section 331, clauses (a) and (b) of section 332 and the word "offender" includes any person who is alleged to have been guilty of any such act.
key_terms: furnishing false information to a public servant
extraterritorial offence and offender for Sections 211-212

breakdown.plain_summary: The active-falsehood counterpart to Section 211's omission offence: actually furnishing information known or believed false, as if true, to a public servant one is legally bound to inform -- base punishment up to six months, escalated to up to two years where the false information concerned an offence's commission, prevention, or an offender's apprehension, illustrated by a landholder misreporting a murder as a snakebite death and a watchman misdirecting police away from actual dacoits.
essential_elements: The accused is legally bound to furnish information on a subject to a public servant
Furnishing information as true which the accused knows or has reason to believe is false
Limb (b) escalation applies where the information concerns offence commission, prevention, or offender apprehension
breakdown.how_to_read: The shared Explanation with Section 211 extends 'offence' to specified extraterritorial acts (cross-referencing BNS Sections 103, 105, 307, 309(2)-(4), 310(2)-(5), 311, 312, 326(f)-(g), 331(4)(6)-(8), 332(a)-(b)) and extends 'offender' to persons merely alleged to have committed such acts -- a deliberately broad information-duty trigger reaching beyond India's territorial offences.

sections.title: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it
sections.raw_text: Whoever refuses to bind himself by an oath or affirmation to state the truth, when required so to bind himself by a public servant legally competent to require that he shall so bind himself, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: refusing an oath or affirmation when duly required

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes refusal to take an oath or affirmation to state the truth when lawfully required to do so by a competent public servant, with up to six months' simple imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both -- the foundational offence enabling the truth-telling duties punished in Sections 214-216.
essential_elements: A public servant legally competent to require it demands that the accused bind himself by an oath or affirmation to state the truth
The accused refuses to so bind himself
breakdown.how_to_read: Sections 213, 214, and 215 form a short sequence of procedural non-cooperation offences (refusing the oath itself, refusing to answer, refusing to sign) that typically arise together in the same examination or deposition but are each separately chargeable.

sections.title: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being legally bound to state the truth on any subject to any public servant, refuses to answer any question demanded of him touching that subject by such public servant in the exercise of the legal powers of such public servant, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: refusing to answer a public servant's lawful question

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes refusal to answer a question lawfully put by a public servant exercising their legal powers, where the person is legally bound to state the truth on that subject -- identical six-month/five-thousand-rupee punishment band as Section 213's oath-refusal offence.
essential_elements: The accused is legally bound to state the truth on a subject to a public servant
A question touching that subject is demanded by the public servant in exercise of their legal powers
The accused refuses to answer that question
breakdown.how_to_read: This presupposes the truth-telling duty is already in place (typically following a valid oath under Section 213) -- the wrong here is answer-refusal itself, distinct from giving a false answer, which instead falls under Section 216.

sections.title: Refusing to sign statement
sections.raw_text: Whoever refuses to sign any statement made by him, when required to sign that statement by a public servant legally competent to require that he shall sign that statement, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to three thousand rupees, or with both.

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes refusal to sign one's own statement when lawfully required to do so by a competent public servant, with a comparatively lighter punishment of up to three months' imprisonment, fine up to three thousand rupees, or both.
essential_elements: The accused made a statement
A public servant legally competent to require it demands that the accused sign that statement
The accused refuses to sign it
breakdown.how_to_read: The lightest of the three refusal offences (213-215) -- signature-refusal alone, without more, does not itself constitute giving false evidence, which is reserved for the substantively false-statement offences in Sections 216 and 227 onward.

sections.title: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to administer an oath or affirmation
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being legally bound by an oath or affirmation to state the truth on any subject to any public servant or other person authorised by law to administer such oath or affirmation, makes, to such public servant or other person as aforesaid, touching that subject, any statement which is false, and which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: false statement on oath or affirmation to a public servant

breakdown.plain_summary: A significant escalation from the mere non-cooperation offences preceding it: actually making a false statement -- known or believed false, or not believed true -- while bound by oath or affirmation to a public servant or other legally authorised administrator, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment plus mandatory fine.
essential_elements: The accused is legally bound by an oath or affirmation to state the truth on a subject, to a public servant or other person authorised by law to administer such oath/affirmation
The accused makes a statement touching that subject which is false
The accused knows or believes it false, or does not believe it true
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the Chapter XIII sibling of Section 227's 'giving false evidence' offence in Chapter XIV -- Section 216 covers false sworn statements to public servants generally (e.g. in administrative or investigative proceedings), while Section 227 onward governs false evidence specifically within judicial proceedings, with materially heavier judicial-proceeding punishments.

sections.title: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of another person
sections.raw_text: Whoever gives to any public servant any information which he knows or believes to be false, intending thereby to cause, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause, such public servant-- (a) to do or omit anything which such public servant ought not to do or omit if the true state of facts respecting which such information is given were known by him; or (b) to use the lawful power of such public servant to the injury or annoyance of any person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both. Illustrations. (a) A informs a Magistrate that Z, a police officer, subordinate to such Magistrate, has been guilty of neglect of duty or misconduct, knowing such information to be false, and knowing it to be likely that the information will cause the Magistrate to dismiss Z. A has committed the offence defined in this section. (b) A falsely informs a public servant that Z has contraband salt in a secret place, knowing such information to be false, and knowing that it is likely that the consequence of the information will be a search of Z's premises, attended with annoyance to Z. A has committed the offence defined in this section. (c) A falsely informs a policeman that he has been assaulted and robbed in the neighbourhood of a particular village. He does not mention the name of any person as one of his assailants, but knows it to be likely that in consequence of this information the police will make enquiries and institute searches in the village to the annoyance of the villagers or some of them. A has committed an offence under this section.
key_terms: false information intended to misuse a public servant's lawful power
false information causing wrongful dismissal or search

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes knowingly or believingly false information given to a public servant, intending or knowing it likely to cause that public servant to act wrongly or to misuse their lawful power to someone's injury or annoyance -- punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both, illustrated by a false neglect-of-duty complaint engineered to get an officer dismissed, a false contraband tip engineered to trigger an annoying search, and a vague false robbery report engineered to trigger annoying village-wide searches.
essential_elements: The accused gives information to a public servant which the accused knows or believes to be false
Intention to cause, or knowledge it is likely to cause, that public servant to act wrongly on the false factual premise, or to use their lawful power to another's injury or annoyance
breakdown.how_to_read: The third illustration shows the offence does not require naming a specific victim -- knowingly likely collateral annoyance to an entire village from an engineered false report suffices, since the test is the public servant's power being misdirected to someone's (anyone's) injury or annoyance.

sections.title: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant
sections.raw_text: Whoever offers any resistance to the taking of any property by the lawful authority of any public servant, knowing or having reason to believe that he is such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: resistance to lawful taking of property by a public servant

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes resisting the lawful taking of property by a public servant's authority, where the accused knows or has reason to believe the taker is such a public servant, with up to six months' imprisonment, fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both.
essential_elements: Property is being taken under the lawful authority of a public servant
The accused offers resistance to that taking
The accused knows or has reason to believe the person taking it is a public servant
breakdown.how_to_read: Covers conduct such as physically resisting a lawful seizure or attachment -- resistance to an unlawful taking falls outside this section entirely, since the taking's lawfulness is itself an element.

sections.title: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant
sections.raw_text: Whoever intentionally obstructs any sale of property offered for sale by the lawful authority of any public servant, as such, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: obstructing a sale of property conducted by lawful public-servant authority

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes intentionally obstructing a sale of property being conducted under a public servant's lawful authority, with up to one month's imprisonment, fine up to five thousand rupees, or both -- a lighter offence than Section 218's resistance-to-taking, reflecting the lesser disruption of merely obstructing a sale rather than resisting a seizure.
essential_elements: A sale of property is being conducted under the lawful authority of a public servant
The accused intentionally obstructs that sale
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Section 220, which targets a different but related evil at the same lawful public-servant sale -- illegitimate participation in bidding/purchase rather than outright obstruction of the sale process.

sections.title: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant
sections.raw_text: Whoever, at any sale of property held by the lawful authority of a public servant, as such, purchases or bids for any property on account of any person, whether himself or any other, whom he knows to be under a legal incapacity to purchase that property at that sale, or bids for such property not intending to perform the obligations under which he lays himself by such bidding, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to two hundred rupees, or with both.
key_terms: illegal purchase or bid at a lawful public-servant sale
sham bidding without intent to perform

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes two distinct abuses at a lawful public-servant-authority sale: purchasing or bidding on behalf of someone (oneself or another) known to be legally incapable of purchasing at that sale, or bidding without any genuine intention to honour the resulting obligations -- a modest fine-up-to-two-hundred-rupees offence reflecting the IPC-era monetary scale, alongside up to one month's imprisonment.
essential_elements: A sale of property is held under the lawful authority of a public servant
The accused purchases or bids for property at that sale either on account of a person known to be legally incapable of purchasing, or without intending to perform the bidding obligations
breakdown.how_to_read: The fine ceiling here (two hundred rupees) is a legacy-scale figure far below the thousands-of-rupees fines typical elsewhere in the Sanhita -- a notable drafting artifact worth flagging rather than assuming a typo.

sections.title: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions
sections.raw_text: Whoever voluntarily obstructs any public servant in the discharge of his public functions, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand and five hundred rupees, or with both.
key_terms: obstructing a public servant in discharge of public functions

breakdown.plain_summary: A general-purpose obstruction offence: voluntarily obstructing a public servant in the discharge of their public functions, punishable with up to three months' imprisonment, fine up to two thousand five hundred rupees, or both.
essential_elements: The accused voluntarily obstructs a public servant
The obstruction occurs while the public servant is discharging their public functions
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the broad catch-all obstruction offence; Sections 218-220 and 195 (riot-suppression obstruction) are specific, more heavily punished instances of obstruction in particular contexts, so always check whether a more specific section applies before defaulting to Section 221.

sections.title: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being bound by law to render or furnish assistance to any public servant in the execution of his public duty, intentionally omits to give such assistance,-- (a) shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to two thousand and five hundred rupees, or with both; (b) and where such assistance be demanded of him by a public servant legally competent to make such demand for the purposes of executing any process lawfully issued by a Court or of preventing the commission of an offence, or suppressing a riot, or affray, or of apprehending a person charged with or guilty of an offence, or of having escaped from lawful custody, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
key_terms: omission to assist a public servant when legally bound to

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes intentional failure to render legally mandated assistance to a public servant in execution of public duty -- base punishment up to one month, escalated to up to six months where the demanded assistance concerned executing a Court process, preventing an offence, suppressing a riot or affray, or apprehending an offender or escaped-custody person.
essential_elements: The accused is bound by law to render or furnish assistance to a public servant in execution of public duty
Intentional omission to give such assistance
Limb (b) escalation applies where the assistance was demanded for Court-process execution, offence prevention, riot/affray suppression, or apprehension of an offender or escapee
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the modern equivalent of the common-law 'posse comitatus' duty -- ordinary citizens can be legally compelled to assist, and refusal in the more serious listed circumstances (riot suppression, apprehending escapees) draws the heavier six-month band.

sections.title: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant
sections.raw_text: Whoever, knowing that, by an order promulgated by a public servant lawfully empowered to promulgate such order, he is directed to abstain from a certain act, or to take certain order with certain property in his possession or under his management, disobeys such direction,-- (a) shall, if such disobedience causes or tends to cause obstruction, annoyance or injury, or risk of obstruction, annoyance or injury, to any person lawfully employed, be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand and five hundred rupees, or with both; (b) and where such disobedience causes or tends to cause danger to human life, health or safety, or causes or tends to cause a riot or affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both. Explanation.--It is not necessary that the offender should intend to produce harm, or contemplate his disobedience as likely to produce harm. It is sufficient that he knows of the order which he disobeys, and that his disobedience produces, or is likely to produce, harm. Illustration. An order is promulgated by a public servant lawfully empowered to promulgate such order, directing that a religious procession shall not pass down a certain street. A knowingly disobeys the order, and thereby causes danger of riot. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
key_terms: disobedience to a lawfully promulgated public order

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes knowing disobedience of a lawfully promulgated public order directing abstention from an act or specified handling of property, with a two-tier consequence-based structure -- up to six months where the disobedience causes or risks obstruction/annoyance/injury to a lawfully employed person, escalating to up to one year where it causes or risks danger to life/health/safety or a riot/affray, illustrated by someone knowingly violating a religious-procession route order and thereby risking a riot.
essential_elements: A public servant lawfully empowered to promulgate the order has done so
The accused knows of the order's direction to abstain from an act or handle certain property in a certain way
The accused disobeys that direction
Limb (a): disobedience causes, tends to cause, or risks obstruction/annoyance/injury to a lawfully employed person
Limb (b) escalation: disobedience causes, tends to cause, danger to life/health/safety, or a riot/affray
breakdown.how_to_read: The Explanation is doctrinally important: no intent or contemplation of harm is required at all -- mere knowledge of the order plus the disobedience producing or likely producing harm suffices, making this closer to a strict/negligence-based liability standard than most Sanhita offences.

sections.title: Threat of injury to public servant
sections.raw_text: Whoever holds out any threat of injury to any public servant, or to any person in whom he believes that public servant to be interested, for the purpose of inducing that public servant to do any act, or to forbear or delay to do any act, connected with the exercise of the public functions of such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: threat of injury to a public servant to influence official conduct

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes holding out a threat of injury to a public servant, or to a person believed to interest that public servant, for the purpose of inducing them to act, forbear, or delay in exercising their public functions -- punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
essential_elements: A threat of injury is held out to a public servant, or to a person the accused believes the public servant to be interested in
The purpose is to induce the public servant to do, forbear, or delay an act connected with their public functions
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'person in whom he believes that public servant to be interested' language extends the offence to threats against a public servant's family or close associates, not just the official personally -- coercion-by-proxy is treated the same as direct coercion.

sections.title: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public servant
sections.raw_text: Whoever holds out any threat of injury to any person for the purpose of inducing that person to refrain or desist from making a legal application for protection against any injury to any public servant legally empowered as such to give such protection, or to cause such protection to be given, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: threat to deter a legal application for protection from a public servant

breakdown.plain_summary: Punishes holding out a threat of injury to someone, for the purpose of inducing them to refrain from making, or to abandon, a legal application for protection to a public servant legally empowered to give such protection -- punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, fine, or both.
essential_elements: A threat of injury is held out to a person
The purpose is to induce that person to refrain or desist from a legal application for protection against injury, made to a public servant empowered to give such protection
breakdown.how_to_read: Complements Section 224: where 224 punishes threatening the public servant directly to influence their official conduct, Section 225 punishes threatening a private citizen to stop them from ever seeking that official protection in the first place -- an access-to-justice protection provision.

sections.title: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power
sections.raw_text: Whoever attempts to commit suicide with the intent to compel or restrain any public servant from discharging his official duty shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both, or with community service.
key_terms: attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain a public servant

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Chapter XIII with a narrow, specific offence: attempting suicide with the intent to compel or restrain a public servant from discharging official duty, punishable with up to one year's simple imprisonment, fine, or both, or with community service.
essential_elements: The accused attempts to commit suicide
The intent behind the attempt is to compel or restrain a public servant from discharging official duty
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a narrowly targeted provision distinct from any general offence relating to attempted suicide -- the public-duty-coercion intent element is what brings it within this public-servant-contempt chapter rather than elsewhere in the Sanhita; the community-service sentencing option again reflects a deliberately rehabilitative rather than purely punitive approach.
